title: Empirical Calibration: mlsysim vs. Published Benchmarks
text:
This document compares mlsysim analytical predictions against published benchmark results for common ML workloads. The goal is to validate that the framework’s first-principles models produce results in the correct physical range, and to characterize the accuracy envelope that users should expect.
Date: 2026-04-01 mlsysim version: 0.1.0 Methodology: Each configuration was run through the appropriate solver (SingleNodeModel for training throughput, ServingModel for inference latency, calc_transformer_training_flops for FLOPs estimates). Default efficiency parameters were used (eta=0.10 for training, eta=0.50 for serving) unless otherwise noted.
The benchmark scalar values live in Literature.Benchmarks, beside the other cited literature anchors. The executable validation contract in mlsysim.engine.empirical only composes those literature values with canonical Models.* and Hardware.* registry entries, plus the tolerance/range and review rationale. This keeps model definitions, hardware specifications, and published benchmark numbers single-sourced inside MLSys·im.

LLM inference latency (Configs 3-5). The decode ITL predictions land squarely within published ranges. This is expected: decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, and the model correctly computes (weights + KV_cache) / bandwidth. The decode ITL is insensitive to the efficiency parameter because compute is not on the critical path, which exactly matches the physical regime where auto-regressive decoding is a streaming memory read, not a compute problem.
Training FLOPs (Config 6). The 6ND approximation (6 * parameters * tokens) for transformer training FLOPs matches the GPT-3 paper’s reported value to within 0.3%. This validates the fundamental FLOP counting formula.



CNN training throughput (Configs 1-2). The default efficiency parameter (eta=0.10) produces predictions that bracket reality but do not hit both targets simultaneously:

A100 prediction is 22% low at eta=0.10. Setting eta=0.13 brings the prediction into the Literature.Benchmarks.ResNet50A100TrainThroughput validation band.
H100 prediction is 54% high at eta=0.10. Setting eta=0.065 brings the prediction into the Literature.Benchmarks.ResNet50H100TrainThroughput validation band.

This asymmetry reveals a real insight: the efficiency parameter is not a universal constant. It encodes the gap between peak datasheet FLOP/s and actual sustained throughput, which depends on:

Tensor core utilization: ResNet-50 has many small convolutions that may not saturate H100’s larger tensor cores as efficiently as A100’s.
Memory system pressure: H100’s 3x higher peak FLOP/s amplifies any memory bottleneck (the model uses peak FP16 FLOP/s of 989 TFLOP/s for H100 vs. 312 TFLOP/s for A100, but real ResNet-50 kernels achieve a lower fraction of the H100 peak).
Framework overhead: Batch normalization layers, data loading, and gradient synchronization are not modeled in the roofline calculation.




The single-parameter efficiency model works well within a hardware family but does not transfer across hardware generations without re-calibration. This is a known limitation of roofline-based analytical models and is explicitly surfaced to students in the textbook.

Efficiency parameter (eta). This is the fraction of peak hardware throughput (FLOP/s or GB/s) that the workload actually achieves. It consolidates all sources of inefficiency: tensor core utilization, memory stalls, kernel launch overhead, data pipeline stalls, and framework overhead. It is NOT the same as MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization), which is defined as observed_throughput / theoretical_peak_throughput.
Published benchmarks. We compare against:

MLPerf Training v3.0/v3.1: Industry-standard training benchmarks. Single-accelerator numbers used (not multi-GPU or multi-node). ResNet-50 throughput measured as images/second during convergence training.
TensorRT-LLM benchmarks: NVIDIA’s optimized inference engine. H100-80GB SXM, FP16 precision, KV-cache enabled.
vLLM benchmarks: Open-source LLM serving engine. Batched decode latency with PagedAttention.
Brown et al. (2020): “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners.” GPT-3’s benchmark target is exposed as Models.Language.GPT3.training_ops.

Decode ITL is efficiency-insensitive. The serving model correctly identifies decode as memory-bandwidth-bound. The ITL formula is: ITL = (model_weights + KV_cache) / memory_bandwidth + framework_tax. Since this does not involve the compute efficiency parameter, varying eta from 0.3 to 0.8 produces identical ITL values. This matches the physical reality of auto-regressive decoding.
Hardware specs used. Hardware values come from the Silicon Zoo: Hardware.Cloud.A100 and Hardware.Cloud.H100. Do not copy peak FLOP/s, memory bandwidth, or capacity numbers into calibration scripts.





import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import SingleNodeModel, ServingModel
from mlsysim.physics import calc_transformer_training_flops

# Config 1: ResNet-50 / A100 / training
resnet = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
a100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
r1 = SingleNodeModel().solve(
    resnet, a100,
    batch_size=256, efficiency=0.10, is_training=True
)
print(f"ResNet-50 A100: {r1.throughput.m_as('1/s'):.0f} img/s")

# Config 2: ResNet-50 / H100 / training
h100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100
r2 = SingleNodeModel().solve(
    resnet, h100,
    batch_size=256, efficiency=0.10, is_training=True
)
print(f"ResNet-50 H100: {r2.throughput.m_as('1/s'):.0f} img/s")

# Config 3: Llama-3-8B / H100 / decode bs=1
llama = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B
r3 = ServingModel().solve(
    llama, h100,
    seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, efficiency=0.50
)
print(f"Llama-3-8B bs=1 ITL: {r3.itl.m_as('ms'):.1f} ms")

# Config 4: Llama-3-8B / H100 / decode bs=32
r4 = ServingModel().solve(
    llama, h100,
    seq_len=2048, batch_size=32, efficiency=0.50
)
print(f"Llama-3-8B bs=32 ITL: {r4.itl.m_as('ms'):.1f} ms")

# Config 6: GPT-3 training FLOPs
gpt3 = mlsysim.Models.Language.GPT3
target = mlsysim.Models.Language.GPT3.training_ops
flops = calc_transformer_training_flops(gpt3.parameters, gpt3.training_tokens)
print(f"GPT-3 FLOPs: {flops.to('flop').magnitude:.2e}")
print(f"GPT-3 target: {float(target):.2e}")

title: engine.solvers.agents
text:
engine.solvers.agents
Agent solvers: reliability, cost, and context over a whole trajectory.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__); kept per-domain so the logic stays reviewable. The unit of account is the delegated task, not the model call: a task succeeds only if every unchecked turn does, costs every attempt it takes until one is accepted, and re-reads its own history on every turn.





Name
Description




AcceptedTaskCostModel
Cost per accepted task, C_eff = E[C_attempt] / p_acc, and two levers on it.


AppendOnlyContextModel
Context read by the last call, and input resent in total, by an append-only trajectory.


HorizonCompoundingModel
Unchecked task success over a horizon of independent steps.





engine.solvers.agents.AcceptedTaskCostModel()
Cost per accepted task, C_eff = E[C_attempt] / p_acc, and two levers on it.
An attempt costs model tokens plus everything else (sandbox, tests, review); attempts repeat until one is accepted. A price cut removes a fraction of one component; an acceptance gain divides the whole attempt. The break-even acceptance is the acceptance the price cut is worth. Charging only the accepted attempt understates cost by 1 / p_acc. Growing the model cost by a fraction g raises the attempt to C' = (1 + g) C_model + C_other; cost per accepted task holds only if acceptance rises to p_acc C' / C.



engine.solvers.agents.AppendOnlyContextModel()
Context read by the last call, and input resent in total, by an append-only trajectory.
Each turn appends its output and observation to the prompt and resends the whole history, so the last of H calls reads s0 + delta (H - 1) tokens while the run sends H s0 + delta H (H - 1) / 2: the window can hold the history while the resend grows quadratically with the horizon.



engine.solvers.agents.HorizonCompoundingModel()
Unchecked task success over a horizon of independent steps.
Every step is right with probability p, nothing checks a step before the next builds on it, and nothing recovers, so a task of H turns succeeds with probability p^H. Holding target at H turns needs a per-step error of 1 - target^(1/H); for small error the product eps H approaches -ln(target) at any horizon. The first horizon whose success falls below target is floor(ln target / ln p) + 1.

title: physics.power
text:
physics.power
Power delivery: load steps on a supply rail and their voltage droop.





Name
Description




calc_dynamic_power_ratio
Ratio of dynamic power after scaling the clock by frequency_ratio.


calc_inductive_droop
Voltage droop across a loop inductance: dV = L * dI / dt.


calc_rail_current_step
Current change on a supply rail for a power step: dI = dP / V.





physics.power.calc_dynamic_power_ratio(
    frequency_ratio,
    voltage_tracks_frequency=True,
)
Ratio of dynamic power after scaling the clock by frequency_ratio.
Dynamic CMOS power is P = C V^2 f. When the supply voltage must rise in proportion to frequency (V ~ f), power grows with the cube of the frequency ratio; at fixed voltage it grows linearly. Capacitance is held constant. Dimensionless.



physics.power.calc_inductive_droop(inductance, current_step, rise_time)
Voltage droop across a loop inductance: dV = L * dI / dt.
The droop a supply loop of inductance L shows when its current changes by dI over dt. The shorter the edge, the larger the droop, which is why on-package and on-die capacitance must answer the fastest edges. Returns volts.



physics.power.calc_rail_current_step(power_step, rail_voltage)
Current change on a supply rail for a power step: dI = dP / V.
power_step in watts, rail_voltage in volts. Returns amperes.

title: physics.motors
text:
physics.motors
Electric-motor and actuator equations: winding heat, copper resistance, voltage-limited speed, and the inertia match of a geared joint (added 2026-10-20).
Sources: the first-order lumped thermal model and copper’s linear resistance coefficient are standard (Incropera and DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, lumped capacitance; NBS Handbook 100, Copper Wire Tables); the inertia match N* = sqrt(J_load / J_rotor) and the brushless terminal equation follow Lynch and Park, Modern Robotics (2017), Sec. 8.9, and Krishnan, Permanent Magnet Synchronous and Brushless DC Motor Drives (CRC Press, 2010).





Name
Description




calc_contact_force_rate
Rate at which contact force rises against a stiff surface at constant approach speed: dF/dt = k v.


calc_copper_resistance_factor
Winding resistance relative to its reference value: R(T)/R_0 = 1 + alpha (T - T_0).


calc_first_order_temperature
Lumped winding temperature after elapsed at constant power:


calc_first_order_time_to_temperature
Time for a first-order body to move from start to target:


calc_inertia_matched_ratio
Gear ratio that maximizes joint acceleration for a given motor torque: N* = sqrt(J_load / J_rotor).


calc_peak_normalized_response
2x / (1 + x^2): a response relative to its peak at x = 1.


calc_periodic_burst_peak_rise
Peak temperature rise of a first-order winding under a periodic burst at steady state:


calc_voltage_limited_speed
Speed at which a brushless motor delivering torque runs out of supply voltage.





physics.motors.calc_contact_force_rate(stiffness, approach_velocity)
Rate at which contact force rises against a stiff surface at constant approach speed: dF/dt = k v.



physics.motors.calc_copper_resistance_factor(
    temperature,
    alpha,
    reference_temperature,
)
Winding resistance relative to its reference value: R(T)/R_0 = 1 + alpha (T - T_0).



physics.motors.calc_first_order_temperature(
    elapsed,
    start,
    asymptote,
    time_constant,
)
Lumped winding temperature after elapsed at constant power: T(t) = T_inf - (T_inf - T_0) exp(-t / tau).



physics.motors.calc_first_order_time_to_temperature(
    start,
    target,
    asymptote,
    time_constant,
)
Time for a first-order body to move from start to target: t = tau ln((T_inf - T_0) / (T_inf - T_target)); None if the asymptote never reaches it.
Rising toward a higher asymptote, or (added 2026-10-20) cooling toward a lower one when target lies between the asymptote and start.



physics.motors.calc_inertia_matched_ratio(load_inertia, rotor_inertia)
Gear ratio that maximizes joint acceleration for a given motor torque: N* = sqrt(J_load / J_rotor).



physics.motors.calc_peak_normalized_response(ratio)
2x / (1 + x^2): a response relative to its peak at x = 1.
Joint acceleration against gear ratio (x = N / N*) and phase-short braking torque against speed (x = omega / omega_peak) both follow this curve.



physics.motors.calc_periodic_burst_peak_rise(
    power,
    thermal_resistance,
    on_time,
    period,
    time_constant,
)
Peak temperature rise of a first-order winding under a periodic burst at steady state: P theta (1 - e^{-t_on/tau}) / (1 - e^{-t_cycle/tau}).



physics.motors.calc_voltage_limited_speed(
    torque,
    torque_constant,
    terminal_resistance,
    supply_voltage,
    no_load_speed,
)
Speed at which a brushless motor delivering torque runs out of supply voltage.

title: solvers.CompressionModel
text:
solvers.CompressionModel()
Analyzes model compression trade-offs (Accuracy vs. Efficiency).
This model simulates the ‘Compression Tax’ — the accuracy degradation that occurs when reducing model size via quantization or pruning, balanced against the gains in memory footprint and inference latency.
Literature Source: 1. Han et al. (2015), “Deep Compression: Compressing Deep Neural Networks with Pruning, Trained Quantization and Huffman Coding.” 2. Gholami et al. (2021), “A Survey of Quantization Methods for Efficient Neural Network Inference.” 3. Blalock et al. (2020), “What is the State of Neural Network Pruning?”





Name
Description




candidate
Evaluate one compression configuration with feasibility metadata.


solve
Solves for compression gains and estimated accuracy impact.


sweep
Evaluate a compression design space and mark Pareto candidates.





solvers.CompressionModel.candidate(
    model,
    hardware,
    *,
    label=None,
    method='quantization',
    target_bitwidth=8,
    sparsity=0.0,
    sparsity_type='unstructured',

    min_speedup=None,
    require_hardware_support=False,
    baseline_precision='fp32',
)
Evaluate one compression configuration with feasibility metadata.
Sizes, ratios, and speedups are relative to baseline_precision (see solve).

)

required

'quantization'


target_bitwidth
int
Target numerical precision in bits (e.g., 8 for INT8/FP8, 4 for INT4). At 8-bit, accuracy delta uses the FP8 estimate (near-lossless) by default.
8


sparsity
float
Target sparsity ratio (0.0 to 1.0) for pruning.
0.0


sparsity_type
str
Type of sparsity pattern: ‘unstructured’, ‘structured’, or ‘n_m’ (2:4). - unstructured: storage savings only, no inference speedup - structured: both storage and compute savings - n_m: hardware 2:4 sparsity with 2x speedup at 50% sparsity (Ampere+)
'unstructured'


baseline_precision
str
Configurable precision of the uncompressed model that ratios and sizes are measured against, resolved through core.units.PRECISION_MAP. Defaults to "fp32" (INT8 is 4x, INT4 is 8x). Pass "fp16" for models trained and served from FP16/BF16 weights, such as most LLMs, where INT4 is quoted as 4x.
'fp32'














Name
Type
Description





CompressionResult
Compression metrics including memory savings, inference speedup, and estimated accuracy delta, plus the baseline_precision they are relative to.






Conventions and branch logic:

Sizes are measured against the configurable baseline_precision (FP32 by default, 4 bytes/param), so quantization’s compression_ratio = b_base / target_bitwidth (32/4 = 8x for INT4 by default; 16/4 = 4x with baseline_precision="fp16"). A target wider than the baseline is an upcast and yields a ratio < 1.
estimated_accuracy_delta is a signed fraction (e.g. -0.005 = -0.5 percentage points top-1), taken from survey medians in engine/calibration.py (Gholami 2021 for quantization; Blalock 2020 for pruning, where degradation goes exponential past the ~50% sparsity threshold).
inference_speedup depends on the Roofline regime: memory-bound workloads gain the full compression ratio (less data to move); compute-bound workloads gain only what the hardware’s low-precision path provides (1.0 when unsupported). For pruning, only structured and 2:4 N:M sparsity translate into compute speedup; unstructured sparsity saves storage only.
Unknown method values fall through to a no-op result (ratio 1.0, delta 0.0).





solvers.CompressionModel.sweep(
    model,
    hardware,
    candidate_configs,
    *,
    size_limit=None,
    max_accuracy_drop=None,
    min_speedup=None,
    require_hardware_support=False,
    objective='min_size_max_speed_preserve_quality',
    baseline_precision='fp32',
)
Evaluate a compression design space and mark Pareto candidates.
Every candidate is measured against the same baseline_precision so sizes, ratios, and speedups are comparable across the sweep.

physics.transformer.calc_attention_crossover(
    width,
    ffn_multiple=4,
    attention_projections=4,
)
Context length at which a block’s attention products equal its dense products: (weights per block) S = 2 S^2 d gives S = (weights per block) / 2d, six times the width for the classic block.



physics.transformer.calc_attention_score_macs(seq_len, width)
Multiply-adds of one block’s two attention products, Q K^T and the weighted sum of V: S^2 d each, 2 S^2 d in all (summed over heads, which split d without changing the total).



physics.transformer.calc_online_softmax(scores, values, block_size)
Softmax-weighted sum of values over scores, one block of scores at a time.
Each block updates a running maximum m, a running sum l = sum exp(x - m), and a running output O = sum exp(x - m) v; when the maximum rises, the old l and O are rescaled by exp(m_old - m_new) (Milakov and Gimelshein 2018; the inner loop of FlashAttention, Dao et al. 2022). The result after the last block equals the whole-row computation exactly.
Returns a list with one dict per block: max, rescale (the factor applied to the previous l and O), sum, and output (added 2026-10-20).



physics.transformer.calc_score_matrix_intensity(head_dim, bytes_per_value)
Arithmetic intensity of materializing one head’s attention scores in memory.
Each score costs 2 d_head FLOPs (a dot product of length d_head) and is written once and read back once, 2 x bytes_per_value bytes, so the intensity is d_head / bytes_per_value FLOP per byte: 32 for 64-wide heads in FP16, far below an accelerator’s ridge point (added 2026-10-20).



physics.transformer.calc_transformer_block_weights(
    width,
    ffn_multiple=4,
    attention_projections=4,
)
Weights of one classic decoder block, biases and norms aside.
Attention holds attention_projections square projections (query, key, value, output: 4 d^2); the feed-forward network goes d -> ffn_multiple d -> d (8 d^2 at the usual multiple of four). Returns (attention, mlp, total); the classic block is 12 d^2 (Vaswani et al. 2017; Radford et al. 2019).



physics.transformer.calc_transformer_decode_flops(n_params, n_tokens=1)
Autoregressive decode FLOPs using the 2P rule.
Forward pass ~ 2 FLOPs per parameter per token (Kaplan et al. 2020, Sec. 2.1). Deliberately EXCLUDES per-token attention-over-KV FLOPs (~ 2 * layers * context * kv_width per token, linear in context length), so it holds in the parameter-dominated regime (short/moderate context); do not apply it unmodified at very long contexts (e.g. 128K).



physics.transformer.calc_transformer_prefill_flops(
    n_params,
    seq_len,
    n_layers=None,
    hidden_dim=None,
    causal=True,
)
Calculate prompt prefill FLOPs for a Transformer.
Prefill computation comprises: 1. Linear projections and FFN layers: 2 * n_params * seq_len 2. Self-attention matrix multiplications (QK^T and Softmax * V): - Causal (lower-triangular): 2 * n_layers * hidden_dim * seq_len^2 - Bidirectional (full): 4 * n_layers * hidden_dim * seq_len^2

physics.transformer.calc_vla_inference_latency(
    n_params,
    weight_memory,
    input_tokens,
    action_tokens,
    peak_flops,
    memory_bandwidth,
    *,
    bus_efficiency=1.0,
    compute_utilization=1.0,
    parallel_decode=False,
    n_layers=None,
    hidden_dim=None,
)
Roofline latency of one fresh vision-language-action (VLA) evaluation.
One evaluation of a decoder-only VLA backbone has two phases that bind on different resources:

Prefill. The input tokens (image patches plus prompt) pass through the backbone together. Each weight fetched from memory is reused across all S tokens, so at 16-bit activations the arithmetic intensity is about S FLOP/byte and the pass is compute-bound once S exceeds the ridge point. The pass cannot finish before its own weight sweep either: t_prefill = max(F_prefill / (Pi * u), M_weights / (B * eta)), with F_prefill from :func:calc_transformer_prefill_flops.
Decode. An autoregressive action decoder emits one action token per step (OpenVLA emits one token per action dimension). The prefill pass emits the first token; each of the remaining action_tokens - 1 steps is a matrix-vector pass that re-reads every weight, so it is bandwidth-bound: t_step = max(2 N / (Pi * u), M_weights / (B * eta)).

With parallel_decode=True (OpenVLA-OFT) the action tokens enter the same forward pass as empty placeholder embeddings under bidirectional attention: the prefill grows by action_tokens and the decode phase vanishes.
Weight-only quantization (for example INT4 weights with 16-bit activations) shrinks weight_memory and therefore the decode term, but not the prefill FLOPs, which still execute at the 16-bit peak_flops the caller passes in.
Source: Pope et al., “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference,” MLSys 2023 (prefill compute-bound, decode memory-bound); Williams, Waterman and Patterson, “Roofline,” CACM 52(4), 2009; Kim et al., “OpenVLA,” arXiv:2406.09246, 2024 (one autoregressive token per action dimension); Kim, Finn and Liang, “Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success,” RSS 2025 (parallel decoding).
Excludes a separately timed vision encoder, KV-cache traffic, kernel launch and framework overhead, and contention from other bus clients. compute_utilization (achieved fraction of peak_flops) and bus_efficiency (sustained fraction of memory_bandwidth) are the two calibration knobs.










Name
Type
Description





dict
Quantities prefill_flops, t_prefill_compute, t_weight_sweep, t_prefill, t_decode_step, t_decode, t_total, f_max; ints prefill_tokens and decode_steps; and prefill_bound (“compute” or “memory”).







physics.transformer.calc_weight_only_step_time(
    n_params,
    n_tokens,
    sustained_rate,
    weight_read_time,
)
Time for one forward pass over n_tokens positions, weight work only.
T(N) = max(T_weights, 2 P N / R)
The pass either waits to read every weight once (weight_read_time) or does 2 P N weight operations at sustained_rate, whichever is longer. Attention traffic is left out, so long contexts take longer than this bound (added 2026-10-20).

Weight-only quantization (for example INT4 weights with 16-bit activations) shrinks weight_memory and therefore the decode term, but not the prefill FLOPs, which still execute at the 16-bit peak_flops the caller passes in.
Source: Pope et al., “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference,” MLSys 2023 (prefill compute-bound, decode memory-bound); Williams, Waterman and Patterson, “Roofline,” CACM 52(4), 2009; Kim et al., “OpenVLA,” arXiv:2406.09246, 2024 (one autoregressive token per action dimension); Kim, Finn and Liang, “Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success,” RSS 2025 (parallel decoding).
Excludes a separately timed vision encoder, KV-cache traffic, kernel launch and framework overhead, and contention from other bus clients. compute_utilization (achieved fraction of peak_flops) and bus_efficiency (sustained fraction of memory_bandwidth) are the two calibration knobs.










Name
Type
Description





dict
Quantities prefill_flops, t_prefill_compute, t_weight_sweep, t_prefill, t_decode_step, t_decode, t_total, f_max; ints prefill_tokens and decode_steps; and prefill_bound (“compute” or “memory”).







physics.transformer.calc_weight_only_step_time(
    n_params,
    n_tokens,
    sustained_rate,
    weight_read_time,
)
Time for one forward pass over n_tokens positions, weight work only.
T(N) = max(T_weights, 2 P N / R)
The pass either waits to read every weight once (weight_read_time) or does 2 P N weight operations at sustained_rate, whichever is longer. Attention traffic is left out, so long contexts take longer than this bound (added 2026-10-20).

title: solvers.SeriesFailureModel
text:
solvers.SeriesFailureModel
solvers.SeriesFailureModel()
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.
Any single component failure stops the job, so failure rates add (a series system with independent, exponentially distributed failures). Each component is stated per node, with its MTTF and its count per node; its share per device is count / devices_per_node / MTTF. A redundant part that cannot fail the node singly (an N+M power supply) enters with count 0. Added 2026-10-20.

title: solvers.TrainingMemoryModel
text:
solvers.TrainingMemoryModel()
Decomposes per-accelerator training memory into teachable components.
This model answers a different question than SingleNodeModel. Roofline feasibility asks whether a workload’s inference weights fit; training feasibility must also account for gradients, optimizer state, activations, and communication buffers. The accounting follows the common mixed-precision state breakdown used by Megatron-LM and ZeRO.
Literature Source: 1. Shoeybi et al. (2019), “Megatron-LM” (tensor/pipeline parallel state). 2. Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO” (data-parallel state sharding). 3. Korthikanti et al. (2023), activation recomputation accounting.
Formula contract: - parameter states are sharded by TP * PP * EP before ZeRO sharding. - ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state, ZeRO-2 also shards gradients, and ZeRO-3 also shards weights across DP. - activation memory is based on local microbatch, layers per pipeline stage, hidden dimension, and the actual bytes per element for the precision.





Name
Description




solve
Estimate per-accelerator training memory.





solvers.TrainingMemoryModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    batch_size,
    seq_len=2048,
    precision='fp16',
    optimizer='adam',
    activation_checkpointing='selective',
    tp_size=1,
    pp_size=1,
    dp_size=1,
    ep_size=1,
    zero_stage=0,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=1,
    trainable_fraction=1.0,
    communication_buffer_fraction=0.05,
    sequence_parallel=True,
)
Estimate per-accelerator training memory.
batch_size is the global batch. The activation term uses the local microbatch implied by data parallelism and gradient accumulation. Model states are sharded by tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism first; ZeRO then shards optimizer, gradient, and parameter states across the data-parallel group according to its stage.
With tp_size > 1 and sequence_parallel (the Megatron-LM recipe Korthikanti et al. 2023 evaluate), every stored activation is split across the tensor-parallel group, so the activation term divides by tp_size (their Table 2). Without sequence parallelism the LayerNorm and dropout activations stay replicated; that case keeps the unsharded activation term as a conservative upper bound.

title: engine.solvers.goodput
text:
engine.solvers.goodput
Fleet goodput solvers: ML productivity goodput and runtime goodput.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). Added 2026-10-20.





Name
Description




GoodputModel
ML productivity goodput: the share of offered capacity-time that becomes


RuntimeGoodputModel
Runtime goodput of one job: the share of its held time spent on retained steps.





engine.solvers.goodput.GoodputModel()
ML productivity goodput: the share of offered capacity-time that becomes ideal-rate work, MPG = S x R x P.
Scheduling goodput S is held over offered capacity-time, runtime goodput R retained over held time, and program goodput P ideal over retained time. Each factor divides by what the previous one passed, so the factors multiply and every lost interval is charged once, at the first boundary it fails: 1 = (1 - S) + S(1 - R) + SR(1 - P) + SRP. One point of a factor is worth the product of the other two, and a lever that lifts a factor to its ceiling multiplies MPG by the ceiling’s ratio. A useful accelerator-hour costs the offered rate divided by MPG.
Literature Source: 1. Wongpanich et al. (2025), “Machine Learning Fleet Efficiency: Analyzing and Optimizing Large-Scale Google TPU Systems with ML Productivity Goodput.”



engine.solvers.goodput.RuntimeGoodputModel()
Runtime goodput of one job: the share of its held time spent on retained steps.
The loss is the sum of five owners’ terms on one denominator, held time (first order; each term is small):

startup: restart, checkpoint load, and warmup once per held window;
input waits: complete allocations stalled on the input pipeline;
checkpoint waste at the Young-Daly interval, write share plus rework;
recovery: the four-term cold-restart budget over the failure interval (rework is already counted in the checkpoint term);
forced preemption: rate times (work since the last save + startup).

Reuses CheckpointIntervalModel for the checkpoint term and the recovery profile’s cold_restart_time for recovery, startup, and the preemption relaunch (the same source as RecoveryBudgetModel and PreemptionTaxModel).
Literature Source: 1. Young (1974); Daly (2006), optimal checkpoint interval. 2. Wongpanich et al. (2025), runtime goodput.

title: engine.solvers.harness
text:
engine.solvers.harness
Agent-harness solvers: what the runtime holds, shares, and admits (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers. Each model is arithmetic on stated inputs: approval escrow sized by Little’s law, weighted deficit round-robin between request classes, bounded-liability admission of the next model call, one trajectory metered against its budget vector, and call or step ceilings read from public agent runs. None models a particular serving engine, provider quota, or queueing burst.





Name
Description




ApprovalEscrowModel
What approval escrow holds for a long-running workload and an urgent one.


BoundedLiabilityAdmissionModel
Bounded-liability admission of the next model call, against a check of settled spend.


DeficitRoundRobinModel
Weighted deficit round-robin between backlogged request classes.


TrajectoryBudgetMeterModel
One append-only trajectory metered against a budget vector of turns, tokens, time, and dollars.





engine.solvers.harness.ApprovalEscrowModel()
What approval escrow holds for a long-running workload and an urgent one.
Little’s law gives the trajectories waiting for a decision, L = lambda W. For the repair workload each keeps its workspace lease, so escrow binds on retained memory; for the remediation workload fewer than one waits, and the decision binds on time to mitigate, T = diagnose + decide + apply. Means only: bursts and batch review hold more for as long as they last.



engine.solvers.harness.BoundedLiabilityAdmissionModel()
Bounded-liability admission of the next model call, against a check of settled spend.
A spend check admits when the call’s liability fits allowance - settled. The reservation test admits only when settled spend, outstanding reservations, the call’s liability, and the protected finalization reserve together fit the allowance. Liability prices every input token at the undiscounted rate and the whole output allowance (calc_bounded_liability). Dollars throughout.



engine.solvers.harness.DeficitRoundRobinModel()
Weighted deficit round-robin between backlogged request classes.
Each round a class earns w q charge units and spends c per call (input tokens plus the full output allowance), carrying unspent credit forward. Weights fix the token-charge shares, w / sum(w); the call shares follow w q / c and so depend on call size. A direct simulation of rounds rounds checks the long-run formula.



engine.solvers.harness.TrajectoryBudgetMeterModel()
One append-only trajectory metered against a budget vector of turns, tokens, time, and dollars.
With prefix reuse every turn’s earlier prompt is billed at the cached rate and only the newly appended tokens (and the whole first prompt) at the input rate; without reuse every input token is billed uncached. The token meter counts cached input in full, so only the dollar meter sees a cache miss. Each used fraction is used / allowance; the leading meter is the largest.

title: engine.solvers.serving_scale
text:
engine.solvers.serving_scale
Serving-at-scale solvers: request traces, measured frontiers, KV admission, routing.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). The equations live in physics.serving (Little’s law, the batching knee, padding waste, speculative rounds) and physics.memory (KV-cache size); these models apply them to a published trace, a benchmark table, or one stated replica (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




KvAdmissionModel
How many requests of one context length a replica’s KV budget admits.


PrecisionDividendModel
The maximum batch before and after lower-precision weights and KV cache.





engine.solvers.serving_scale.KvAdmissionModel()
How many requests of one context length a replica’s KV budget admits.
The budget is the replica’s HBM minus its weights and a runtime reserve; each request holds 2 L H_kv d_head b bytes per token for its whole context (calc_kv_cache_size). Paging changes none of these bytes, only the waste around them.



engine.solvers.serving_scale.PrecisionDividendModel()
The maximum batch before and after lower-precision weights and KV cache.
Weights and each request’s KV cache split evenly across tp_size devices. Lower-precision weights raise each device’s KV budget once; lower-precision KV shrinks every request’s share. The dividend is the ratio of the two maximum batches.

title: solvers.SensitivitySolver
text:
solvers.SensitivitySolver()
Identifies the binding constraint via numerical sensitivity analysis (Wall 21).
This solver computes numerical partial derivatives of performance with respect to hardware parameters to identify the ‘binding constraint.’
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” 2. Ofenbeck et al. (2014), “Applying the Roofline Model.”





Name
Description




solve
Solve for parameter sensitivities and identify the binding constraint.





solvers.SensitivitySolver.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    precision='fp16',
    perturbation_pct=10.0,
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Solve for parameter sensitivities and identify the binding constraint.
Numerically perturbs each hardware parameter (peak FLOPS, memory bandwidth, memory capacity) by perturbation_pct and re-solves the single-node Roofline. Each sensitivity is the normalized latency response (T_perturbed - T_base) / T_base (dimensionless; negative means the upgrade helps). The binding constraint is the parameter with the largest absolute sensitivity — the resource whose improvement moves latency the most.

float

Name
Type
Description





SensitivityResult
Per-parameter sensitivities, the binding constraint name, the baseline latency, and feasible. If the baseline does not fit in memory, feasible is False, binding_constraint is "memory_capacity", and constraint_trace carries the Memory Wall failure: the offload path pins latency, so the sensitivities (typically all zero) do not rank hardware levers.

title: engine.solvers.sandboxes
text:
engine.solvers.sandboxes
Agent-sandbox solvers: the cost of an isolation envelope (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers. Each model is arithmetic on stated per-call, per-byte, or per-lease inputs: the system-call tax each envelope pays, setup paid per call or once per trajectory, workspace provisioning by copy or copy-on-write, and a warm pool sized by Little’s law and a Poisson reserve. None models queueing inside a host, restore contention, or a particular hypervisor.





Name
Description




EnvelopeAmortizationModel
Setup paid on every call against once per trajectory, under equal useful work.


SandboxPoolReserveModel
A warm sandbox pool under steady Poisson arrivals.


SyscallTaxModel
The added time of calls ordinary system calls under each envelope.


WorkspaceProvisioningModel
Bytes to provision workspaces by full copy or copy-on-write, and the





engine.solvers.sandboxes.EnvelopeAmortizationModel()
Setup paid on every call against once per trajectory, under equal useful work.
Fresh per call: N (T_setup + W); retained: T_setup + N W. Setup is T_setup / (T_setup + W) of a fresh call, and holding it to a share phi needs W >= T_setup (1 - phi) / phi. Serialized, no overlap.



engine.solvers.sandboxes.SandboxPoolReserveModel()
A warm sandbox pool under steady Poisson arrivals.
Active leases follow Little’s law, N = lambda T_hold. With s standby instances and a constant restore lead time T_init, a request misses when at least s earlier replacements are outstanding: P(Poisson(lambda T_init) >= s). Resident guest memory is a private image per lease, or one shared image plus dirty pages per lease and private state per standby under copy-on-write.



engine.solvers.sandboxes.SyscallTaxModel()
The added time of calls ordinary system calls under each envelope.
A shared-kernel container pays a trap and an in-kernel filter per call, a microVM a native trap in its guest (device exits counted separately), and a user-space kernel a trap, emulation, and a switch to the emulator.



engine.solvers.sandboxes.WorkspaceProvisioningModel()
Bytes to provision workspaces by full copy or copy-on-write, and the first-write payload under file or block granularity.
Payload only: drive times are lower bounds at the sequential rate, and metadata, journaling, and caching add traffic.

title: physics.serving
text:
physics.serving
Inference serving and queueing models.





Name
Description




calc_batch_formation_wait
Mean time a request waits for a batch of batch_size to fill.


calc_batch_knee
Batch size at which per-request cost equals the per-batch fixed cost.


calc_batch_throughput_share
Throughput at batch_size as a share of the ceiling 1 / t_req: B t_req / (t_0 + B t_req).


calc_exponential_quantile_factor
A quantile of an exponential distribution as a multiple of its mean.


calc_kingman_wait_ratio
Mean queue wait of one server as a multiple of the mean service time (Kingman 1961).


calc_littles_law_occupancy
Mean requests in a stable system, by Little’s law.


calc_littles_law_rate
Turns per unit time that occupied_slots sustain, by Little’s law.


calc_mg1_wait_ratio
Mean M/G/1 queue wait as a multiple of the mean service time.


calc_mm1_max_utilization
Highest utilization at which an M/M/1 tail stays within tail_budget.


calc_mm1_time_in_system
Mean time a request spends in an M/M/1 server, waiting plus service.


calc_padding_waste_fraction
Share of slot time a fixed-membership batch leaves idle.


calc_queue_latency_mmc
M/M/c queueing model for inference tail latency (Erlang C).


calc_residency_factor
How much holding a slot through a wait divides the turn rate.


calc_speculative_expected_tokens
Expected tokens one speculative round emits.


calc_speculative_round_speedup
Decode-stream speedup of speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023).





physics.serving.calc_batch_formation_wait(batch_size, arrival_rate)
Mean time a request waits for a batch of batch_size to fill.
W_form = (B - 1) / (2 lambda)
With arrivals at a steady arrival_rate (lambda), the first request of a batch waits for B - 1 more and the last for none; the mean is half.



physics.serving.calc_batch_knee(fixed_time, per_request_time)
Batch size at which per-request cost equals the per-batch fixed cost.
B_knee = t_0 / t_req
With batch service time S(B) = t_0 + B t_req, throughput B / S(B) reaches half its ceiling 1 / t_req at this batch.



physics.serving.calc_batch_throughput_share(
    batch_size,
    fixed_time,
    per_request_time,
)
Throughput at batch_size as a share of the ceiling 1 / t_req: B t_req / (t_0 + B t_req).



physics.serving.calc_exponential_quantile_factor(quantile)
A quantile of an exponential distribution as a multiple of its mean.
k_q = ln(1 / (1 - q))
Time in an M/M/1 system is exponential, so its p99 is ln(100) = 4.605 times its mean at every load.



physics.serving.calc_kingman_wait_ratio(utilization, arrival_scv, service_scv)
Mean queue wait of one server as a multiple of the mean service time (Kingman 1961).
E[W] / E[S] ~ (c_a^2 + c_s^2) / 2 * rho / (1 - rho)
A heavy-traffic approximation for a G/G/1 queue: arrival_scv and service_scv are the squared coefficients of variation of interarrival and service times. Exact for M/M/1 (both 1); a mean, not a tail.



physics.serving.calc_littles_law_occupancy(arrival_rate, time_in_system)
Mean requests in a stable system, by Little’s law.
L = lambda W
arrival_rate (requests per unit time) times time_in_system (the mean time each request spends inside). The law needs only stability, not a distribution, so it gives a mean and says nothing about the tail.



physics.serving.calc_littles_law_rate(occupied_slots, residence_time)
Turns per unit time that occupied_slots sustain, by Little’s law.
L = lambda W   =>   lambda = L / W
residence_time is the time each turn holds its slot. The law assumes only a stable system, so the rate is an average, not a peak.



physics.serving.calc_mg1_wait_ratio(utilization, service_cv)
Mean M/G/1 queue wait as a multiple of the mean service time.
The Pollaczek-Khinchine formula for one server with Poisson arrivals and a general service-time distribution:
W_q / (1/mu) = rho / (1 - rho) * (1 + C_s^2) / 2
The first factor (load) grows without bound as utilization approaches 1; the second (variability) scales the whole curve by the spread of service times, service_cv being their coefficient of variation (1 for exponential service). Added 2026-10-20 for scheduler queueing, where a fleet is modeled as one server working through jobs.

Type
Description
Default




utilization
float
Offered load rho, in [0, 1).
required


service_cv
float
Coefficient of variation of service time, C_s >= 0.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Mean queue wait divided by the mean service time (inf at rho >= 1).







physics.serving.calc_mm1_max_utilization(service_time, tail_budget, tail_factor)
Highest utilization at which an M/M/1 tail stays within tail_budget.
k S / (1 - rho) <= T   =>   rho <= 1 - k S / T
tail_factor (k) is the tail as a multiple of the mean time in system (calc_exponential_quantile_factor).



physics.serving.calc_mm1_time_in_system(service_time, utilization)
Mean time a request spends in an M/M/1 server, waiting plus service.
W = S / (1 - rho)
service_time (S) is the mean service time and utilization (rho) the fraction of time the server is busy. W grows without bound as rho approaches 1: the queueing knee.



physics.serving.calc_padding_waste_fraction(lengths)
Share of slot time a fixed-membership batch leaves idle.
W = 1 - mean(L) / max(L)
Every member holds its slot until the longest member finishes, so slot time is n max(L) while useful work is sum(L).



physics.serving.calc_queue_latency_mmc(
    arrival_rate_hz,
    service_rate_hz,
    num_servers,
)
M/M/c queueing model for inference tail latency (Erlang C).
Calculates the expected queueing delays (P50 and P99) for a system with Markovian arrivals, Markovian service times, and c parallel servers.
This implementation uses the Log-Sum-Exp trick to calculate the Erlang C formula. This prevents floating-point overflow (math.inf) or underflow to 0.0 when dealing with large-scale clusters (e.g., c > 100).

Type
Description
Default

Quantity or float
The average rate of incoming requests (λ) in requests per second (Hz).
required

Quantity or float
The average rate at which a single server completes requests (μ) in Hz.
required

physics.serving.calc_residency_factor(generation_time, wait_time)
How much holding a slot through a wait divides the turn rate.
1 + T_wait / T_gen
Keeping state through a wait stretches each turn’s residence from generation_time to generation_time + wait_time; for the same slots, Little’s law divides the rate by this factor (the residency tax).



physics.serving.calc_speculative_expected_tokens(acceptance, draft_length)
Expected tokens one speculative round emits.
E[tokens] = (1 - alpha^(K+1)) / (1 - alpha)
A draft proposes draft_length (K) tokens, each accepted independently with probability acceptance (alpha) until the first rejection; the target’s verification pass always contributes one token.



physics.serving.calc_speculative_round_speedup(
    accepted_per_round,
    draft_length,
    draft_cost_ratio,
)
Decode-stream speedup of speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023).
S = (m + 1) / (gamma r + 1)
Each round drafts draft_length (gamma) tokens at draft_cost_ratio (r) of a target step each, and the target’s one verification step keeps accepted_per_round (m) drafted tokens plus one of its own. Faster only while m > gamma r.

title: physics.fine_tuning
text:
physics.fine_tuning
Fine-tuning on serialized trajectories: weighting, packing, and preference pairs.
Closed forms behind supervised and preference fine-tuning of a policy on recorded trajectories (added 2026-10-20). Each takes stated counts: selected target tokens per example, stored example lengths against a fixed buffer, or log-probability sums of two scored records. None models a trained network. The solvers in engine/solvers/fine_tuning.py compose them.





Name
Description




calc_example_average_share
A group’s weight in an example-averaged loss: k / N.


calc_first_fit_decreasing
Buffer loads when examples are packed longest first into the first buffer with room.


calc_preference_pair
One preference pair under the DPO loss (Rafailov et al. 2023).


calc_token_average_shares
Each example’s weight in a token-averaged loss: n_i / sum_j n_j.





physics.fine_tuning.calc_example_average_share(group_examples, total_examples)
A group’s weight in an example-averaged loss: k / N.
Every example’s mean loss counts once, so a trajectory split into k records carries k times the weight of an unsplit example.



physics.fine_tuning.calc_first_fit_decreasing(lengths, capacity)
Buffer loads when examples are packed longest first into the first buffer with room.
Returns the stored tokens of each fixed-capacity buffer. An example longer than capacity cannot be packed.



physics.fine_tuning.calc_preference_pair(
    policy_preferred,
    reference_preferred,
    policy_dispreferred,
    reference_dispreferred,
    beta,
)
One preference pair under the DPO loss (Rafailov et al. 2023).
Each record’s score is its policy log-probability sum minus the reference’s, z = log pi_theta - log pi_ref; the pair margin is beta (z_w - z_l); the logistic score is sigma(margin); the loss is -log sigma(margin) = log(1 + e^-margin); the gradient’s saturation factor is sigma(-margin), and the full coefficient on the pair is beta sigma(-margin).
Returns (score_w, score_l, margin, preference_score, loss, saturation, coefficient).



physics.fine_tuning.calc_token_average_shares(target_counts)
Each example’s weight in a token-averaged loss: n_i / sum_j n_j.
Every selected target token counts once, so an example’s weight grows with its target count.

solvers.InferenceScalingModel()
Models inference-time compute scaling (Wall 12: Reasoning/CoT Cost).
This model quantifies the cost of ‘System-2 thinking’ — inference-time compute scaling via chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the model generates K intermediate reasoning steps before producing the final answer. Each step incurs the full cost of autoregressive decoding.

solvers.TopologyModel()
Models bisection bandwidth for different network topologies (Wall 10).

title: engine.solvers.storage
text:
engine.solvers.storage
Storage solvers: what a training fleet reads, saves, and pays to move.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__); kept per-domain so the logic stays reviewable. Each model is a bandwidth or rate bound: it counts bytes and divides by a stated rate, and leaves queueing, contention, and protocol overheads out.





Name
Description




CheckpointStormModel
Synchronized saves when every replica writes its own copy of the state.


DataStallModel
Input wait per step when delivery and compute run in sequence or overlap.


HostIoCpuModel
Host CPU time spent issuing and completing I/O requests.


InputDemandModel
The input bandwidth a fleet draws: consumers x busy fraction x batch bytes / compute time.


ObjectStorageBillModel
The object-storage bill beyond capacity: egress per read, GET requests, archive retrieval.


PrefetchDepthModel
Ready batches a prefetch queue needs to cover a tier’s tail read latency.


StorageFootprintModel
The bytes a training run reads once and the bytes it saves again and again.


StreamVsStageModel
Streaming every epoch from remote object storage against staging once per run.


SyntheticFootprintModel
Generated training data at rest and in motion.


TieredCacheModel
Mean service of a two-tier cache: E[T] = h T_hit + (1 - h) T_miss.


TieredCheckpointModel
A checkpoint staged on each node’s local storage, then drained to a durable tier.


UtilizationLossModel
Dollars of accelerator time idled when utilization falls from one level to another.





engine.solvers.storage.CheckpointStormModel()
Synchronized saves when every replica writes its own copy of the state.
replicas copies of the full resumable state cross one shared ingest bandwidth; writing one logical copy, split across the ranks that own it, moves the state once. The ratio is the replica count.



engine.solvers.storage.DataStallModel()
Input wait per step when delivery and compute run in sequence or overlap.
In sequence a step costs delivery plus compute; overlapped, the loader fetches the next batch during compute, so a step costs the longer of the two. The stall is the share of the step not spent computing.



engine.solvers.storage.HostIoCpuModel()
Host CPU time spent issuing and completing I/O requests.
Each request costs a stated CPU service time on the host; at a request rate r the host spends r x service CPU-seconds per second, the number of cores kept busy by data movement alone.



engine.solvers.storage.InputDemandModel()
The input bandwidth a fleet draws: consumers x busy fraction x batch bytes / compute time.
Each consumer reads a distinct batch of samples_per_step samples of bytes_per_sample every step_time of compute; busy_fraction is the share of wall-clock time spent computing.



engine.solvers.storage.ObjectStorageBillModel()
The object-storage bill beyond capacity: egress per read, GET requests, archive retrieval.
Capacity is billed per byte-month; every read that leaves the region or provider pays egress per byte; each file read pays a GET fee; an archive restore pays a retrieval fee and then egress for one read.



engine.solvers.storage.PrefetchDepthModel()
Ready batches a prefetch queue needs to cover a tier’s tail read latency.
One read at a tier’s tail latency spans latency / compute_time compute windows, so the queue needs the ceiling of that many ready batches. A deeper safety depth costs depth x batch of host memory per consumer.



engine.solvers.storage.StorageFootprintModel()
The bytes a training run reads once and the bytes it saves again and again.
A resumable checkpoint holds bytes_per_param for every parameter and is written once per save interval, so a run of duration D saves D / interval times. Against a corpus read once, the written bytes can exceed the read bytes by orders of magnitude. The corpus is packaged into shards of shard_bytes; the archive keeps every archive_every-th checkpoint (and the final one when the count is not a multiple) plus the source and the tokenized corpus.



engine.solvers.storage.StreamVsStageModel()
Streaming every epoch from remote object storage against staging once per run.
Both options keep the dataset in object storage as the source of truth. Streaming pays egress for every epoch of every run; staging adds a year of local capacity and pays egress once per run. They break even where the streaming egress per run equals staging’s extra cost per run.



engine.solvers.storage.SyntheticFootprintModel()
Generated training data at rest and in motion.
Each sample carries provenance metadata (a fraction of its payload) at rest; the pipeline writes payload and metadata once and reads the payload once per verification pass.



engine.solvers.storage.TieredCacheModel()
Mean service of a two-tier cache: E[T] = h T_hit + (1 - h) T_miss.
With service times in units of one hit, E[T] = h + (1 - h) x penalty, and the delivered rate is 1 / E[T] of the all-hit rate. Given tier bandwidths, the penalty is their ratio and the delivered rate is the hot bandwidth times that fraction (time per byte averaged over the mix).



engine.solvers.storage.TieredCheckpointModel()
A checkpoint staged on each node’s local storage, then drained to a durable tier.
Each node writes its shard (checkpoint / nodes) to local storage and training pauses only for that write. The durable copy proceeds in the background at the shared tier’s aggregate bandwidth, which is the same time as each node’s shard at its per-node share of that bandwidth.



engine.solvers.storage.UtilizationLossModel()
Dollars of accelerator time idled when utilization falls from one level to another.
A fleet of n_devices billed at device_hour_rate costs its full rate every day whether it computes or waits; a drop in the busy fraction wastes that share of the daily cost.

Input wait per step when delivery and compute run in sequence or overlap.
In sequence a step costs delivery plus compute; overlapped, the loader fetches the next batch during compute, so a step costs the longer of the two. The stall is the share of the step not spent computing.



engine.solvers.storage.HostIoCpuModel()
Host CPU time spent issuing and completing I/O requests.
Each request costs a stated CPU service time on the host; at a request rate r the host spends r x service CPU-seconds per second, the number of cores kept busy by data movement alone.



engine.solvers.storage.InputDemandModel()
The input bandwidth a fleet draws: consumers x busy fraction x batch bytes / compute time.
Each consumer reads a distinct batch of samples_per_step samples of bytes_per_sample every step_time of compute; busy_fraction is the share of wall-clock time spent computing.



engine.solvers.storage.ObjectStorageBillModel()
The object-storage bill beyond capacity: egress per read, GET requests, archive retrieval.
Capacity is billed per byte-month; every read that leaves the region or provider pays egress per byte; each file read pays a GET fee; an archive restore pays a retrieval fee and then egress for one read.



engine.solvers.storage.PrefetchDepthModel()
Ready batches a prefetch queue needs to cover a tier’s tail read latency.
One read at a tier’s tail latency spans latency / compute_time compute windows, so the queue needs the ceiling of that many ready batches. A deeper safety depth costs depth x batch of host memory per consumer.



engine.solvers.storage.StorageFootprintModel()
The bytes a training run reads once and the bytes it saves again and again.
A resumable checkpoint holds bytes_per_param for every parameter and is written once per save interval, so a run of duration D saves D / interval times. Against a corpus read once, the written bytes can exceed the read bytes by orders of magnitude. The corpus is packaged into shards of shard_bytes; the archive keeps every archive_every-th checkpoint (and the final one when the count is not a multiple) plus the source and the tokenized corpus.



engine.solvers.storage.StreamVsStageModel()
Streaming every epoch from remote object storage against staging once per run.
Both options keep the dataset in object storage as the source of truth. Streaming pays egress for every epoch of every run; staging adds a year of local capacity and pays egress once per run. They break even where the streaming egress per run equals staging’s extra cost per run.



engine.solvers.storage.SyntheticFootprintModel()
Generated training data at rest and in motion.
Each sample carries provenance metadata (a fraction of its payload) at rest; the pipeline writes payload and metadata once and reads the payload once per verification pass.



engine.solvers.storage.TieredCacheModel()
Mean service of a two-tier cache: E[T] = h T_hit + (1 - h) T_miss.
With service times in units of one hit, E[T] = h + (1 - h) x penalty, and the delivered rate is 1 / E[T] of the all-hit rate. Given tier bandwidths, the penalty is their ratio and the delivered rate is the hot bandwidth times that fraction (time per byte averaged over the mix).



engine.solvers.storage.TieredCheckpointModel()
A checkpoint staged on each node’s local storage, then drained to a durable tier.
Each node writes its shard (checkpoint / nodes) to local storage and training pauses only for that write. The durable copy proceeds in the background at the shared tier’s aggregate bandwidth, which is the same time as each node’s shard at its per-node share of that bandwidth.



engine.solvers.storage.UtilizationLossModel()
Dollars of accelerator time idled when utilization falls from one level to another.
A fleet of n_devices billed at device_hour_rate costs its full rate every day whether it computes or waits; a drop in the busy fraction wastes that share of the daily cost.

title: solvers.TransformationModel

title: engine.solvers.embodied
text:
engine.solvers.embodied
Embodied solvers: how far a machine travels before it stops, and what the floor allows.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). The equations live in physics.robotics.stopping and physics.drivetrain; these models compose them for one stated situation (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




OnsetTrialModel
One stopping trace scored against a precommitted oracle (added 2026-10-20).


RailHoldUpModel
A capacitor-backed rail that must carry the protective response from the


ShieldCoverageBillModel
The evidence a shielded hazard-rate claim needs (added 2026-10-20).


StoppingBudgetModel
The elementary stopping budget: travel during the pre-brake delay plus braking travel.


TakeoverBudgetModel
A request for a person to take over, priced against the finished stopping budget.


TractionLossModel
A drop in floor friction against the deceleration a machine’s budget assumes.





engine.solvers.embodied.OnsetTrialModel()
One stopping trace scored against a precommitted oracle (added 2026-10-20).
The oracle bounds powered-deceleration onset at onset_bound after the reference event and travel to rest at travel_bound (onset-bound travel, the resident stop, and the tracking inset). A trace that begins braking at onset travels speed * onset plus the same resident stop. Each predicate keeps its own signed margin; a combined score needs scales fixed in advance, here the bounds themselves. The trace passes only when both margins are non-negative.



engine.solvers.embodied.RailHoldUpModel()
A capacitor-backed rail that must carry the protective response from the loss-of-feed flag until the holding brakes are set (added 2026-10-20).
t_set = flag_path + (v/a + a/j) + t_engage: the path from the flag to powered-deceleration onset, the S-curve stop from the entry speed v (calc_scurve_stop_time), and the holding brake’s engagement. The margin is the hold-up time less t_set.



engine.solvers.embodied.ShieldCoverageBillModel()
The evidence a shielded hazard-rate claim needs (added 2026-10-20).
A fleet of fleet_units logs hours_per_day for one release cycle of cycle_days with zero hazardous proposals; the one-sided Poisson bound is -ln(1 - C) / T. The shield passes 1 - coverage of hazardous proposals (calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate), plus the common-cause rate. Against target_rate the model reports the coverage the bound would need, the proposal bound the stated coverage would need, the failure-free exposure and fleet days that bound it (calc_empirical_testing_exposure), and the seeded-hazard campaign that bounds the coverage itself (calc_zero_failure_sample_size), alone and with both bounds held jointly at 1 - alpha/2 each.



engine.solvers.embodied.StoppingBudgetModel()
The elementary stopping budget: travel during the pre-brake delay plus braking travel.
d_stop = travel(delay) + v^2 / (2 a) <= D_clear. The delay travel is v * tau at constant speed, or the trapezoid between speed and speed_at_delay_end when two speeds were recorded. Braking travel and braking time are from speed, the speed when the hazard appears, as the elementary budget assumes. The crossover speed 2 a tau is where the two terms are equal; the speed ceiling is the fastest speed whose stop fits clear_distance. A localization bound and a protective margin, when stated, add to the required distance and lower the ceiling (calc_safe_stopping_distance). added_delay prices one more delay step as travel at speed. The delay ceiling is the longest constant-speed pre-brake delay whose stop, with the overhead, still fits (calc_watchdog_lease_bound): (D_clear - overhead - v^2/2a) / v.
The finished budget (added 2026-10-20) takes three optional terms. A jerk bound replaces constant-deceleration braking with the resident S-curve stop (calc_scurve_stop_distance); its extra travel over v^2/2a is the jerk-ramp travel, and above a^2/j it equals v a / (2 j), a delay of a / (2 j). A tracking_bound (the tracking inset) joins the required distance after the two allowances. An approach_speed charges a person who keeps closing the gap for the whole delay and stop (v_h (tau + T_stop)). With a jerk bound the speed ceiling is the S-curve root (calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity) and the delay ceiling is (D_clear - overhead - inset - d_S(v)) / v. The same case reports the weakest deceleration whose S-curve stop still fits the braking room, jerk fixed, and its shortfall from the stated one (added 2026-10-20).



engine.solvers.embodied.TakeoverBudgetModel()
A request for a person to take over, priced against the finished stopping budget.
The takeover T_Sigma (the human response plus the console transport) adds to the machine’s pre-brake delay tau: until the person commits, the machine keeps moving at the request speed. Four finished budgets (StoppingBudgetModel with the S-curve jerk bound and the tracking inset) are solved at that speed: the machine alone, the machine with the dispatch-to-admission allocation Delta_da charged, and each with the takeover waited out before braking. The fallback deadline T_latest is the machine-alone delay spare: the longest wait after the request before the machine’s own stop must begin,
T_latest = (D_clear - delta - d_S(v)) / v - tau.
Configured timeouts are clipped to it, T = max(0, min(T_cfg, T_latest)), and dispatched on the last whole permission tick. Once the operator holds the channel, a manual lease longer than the chunk lease adds its excess to the delay as travel at the request speed (added 2026-10-20).



engine.solvers.embodied.TractionLossModel()
A drop in floor friction against the deceleration a machine’s budget assumes.
At the traction limit the deceleration is mu g phi, so braking distance v^2 / (2 mu g phi) scales as 1 / mu and the ratio of the two braking distances is mu_before / mu_after. The stated deceleration holds only while the lower friction still supplies it (calc_required_friction).

title: engine.solvers.recovery
text:
engine.solvers.recovery
Failure-recovery solvers: what the runtime does once an effect has failed (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers. Each model is arithmetic on stated inputs: one bounded repair priced against unwinding and rebuilding to the same endpoint, the expected irreversible loss of a plan whose checks run before or after its pivot, an append-only loop run to its turn ceiling or stopped early, retries multiplied through nested layers, a capped dependency under one burst of blocking calls, a retry cohort synchronized or jittered, a cleanup graph against a reverse stack, a breaker window classified two ways, and the incidents a published table lists as sustained by retries. None models a particular framework, provider, or queueing burst beyond what it states.





Name
Description




BulkheadAdmissionModel
One burst of blocking calls to a stalled dependency, before any completes.


IrreversibleLossModel
Expected irreversible loss of a plan with its check after, or before, the pivot.


RepairBreakEvenModel
One bounded repair attempt against compensating and rebuilding to the same endpoint.


RetryAmplificationModel
Attempts one failing logical operation sends when each layer retries on its own allowance.


RetryJitterModel
A cohort of retries released together: all inside a burst window, or jittered.


UndetectedLoopModel
An append-only loop run to its turn ceiling, or stopped after an earlier turn.





engine.solvers.recovery.BulkheadAdmissionModel()
One burst of blocking calls to a stalled dependency, before any completes.
Uncapped, every call takes a worker until the pool is full. Capped, at most worker_cap occupy workers and queue_cap wait without one; the rest are rejected at admission, and the cap protects the remaining workers however long the stall lasts. Worker slots only: not CPU, storage, or remote jobs that outlive a timeout.



engine.solvers.recovery.IrreversibleLossModel()
Expected irreversible loss of a plan with its check after, or before, the pivot.
Without a check ahead of the pivot nothing recovers: L = P(bad) I. A check that catches a fraction v and reverts with fidelity rho leaves P(bad) v I (1 - rho) from caught changes and P(bad) (1 - v) I from missed ones, which sum to P(bad) I (1 - v rho). Raising v by one step dv removes P(bad) I rho dv.



engine.solvers.recovery.RepairBreakEvenModel()
One bounded repair attempt against compensating and rebuilding to the same endpoint.
The fallback costs the compensation and rebuild times and the rebuild’s model tokens; one repair costs its pre-output startup, its output at the decode rate, local validation, and its whole isolated request. If a failed attempt leaves the fallback unchanged, E[C] = C_repair + (1 - p) C_fallback and repair first pays when p > p* = C_repair / C_fallback, per axis.



engine.solvers.recovery.RetryAmplificationModel()
Attempts one failing logical operation sends when each layer retries on its own allowance.
Every attempt of a layer drives a full set of attempts in the layer below, so a attempts per layer over L layers reach the dependency a^L times; one retry owner with the same allowance sends a (Brooker 2019).



engine.solvers.recovery.RetryJitterModel()
A cohort of retries released together: all inside a burst window, or jittered.
Synchronized, the window average is N / w; each drawing its arrival uniformly over the span J, the expected rate is N / J and a window of length w expects N w / J arrivals. Expectations only: one window can still receive every retry, so only an admission rate limiter bounds the peak.



engine.solvers.recovery.UndetectedLoopModel()
An append-only loop run to its turn ceiling, or stopped after an earlier turn.
Each turn appends its output and an observation and resends the whole history, so h turns send h s0 + delta h (h - 1) / 2 input tokens (calc_append_only_context) and h k_out output tokens; every turn takes the same time. The avoided charge is gross: detector cost, false alarms, and cleanup are not debited.

title: engine.solvers.parallelism
text:
engine.solvers.parallelism
Distributed-training solvers: parallel layouts, ZeRO sharding, data-parallel scale-out, tensor-parallel layer exchanges, and alignment-training state.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). Added 2026-10-20.





Name
Description




AlignmentMemoryModel
Model state of PPO-style RLHF against DPO, and its split over a model-parallel group.


DataParallelScaleOutModel
A data-parallel job inside one node and across nodes, from its one-device profile.


ParallelLayoutModel
One training step of a TP x PP x DP layout, read through the Fleet Law.


TensorParallelLayerModel
One Transformer layer’s forward compute against its tensor-parallel exchange.


ZeroShardingModel
Per-device training state at each ZeRO stage, and what full sharding sends.





engine.solvers.parallelism.AlignmentMemoryModel()
Model state of PPO-style RLHF against DPO, and its split over a model-parallel group.
PPO trains a policy and a value model (16 B per parameter of mixed-precision Adam each) and runs a frozen reference copy of the policy and a reward model forward only (16-bit weights). DPO keeps only the policy and the reference. During rollout the policy also holds a KV cache for every generated sequence.



engine.solvers.parallelism.DataParallelScaleOutModel()
A data-parallel job inside one node and across nodes, from its one-device profile.
Every update reduces the full gradient: a ring AllReduce inside each node on the fast link, and, with more than one node, a ring across all devices on the inter-node link. Gradient accumulation runs accumulation_steps local steps per update, so the same exchange serves more compute and the global batch grows. Speedup is the device count times the compute share of each update; training time and cost follow from the one-device run.



engine.solvers.parallelism.ParallelLayoutModel()
One training step of a TP x PP x DP layout, read through the Fleet Law.
Compute: the step’s 6 P D FLOPs (flops_per_param_token per parameter per token, D tokens per update) spread over every device at a local share of peak. Communication: each data-parallel rank reduces its gradient shard (the full gradient over TP x PP) with a ring AllReduce of about twice the shard; up to overlap_fraction of that transfer hides under the compute window, never more than the window itself. Pipeline stages idle (p-1)/(m+p-1) of the step, which stretches the compute window by 1/(1 - bubble). State: 16 B per parameter of mixed-precision Adam split over TP x PP; ZeRO-1 also shards the 12 B of optimizer state across the data-parallel group.
Literature Source: 1. Narayanan et al. (2021), Megatron-LM 3D parallelism. 2. Rajbhandari et al. (2020), ZeRO (16 B/param, optimizer sharding). 3. Huang et al. (2019), GPipe (bubble fraction).



engine.solvers.parallelism.TensorParallelLayerModel()
One Transformer layer’s forward compute against its tensor-parallel exchange.
The layer’s forward pass is 2 (P/L) FLOPs per token, split over the TP group and run at a sustained share of peak. Megatron-style tensor parallelism sums an activation of tokens x d_model once after attention and once after the MLP, each a ring AllReduce of 2(t-1)/t times the payload per device. The exchange must fit inside the compute on the link that carries it.
Literature Source: 1. Shoeybi et al. (2019), “Megatron-LM” (two AllReduces per layer per pass).



engine.solvers.parallelism.ZeroShardingModel()
Per-device training state at each ZeRO stage, and what full sharding sends.
DDP replicates weights (W), gradients (G), and optimizer state (O) on every device. ZeRO-1 shards O over N devices, ZeRO-2 also G, and ZeRO-3 (FSDP) also W. Stages 1 and 2 move DDP’s bytes (a ring AllReduce, about 2W per device); ZeRO-3 gathers every layer’s weights in forward and again in backward and reduce-scatters the gradients, about 3W, 1.5x as much.
Literature Source: 1. Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO” (stages and communication volume).
