physics.robotics.actuation.calc_alpha_power_gate_delay_stretch(
    nominal_voltage,
    drooped_voltage,
    threshold_voltage=None,
    alpha=1.3,
)
Calculate CMOS logic gate propagation delay expansion under power-rail voltage droop using the alpha-power law.
Sakurai-Newton Alpha-Power Law: stretch_ratio = (V_droop / V_nom) * ((V_nom - V_th) / (V_droop - V_th))^alpha



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_coasting_contact_peak_force(
    contact_velocity,
    effective_mass,
    contact_stiffness,
    preload_force,
)
Peak force when drive torque is removed at a contact tripwire and the mass coasts into a spring.
Energy balance from the tripwire, where the spring already carries preload_force: F0^2 / (2k) + m v^2 / 2 = F_peak^2 / (2k) => F_peak = sqrt(F0^2 + k m v^2)
With preload_force zero this is the unbraked transient force v sqrt(k m) (calc_transient_impact_force). Added 2026-10-20.



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_contact_force(stiffness, displacement)
Calculate linear Hookean elastic contact force upon unconstrained impact.
Equation: F = k * delta_x



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_contact_yield_deadline(
    yield_force,
    stiffness,
    approach_velocity,
)
Calculate maximum allowable software reaction latency before impact force exceeds mechanical yield.
For an arm approaching a rigid fixture of stiffness k at constant velocity v, contact force rises as F(t) = k * v * t. To prevent structural damage (F <= F_yield): t_deadline = F_yield / (k * v)











Name
Type
Description
Default




yield_force
Quantity
Maximum permissible mechanical shock / yield force (e.g. N).
required


stiffness
Quantity
Contact environment stiffness (e.g. N/m).
required


approach_velocity
Quantity
Tool-center-point approach velocity (e.g. m/s).
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Deadline duration in milliseconds.







physics.robotics.actuation.calc_inductive_voltage_droop(
    loop_inductance,
    current_slew_rate,
)
Calculate inductive voltage drop across power distribution network (PDN) during current transients.
Equation: Delta_V_ind = L * (dI / dt)



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_inverted_pendulum_fall_time(
    effective_length,
    gravity=None,
    theta_0=None,
    theta_fall=None,
)
Calculate characteristic instability timescale or fall duration for an inverted pendulum.
Models bipedal/humanoid balance dynamics under gravity. The linearized dynamics d^2 theta / dt^2 = (g / L) * theta yield the characteristic natural timescale: tau_0 = sqrt(L / g)
If initial perturbation theta_0 and fall threshold theta_fall are given: t_fall = tau_0 * ln(2 * theta_fall / theta_0)
Source: the linear inverted pendulum, whose natural frequency is omega_0 = sqrt(g / h), so tau_0 = sqrt(L / g) (Caron, “Biped Stabilization by Linear Feedback of the Variable-Height Inverted Pendulum Model”, arXiv:1909.07732, Sec. II). The t_fall expression is derived here, not taken from a published model. With zero initial angular velocity the linearized solution is theta(t) = theta_0 * cosh(t / tau_0), so t = tau_0 * acosh(theta_fall / theta_0), and ln(2x) approximates acosh(x) for x >> 1 (it overestimates by about 5% at x = 2). The small-angle linearization also loses accuracy as theta_fall grows.











Name
Type
Description
Default




effective_length
Quantity
Center-of-mass height or pendulum leg length L (e.g. meter).
required


gravity
Quantity
Gravitational acceleration g (defaults to 9.80665 m/s^2).
None


theta_0
Quantity or float
Initial angular perturbation from vertical (e.g. radians or degrees).
None


theta_fall
Quantity or float
Critical tipping angle threshold beyond which recovery is kinematically impossible.
None














Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Characteristic timescale or fall duration in seconds.







physics.robotics.actuation.calc_kinetic_energy(mass, velocity)
Calculate kinetic energy of a translating body.
Equation: E_k = 0.5 * m * v^2
Source: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Sec. 7.2, Eq. 7.6.











Name
Type
Description
Default




mass
Quantity
Total mass of the body (e.g. kg).
required


velocity
Quantity
Translational velocity (e.g. m/s).
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Kinetic energy in Joules.







physics.robotics.actuation.calc_passive_compliance_stiffness_bound(
    force_limit,
    tripwire_force,
    detection_speed,
    response_latency,
    arm_deceleration,
)
Largest series stiffness that keeps a driven contact under a force limit after the tripwire.
After the tripwire the arm keeps driving for the response latency, then stops at arm_deceleration; the stroke it drives is s = v t_r + v^2 / (2 a), and the force rises by k s on top of the tripwire force: F_trip + k s <= F_limit <=> k <= (F_limit - F_trip) / (v t_r + v^2 / (2 a))
Returns (stiffness bound, driven stroke). Added 2026-10-20.



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_quasistatic_spill_acceleration(
    inner_radius,
    freeboard,
    gravity=None,
)
Calculate the steady horizontal acceleration at which an open container’s liquid reaches its rim.
Equation: tan(theta) = a / g ; wall rise = R a / g ; a_max = g h_f / R
Under steady acceleration the free surface settles perpendicular to the effective gravity. Sloshing overshoots this steady tilt, so the bound is necessary, not sufficient.
Source: hydrostatics of a uniformly accelerated liquid (free surface normal to effective gravity); container slosh context in Mayer and Krechetnikov 2012, “Walking with coffee: why does it spill?”, Phys. Rev. E 85, 046117.



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_quintic_blend_duration(
    delta_torque,
    max_allowable_jerk,
)
Compute minimum blend duration for quintic polynomial trajectory to bound torque jerk.
Equation: tau_blend >= (1.875 * |Delta_tau|) / jerk_max



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_reduced_mass(mass_a, mass_b)
Calculate the two-body reduced mass of a collision.
Equation: mu = (1/m_a + 1/m_b)^-1
When one body cannot recoil (m_b -> infinity, a clamped contact), mu -> m_a.
Source: ISO/TS 15066:2016 Annex A, transient-contact model (content carried into ISO 10218-2:2025), as reproduced in Kirschner et al. 2022, eq. 2 (arXiv:2203.02706).



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_reflected_inertia(gear_ratio, rotor_inertia)
Calculate reflected rotor inertia felt at the actuator output shaft.
Equation: J_reflected = N^2 * J_rotor
Source: Lynch and Park, Modern Robotics, Cambridge University Press, 2017, Sec. 8.9.2 (“Apparent Inertia”), where G^2 * I_rotor is the rotor’s apparent (often called reflected) inertia for gear ratio G.











Name
Type
Description
Default




gear_ratio
float
Transmission reduction ratio N (>= 1.0).
required


rotor_inertia
Quantity
Unloaded rotor moment of inertia (e.g. kg * m^2).
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Reflected inertia in kg * m^2.







physics.robotics.actuation.calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump(
    gear_ratio,
    rotor_inertia,
    delta_accel,
)
Calculate the impulsive torque spike at an actuator seam transition.
When an unblended trajectory transition injects an acceleration discontinuity delta_accel across a discrete boundary, the transmission’s reflected rotor inertia amplifies the required inertial reaction torque at the output joint.
Equation: tau_spike = J_reflected * delta_accel = (N^2 * J_rotor) * delta_accel
Source: tau = I * alpha (OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Sec. 10.7, Eq. 10.25) applied to the rotor’s apparent (reflected) inertia G^2 * I_rotor (Lynch and Park, Modern Robotics, Cambridge University Press, 2017, Sec. 8.9.2). Link inertia, load, friction, and gear compliance are omitted, so this is the reflected-rotor share of the spike; treating the seam as an instantaneous acceleration step is a modeling assumption.











Name
Type
Description
Default




gear_ratio
float
Transmission reduction ratio N (>= 1.0).
required


rotor_inertia
Quantity
Unloaded rotor moment of inertia (e.g. kg * m^2).
required


delta_accel
Quantity
Discontinuous acceleration step across the seam (e.g. rad / s^2).
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Peak reaction torque spike in Newton-meters.







physics.robotics.actuation.calc_smoothstep_blend_window(change, rate_limit)
Shortest window of a fixed-endpoint quintic smoothstep whose peak rate stays at a limit.
Equation: T >= 1.875 |Delta u| / rate_max
The smoothstep alpha(s) = 10 s^3 - 15 s^4 + 6 s^5 has peak slope d alpha / ds = 30/16 = 1.875 at s = 1/2, so a change Delta u spread over T peaks at 1.875 Delta u / T. Unit-generic form of calc_quintic_blend_duration: an acceleration change against a jerk bound, or a torque change against a torque-rate ceiling (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Window in seconds.







physics.robotics.actuation.calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(
    force_limit,
    effective_mass,
    contact_stiffness,
    human_mass=None,
)
Calculate the highest contact speed whose transient peak force stays at a force limit.
Equation: v_max = F_max / sqrt(k * m)
The inverse of calc_transient_impact_force: human_mass=None gives the clamped case (m = m_eff); a human_mass gives the free, recoiling case (m = mu, the two-body reduced mass).
Source: ISO/TS 15066:2016 Annex A (carried into ISO 10218-2:2025), as used for v_rel,max in Kirschner et al. 2022 (arXiv:2203.02706).



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_transient_impact_force(
    contact_velocity,
    effective_mass,
    contact_stiffness,
    human_mass=None,
)
Calculate peak unbraked transient impact force on an elastic body.
Equation: F_peak = v * sqrt(k * m)
With human_mass=None the robot-side effective_mass acts alone (m = m_eff), the clamped (quasi-static) case in which the body part cannot recoil. With human_mass given, the free body part recoils and the two-body reduced mass acts: m = mu = (1/m_eff + 1/m_H)^-1.
Source: ISO/TS 15066:2016 Annex A energy model F = v * sqrt(mu * k) (content carried into ISO 10218-2:2025), as reproduced in Kirschner et al. 2022, eqs. 1-2 (arXiv:2203.02706).



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_tripwire_contact_force_accumulation(
    tripwire_force,
    contact_stiffness,
    penetration_velocity,
    loop_latency,
)
Calculate total contact force reached before motor deceleration is commanded following a tripwire breach.
Equation: F_lat = F_trip + k * v * t_lat



physics.robotics.actuation.calc_voltage_droop(current, internal_resistance)
Calculate DC bus voltage droop across internal battery and cable resistance.
Equation: Delta_V = I * R_internal
Source: Ohm’s law, V = I * R (OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, Sec. 9.3).











Name
Type
Description
Default




current
Quantity
Total instantaneous draw current across actuators and compute (e.g. Amperes).
required


internal_resistance
Quantity
Combined battery internal DC resistance and harness resistance (e.g. Ohms).
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Voltage droop in Volts.

Calculate the impulsive torque spike at an actuator seam transition.
When an unblended trajectory transition injects an acceleration discontinuity delta_accel across a discrete boundary, the transmission’s reflected rotor inertia amplifies the required inertial reaction torque at the output joint.

title: engine.solvers.neural
text:
engine.solvers.neural
Neural computation solvers: a dense network’s counts, and one training epoch’s time.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




DenseNetworkModel
Parameters, operations, bytes moved, and memory of a dense network at one batch size.


EpochOverheadModel
One training epoch of a small network: arithmetic and data movement against fixed per-operation overhead.





engine.solvers.neural.DenseNetworkModel()
Parameters, operations, bytes moved, and memory of a dense network at one batch size.
The network is its layer widths. Forward work counts each layer’s matrix multiply (2 B n_in n_out) and its bias add and activation (2 B n_out). Traffic assumes each layer runs as its own kernel: the weights are read once, the input and output cross memory once, and each hidden activation is written and read back. Training keeps every layer’s output for the backward pass and holds a gradient per parameter plus the optimizer’s state; inference keeps only the weights and the largest adjacent pair of activation buffers.
Literature Source: 1. Williams, Waterman, and Patterson (2009), “Roofline” (operations per byte moved). 2. Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986), backpropagation (two products per layer).



engine.solvers.neural.EpochOverheadModel()
One training epoch of a small network: arithmetic and data movement against fixed per-operation overhead.
Work: steps x FLOPs per step at the attainable rate, the roofline’s min(peak, bandwidth x intensity) at the network’s batch intensity. Overhead: steps x operations launched per step x a fixed cost per operation, the framework’s dispatch on the host and dispatch plus a kernel launch on the accelerator. Energy: DRAM energy for the bytes behind one FLOP, against the energy of that FLOP.
Literature Source: 1. Williams, Waterman, and Patterson (2009), “Roofline”. 2. Horowitz (2014), “Computing’s energy problem” (per-op and per-byte energy).

title: engine.solvers.collective
text:
engine.solvers.collective
Collective-communication solvers: AllReduce schedules, hierarchy, AllToAll dispatch, gradient compression, and overlap with the backward pass.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__); kept per-domain so the logic stays reviewable. Every model is an alpha-beta bound: a startup alpha per round or message plus bytes over a stated bandwidth beta, with contention, protocol overhead, and the reduction arithmetic left out.





Name
Description




AllReduceAlgorithmModel
Ring, simple-tree, and parameter-server (star) AllReduce of one buffer at several group sizes.


AllToAllDispatchModel
One mixture-of-experts dispatch AllToAll under uniform routing, and one hot receiver.


CompressionRunModel
Time to a quality target with and without gradient compression, per network.


ErrorFeedbackModel
A compressor that sends each value rounded to a whole unit, with error feedback.


HierarchicalAllReduceModel
Three-phase hierarchical AllReduce against one flat ring across every GPU.


OverlapBudgetModel
Layer-by-layer gradient AllReduce, run after the backward pass or overlapped with it.


RingTraceModel
Every step of a ring AllReduce on one small vector per GPU, the vectors split into N chunks.





engine.solvers.collective.AllReduceAlgorithmModel()
Ring, simple-tree, and parameter-server (star) AllReduce of one buffer at several group sizes.
A ring takes 2(N-1) rounds, each paying one startup alpha and moving one chunk of M/N bytes, so each rank sends 2(N-1)/N times the buffer. The simple tree reduces up and broadcasts down in 2 log2 N rounds, forwarding the whole buffer each round. A single parameter server receives and sends N buffers through one port. The crossover is the buffer at which ring and tree cost the same: the log-aware estimate N alpha beta / log2 N and the exact intersection of the two models.
Literature Source: 1. Patarasuk and Yuan (2009), bandwidth-optimal ring AllReduce. 2. Thakur, Rabenseifner, and Gropp (2005), tree and ring collectives.



engine.solvers.collective.AllToAllDispatchModel()
One mixture-of-experts dispatch AllToAll under uniform routing, and one hot receiver.
Each device holds tokens / N tokens and sends an equal share to every device, keeping its own; a token is hidden_dim values. The concurrent peer streams share one injection port, so dispatch takes at least alpha + sent / beta. On the receive side the bound is the receiving port: a device whose experts draw skew times the uniform remote load takes skew times longer, and every device waiting on its outputs waits with it.



engine.solvers.collective.CompressionRunModel()
Time to a quality target with and without gradient compression, per network.
Each step is compute plus exposed communication, with nothing overlapped. Compression divides only the communication term by ratio and needs 1 + step_penalty times the steps to reach the same quality, so it pays only where communication is a large share of the step.



engine.solvers.collective.ErrorFeedbackModel()
A compressor that sends each value rounded to a whole unit, with error feedback.
Without a residual, every value below half a unit is lost. With error feedback the worker adds the carried residual e_t to the gradient, sends the rounded v_t, and keeps e_{t+1} = g_t + e_t - v_t; what is sent plus the last residual equals the true sum at every step.
Literature Source: Karimireddy et al. (2019), “Error Feedback Fixes SignSGD”.



engine.solvers.collective.HierarchicalAllReduceModel()
Three-phase hierarchical AllReduce against one flat ring across every GPU.
Inside each node of G GPUs a ReduceScatter over the fast link leaves each GPU 1/G of the node’s partial sum, sending (G-1)/G of the buffer. GPUs in the same position on every node then ring-AllReduce their M/G shard across nodes, one ring per GPU position, each on its own port; an AllGather inside the node rebuilds the sum. The in-node phases carry no startup term here. The flat ring runs at the slowest edge, the inter-node port; flat_bound_time is its large-N byte bound 2M/beta.
Literature Source: Sergeev and Del Balso (2018); NCCL hierarchical rings.



engine.solvers.collective.OverlapBudgetModel()
Layer-by-layer gradient AllReduce, run after the backward pass or overlapped with it.
Each of L equal layers yields its gradient, reduced in fixed-size buckets that each take time_per_bucket. Sequentially, the step pays the whole backward pass and then every reduction. Overlapped, a layer’s reduction starts when its backward finishes; when a reduction outlasts the next layer’s backward, the excess accumulates, and the last reduction has no compute left to hide under.



engine.solvers.collective.RingTraceModel()
Every step of a ring AllReduce on one small vector per GPU, the vectors split into N chunks.
In ReduceScatter step s, GPU i sends chunk (i - s) mod N to GPU i + 1, which adds it into its own copy; after N - 1 steps GPU i owns the fully reduced chunk (i + 1) mod N. In AllGather step s (from 1), GPU i forwards chunk (i - s + 2) mod N, the one it completed or received most recently, so after N - 1 more steps every GPU holds every chunk.

title: engine.solvers.performance
text:
engine.solvers.performance
Single-node, network-roofline, efficiency, and inverse-design solvers.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__); kept per-domain so the logic stays reviewable.





Name
Description




AmdahlModel
Amdahl’s law for a sequential request path: one stage made speedup


DecodeBoundModel
Weight-streaming bound on one autoregressive decode step.


EfficiencyModel
Models the gap between peak and achieved FLOPS (Wall 3: Software Efficiency).


IronLawModel
The iron law of ML systems on one machine, in its two forms.


NetworkRooflineModel
Analyzes the Distributed Performance Bounds (The Network Wall).


SensitivitySolver
Identifies the binding constraint via numerical sensitivity analysis (Wall 21).


SingleNodeModel
Resolves single-node hardware Roofline bounds and feasibility.


SynthesisSolver
Given an SLA, synthesizes the required hardware specs (Wall 22: Inverse Solve).





engine.solvers.performance.AmdahlModel()
Amdahl’s law for a sequential request path: one stage made speedup times faster, the others untouched. The untouched time caps the overall speedup at total / untouched, however fast the stage becomes.



engine.solvers.performance.DecodeBoundModel()
Weight-streaming bound on one autoregressive decode step.
At small batch every new token multiplies every weight once and must read every weight from memory, so a decode step needs 2P FLOPs per request and P x bytes_per_param of weight traffic. Comparing the two times on one device (one accelerator-equivalent path, capacity assumed) shows which resource binds; the weight-only arithmetic intensity places the step on the roofline. KV-cache reads and launch overhead are excluded (see ServingModel for those).
Literature Source: 1. Williams, Waterman, and Patterson (2009), “Roofline.” 2. Kaplan et al. (2020), the 2P forward-FLOP rule.



engine.solvers.performance.EfficiencyModel()
Models the gap between peak and achieved FLOPS (Wall 3: Software Efficiency).
This model quantifies the software efficiency of a workload — the fraction of peak hardware FLOPS that the software stack actually converts into useful computation. It decomposes Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) by workload type, accounting for kernel fusion efficiency, SM occupancy, and memory access patterns.
Literature Source: 1. Chowdhery et al. (2022), “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” (First systematic MFU reporting for large Transformers.) 2. Dao et al. (2022), “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.” (FlashAttention MFU improvement.) 3. NVIDIA (2023), “Hopper Architecture Tuning Guide.” (SM Occupancy model.)





Name
Description




solve
Estimates achievable MFU and FLOPS for a given workload type.





engine.solvers.performance.EfficiencyModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    workload_type='ffn',
    use_flash_attention=False,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Estimates achievable MFU and FLOPS for a given workload type.











Name
Type
Description
Default

Workload
The model architecture to simulate.
required


hardware
HardwareNode
The target hardware node.
required


workload_type
str
The dominant kernel type (‘attention’, ‘ffn’, ‘conv’).

Type
Description





EfficiencyResult

engine.solvers.performance.IronLawModel()
The iron law of ML systems on one machine, in its two forms.
Sequential: T = memory + compute + overhead, the safe estimate when the stages run one after another. Overlapped: T >= max(memory, compute) + overhead, the best case when loading and computing overlap perfectly. An upgrade divides the memory term by memory_speedup (more bandwidth or fewer bytes) and the compute term by compute_speedup; the overhead stays, which is why the sum falls by less than the upgrade.



engine.solvers.performance.NetworkRooflineModel()
Analyzes the Distributed Performance Bounds (The Network Wall).
This model elevates the single-node Roofline analysis to the fleet scale. It calculates the Communication Intensity (CI) of a workload and identifies if the fleet is Compute-Bound (Wall 1) or Network-Bound (Wall 2).
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” (Theoretical basis) 2. Ghose et al. (2019), “A Survey of Communication-Efficient Distributed Training.”





Name
Description




solve
Solve for the fleet-scale performance bound (network roofline).





engine.solvers.performance.NetworkRooflineModel.solve(
    model,
    fleet,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Solve for the fleet-scale performance bound (network roofline).
Models one data-parallel training step as two independent ceilings — compute and gradient synchronization — and takes the slower as the binding latency (no overlap is assumed, so this is a lower-bound model). The conventions used:

communication intensity CI = training_ops / sync_bytes [FLOP/byte], with training_ops = 6 * P FLOPs per sample (Kaplan/Chinchilla forward+backward convention) and sync_bytes = 2 * P * bytes_per_param (ring all-reduce moves roughly 2x the gradient volume);
network ridge = fleet_peak_FLOPS / bisection_BW [FLOP/byte], the CI above which the fleet is compute-bound.

Type
Description
Default

required

engine.solvers.performance.SensitivitySolver()
Identifies the binding constraint via numerical sensitivity analysis (Wall 21).
This solver computes numerical partial derivatives of performance with respect to hardware parameters to identify the ‘binding constraint.’
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” 2. Ofenbeck et al. (2014), “Applying the Roofline Model.”





Name
Description




solve
Solve for parameter sensitivities and identify the binding constraint.





engine.solvers.performance.SensitivitySolver.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    precision='fp16',
    perturbation_pct=10.0,
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Solve for parameter sensitivities and identify the binding constraint.
Numerically perturbs each hardware parameter (peak FLOPS, memory bandwidth, memory capacity) by perturbation_pct and re-solves the single-node Roofline. Each sensitivity is the normalized latency response (T_perturbed - T_base) / T_base (dimensionless; negative means the upgrade helps). The binding constraint is the parameter with the largest absolute sensitivity — the resource whose improvement moves latency the most.

Type

Default

required

required

If the baseline does not fit in memory, feasible is False, binding_constraint is "memory_capacity", and constraint_trace carries the Memory Wall failure: the offload path pins latency, so the sensitivities (typically all zero) do not rank hardware levers.

Resolves single-node hardware Roofline bounds and feasibility.
This model handles the ‘Iron Law’ of machine learning systems, calculating whether a model fits in memory and predicting its throughput based on arithmetic intensity.

engine.solvers.performance.SynthesisSolver()
Given an SLA, synthesizes the required hardware specs (Wall 22: Inverse Solve).
This solver inverts the Roofline model to derive minimum hardware specifications required to meet a target latency SLA.
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” 2. Jouppi et al. (2017), “In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU.”





Name
Description




solve
Synthesize minimum hardware requirements from a latency SLA.





engine.solvers.performance.SynthesisSolver.solve(
    model,
    target_latency,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Synthesize minimum hardware requirements from a latency SLA.
Inverts the Roofline model: instead of asking “how fast does this hardware run the model?”, asks “what hardware would run the model in target_latency?”. Assumes a single full pass that streams every weight once (batch size 1, no weight reuse), so:

required_bw = weight_bytes / T_target [GB/s] — the bandwidth needed if the workload is memory-bound;
required_flops = total_ops / (T_target * efficiency) [TFLOP/s] — the compute rate needed if it is compute-bound;
compute_memory_ratio = required_flops / required_bw [FLOP/byte] — the hardware balance point a matching part should sit near.

Type
Description
Default

Workload
The workload to serve; sets weight bytes and operation count.
required

required

'fp16'

float

0.5

engine.solvers.performance.AmdahlModel()
Amdahl’s law for a sequential request path: one stage made speedup times faster, the others untouched. The untouched time caps the overall speedup at total / untouched, however fast the stage becomes.



engine.solvers.performance.DecodeBoundModel()
Weight-streaming bound on one autoregressive decode step.
At small batch every new token multiplies every weight once and must read every weight from memory, so a decode step needs 2P FLOPs per request and P x bytes_per_param of weight traffic. Comparing the two times on one device (one accelerator-equivalent path, capacity assumed) shows which resource binds; the weight-only arithmetic intensity places the step on the roofline. KV-cache reads and launch overhead are excluded (see ServingModel for those).
Literature Source: 1. Williams, Waterman, and Patterson (2009), “Roofline.” 2. Kaplan et al. (2020), the 2P forward-FLOP rule.



engine.solvers.performance.EfficiencyModel()
Models the gap between peak and achieved FLOPS (Wall 3: Software Efficiency).
This model quantifies the software efficiency of a workload — the fraction of peak hardware FLOPS that the software stack actually converts into useful computation. It decomposes Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) by workload type, accounting for kernel fusion efficiency, SM occupancy, and memory access patterns.
Literature Source: 1. Chowdhery et al. (2022), “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” (First systematic MFU reporting for large Transformers.) 2. Dao et al. (2022), “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.” (FlashAttention MFU improvement.) 3. NVIDIA (2023), “Hopper Architecture Tuning Guide.” (SM Occupancy model.)

Description

engine.solvers.performance.IronLawModel()
The iron law of ML systems on one machine, in its two forms.
Sequential: T = memory + compute + overhead, the safe estimate when the stages run one after another. Overlapped: T >= max(memory, compute) + overhead, the best case when loading and computing overlap perfectly. An upgrade divides the memory term by memory_speedup (more bandwidth or fewer bytes) and the compute term by compute_speedup; the overhead stays, which is why the sum falls by less than the upgrade.



engine.solvers.performance.NetworkRooflineModel()
Analyzes the Distributed Performance Bounds (The Network Wall).
This model elevates the single-node Roofline analysis to the fleet scale. It calculates the Communication Intensity (CI) of a workload and identifies if the fleet is Compute-Bound (Wall 1) or Network-Bound (Wall 2).
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” (Theoretical basis) 2. Ghose et al. (2019), “A Survey of Communication-Efficient Distributed Training.”





Name
Description




solve
Solve for the fleet-scale performance bound (network roofline).





engine.solvers.performance.NetworkRooflineModel.solve(
    model,
    fleet,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Solve for the fleet-scale performance bound (network roofline).
Models one data-parallel training step as two independent ceilings — compute and gradient synchronization — and takes the slower as the binding latency (no overlap is assumed, so this is a lower-bound model). The conventions used:

communication intensity CI = training_ops / sync_bytes [FLOP/byte], with training_ops = 6 * P FLOPs per sample (Kaplan/Chinchilla forward+backward convention) and sync_bytes = 2 * P * bytes_per_param (ring all-reduce moves roughly 2x the gradient volume);
network ridge = fleet_peak_FLOPS / bisection_BW [FLOP/byte], the CI above which the fleet is compute-bound.

engine.solvers.performance.SensitivitySolver()
Identifies the binding constraint via numerical sensitivity analysis (Wall 21).
This solver computes numerical partial derivatives of performance with respect to hardware parameters to identify the ‘binding constraint.’
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” 2. Ofenbeck et al. (2014), “Applying the Roofline Model.”





Name
Description




solve
Solve for parameter sensitivities and identify the binding constraint.





engine.solvers.performance.SensitivitySolver.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    precision='fp16',
    perturbation_pct=10.0,
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Solve for parameter sensitivities and identify the binding constraint.
Numerically perturbs each hardware parameter (peak FLOPS, memory bandwidth, memory capacity) by perturbation_pct and re-solves the single-node Roofline. Each sensitivity is the normalized latency response (T_perturbed - T_base) / T_base (dimensionless; negative means the upgrade helps). The binding constraint is the parameter with the largest absolute sensitivity — the resource whose improvement moves latency the most.

engine.solvers.performance.SynthesisSolver()
Given an SLA, synthesizes the required hardware specs (Wall 22: Inverse Solve).
This solver inverts the Roofline model to derive minimum hardware specifications required to meet a target latency SLA.
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” 2. Jouppi et al. (2017), “In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU.”





Name
Description




solve
Synthesize minimum hardware requirements from a latency SLA.





engine.solvers.performance.SynthesisSolver.solve(
    model,
    target_latency,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Synthesize minimum hardware requirements from a latency SLA.
Inverts the Roofline model: instead of asking “how fast does this hardware run the model?”, asks “what hardware would run the model in target_latency?”. Assumes a single full pass that streams every weight once (batch size 1, no weight reuse), so:

required_bw = weight_bytes / T_target [GB/s] — the bandwidth needed if the workload is memory-bound;
required_flops = total_ops / (T_target * efficiency) [TFLOP/s] — the compute rate needed if it is compute-bound;
compute_memory_ratio = required_flops / required_bw [FLOP/byte] — the hardware balance point a matching part should sit near.

title: engine.solvers.grounding
text:
engine.solvers.grounding
Grounded-intent solvers: how long a learned target stays true, and the lease that bounds it.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). The equations live in physics.robotics (the evidence horizons, the stopping distance) and physics.statistics (the conformal rank, the chi-square quantile); these models compose them for one stated target, arm, and aisle, so a chapter, a slide deck, and a lab read the same arithmetic (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




ConfidenceRegionModel
A Gaussian estimate’s confidence region compared with a tolerance, axis by axis.


DynamicReachModel
The transit lower bound: no trajectory covers d faster than d / v_max.


ForwardOccupancyModel
Growth term of a person’s forward occupancy set, v_h dt, against an aisle.


IntentCadenceModel
A moving target’s evidence horizons against a slow proposer’s cadence.


IntentLeaseExpiryModel
The intent lease’s expiry: the earliest of evidence, host silence, and the stopping deadline.


ReferentSetModel
Open-vocabulary candidates normalized and screened by a split-conformal threshold.





engine.solvers.grounding.ConfidenceRegionModel()
A Gaussian estimate’s confidence region compared with a tolerance, axis by axis.
The region holding probability coverage has principal semi-axes r sigma_i, where r^2 is the chi-square quantile for one degree of freedom per axis.



engine.solvers.grounding.DynamicReachModel()
The transit lower bound: no trajectory covers d faster than d / v_max.
A terminal move is admissible only if that floor fits the evidence window; otherwise the reach is staged on at least ceil(floor / window) fresh captures. The reach inside a window at the speed ceiling is v_max T.



engine.solvers.grounding.ForwardOccupancyModel()
Growth term of a person’s forward occupancy set, v_h dt, against an aisle.
Over a screening horizon dt the set centered on the last measurement grows by v_h dt (before the body envelope and tracking error); past w / v_h one person’s growth term alone spans an aisle of width w.



engine.solvers.grounding.IntentCadenceModel()
A moving target’s evidence horizons against a slow proposer’s cadence.
Untracked, the target leaves its tolerance after (r_tol - e_0) / v; tracked, only residual slip remains, sqrt(2 (r_tol - e_0) / a_slip). A proposer that renews the target from its own inference computes it from a frame captured one inference earlier and holds it one period, so the oldest evidence behind a model-only target is period + inference, and the drift it can follow is the margin over that age. A stall of T leaves the target e_0 + v T (untracked) or e_0 + a_slip T^2 / 2 (tracked) off; a stop begins one tick, one bus cycle, and one brake onset after expiry.



engine.solvers.grounding.IntentLeaseExpiryModel()
The intent lease’s expiry: the earliest of evidence, host silence, and the stopping deadline.
The credible deceleration is the arm’s worst-case stop averaged over a stop from its velocity limit; at the admitted speed ceiling the stop takes v t_onset + v^2 / (2 a), and the stopping deadline is the time the remaining clearance allows at that speed. With all three countdowns started together, the lease expires at the minimum.



engine.solvers.grounding.ReferentSetModel()
Open-vocabulary candidates normalized and screened by a split-conformal threshold.
Raw per-box scores are normalized over the retained candidates; the set keeps every candidate whose normalized score is at least 1 - qhat, where qhat is the calibration score at rank ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha)). A set of any size other than one is refused.

title: physics.networking
text:
physics.networking
Network latency and distance physics.





Name
Description




calc_great_circle_distance
Great-circle distance between two points on a spherical Earth (haversine).


calc_network_latency_ms
Physical round-trip latency floor for a fiber link.





physics.networking.calc_great_circle_distance(
    lat1_deg,
    lon1_deg,
    lat2_deg,
    lon2_deg,
)
Great-circle distance between two points on a spherical Earth (haversine).
d = 2 R asin(sqrt(sin^2(dphi/2) + cos(phi1) cos(phi2) sin^2(dlambda/2))) with R the Earth’s mean radius. Latitudes and longitudes are in degrees. Real fiber routes are longer than the great circle, so a propagation floor computed from this distance is a lower bound.





Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Distance in kilometers.







physics.networking.calc_network_latency_ms(distance_km)
Physical round-trip latency floor for a fiber link.
Models only signal propagation: RTT = 2 * distance / v_fiber, where v_fiber is the speed of light in optical fiber (refractive index ~1.5 gives ~200,000 km/s, the standard teaching value; see SPEED_OF_LIGHT_FIBER_KM_S). Real links add switching, queueing, and serialization delay on top, so this is a lower bound.











Name
Type
Description
Default




distance_km
Quantity or float
One-way fiber distance; bare floats are interpreted as kilometers.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Round-trip propagation latency in milliseconds (~1 ms per 100 km of one-way distance).

title: engine.solvers.perception
text:
engine.solvers.perception
Sensor-perception solvers: capture timing, observation age, and measured error scales (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). The equations live in physics/robotics/sensing.py, physics/robotics/control.py, and physics/statistics.py; these models compose them for one stated camera, lidar, stereo rig, or loop, so a chapter, a slide deck, and a lab read the same arithmetic.





Name
Description




ClockConversionModel
A free-running clock’s drift between syncs, and the dispatch limit a conversion bound sets.


ConformalInsetModel
The calibration rank behind a split-conformal bound on residuals.


DelayPhaseMarginModel
The delay a loop’s phase margin can absorb, and the share a stated delay spends.


LidarSweepAgeModel
One spinning-lidar sweep’s motion distortion, and a forward sector’s age.


ObservationAgeModel
A camera observation’s age, stage by stage, from the exposure midpoint to dispatch.


RollingShutterSkewModel
Row timing and skew of a rolling-shutter camera on a moving base.


StereoDepthErrorModel
One-sigma stereo depth error against range, and where it spends each clearance.


ThermalExpansionModel
Length change of a uniformly heated member, alpha L dT.


TimingAttitudeErrorModel
Position errors from a timing error and an angle error, for a target at distance.


VisibilityRangeModel
Range at which fog with extinction beta drops a black target’s contrast to the threshold (Koschmieder).





engine.solvers.perception.ClockConversionModel()
A free-running clock’s drift between syncs, and the dispatch limit a conversion bound sets.
Drift accumulates as rate x interval; a producer refuses to dispatch an observation older than its budgeted age plus the conversion bound, whose own uncertainty is travel at speed.



engine.solvers.perception.ConformalInsetModel()
The calibration rank behind a split-conformal bound on residuals.
The bound is the ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha))-th smallest of n residuals, which exists only from n = ceil((1 - alpha) / alpha).



engine.solvers.perception.DelayPhaseMarginModel()
The delay a loop’s phase margin can absorb, and the share a stated delay spends.
A pure delay removes omega_c tau of phase at crossover, so the margin is gone at tau_max = PM / omega_c (calc_delay_phase_margin_ceiling).



engine.solvers.perception.LidarSweepAgeModel()
One spinning-lidar sweep’s motion distortion, and a forward sector’s age.
A sweep lasts one rotation, during which the base travels v T and turns omega T. A sector of width w at distance d is swept in T phi / 360 deg; streaming it as it arrives ages it by that sector time plus the sensor’s data latency and its time-sync bound, waiting for the full sweep by the whole rotation plus the same two terms.



engine.solvers.perception.ObservationAgeModel()
A camera observation’s age, stage by stage, from the exposure midpoint to dispatch.
The capture epoch is the exposure midpoint, so the age starts at half the exposure, then adds readout, link transport, DMA and queueing, the image signal processor, the vision backbone, and dispatch. A stamp taken at DMA completion (arrival) misdates the frame by the age up to that stage; a trigger stamp at exposure start misdates it by half the exposure. Batching batch_frames successive frames holds the oldest n - 1 frame periods. Every interval is also priced as travel at speed.



engine.solvers.perception.RollingShutterSkewModel()
Row timing and skew of a rolling-shutter camera on a moving base.
Rows are read one after another over the readout time, so the last row sees the scene from v t_readout farther along, and a turn at omega shifts a target at range d sideways by d omega t_readout. Each row also blurs over its own exposure, v t_exp.



engine.solvers.perception.StereoDepthErrorModel()
One-sigma stereo depth error against range, and where it spends each clearance.
sigma_z = z^2 sigma_d / (f b) grows with squared range; the range at which one sigma equals a clearance C is sqrt(C f b / sigma_d). Adding one sigma to a clearance kept along the viewing ray is the shortcut inset; an unmodeled baseline change db biases depth by z db / b.



engine.solvers.perception.ThermalExpansionModel()
Length change of a uniformly heated member, alpha L dT.



engine.solvers.perception.TimingAttitudeErrorModel()
Position errors from a timing error and an angle error, for a target at distance.
A timestamp off by dt places the target v dt along the travel and, while turning at omega, misorients the view by omega dt, which at range is d omega dt sideways. An angle error theta moves the target d theta sideways (calc_lever_arm_error, small angle).



engine.solvers.perception.VisibilityRangeModel()
Range at which fog with extinction beta drops a black target’s contrast to the threshold (Koschmieder).

Length change of a uniformly heated member, alpha L dT.



engine.solvers.perception.TimingAttitudeErrorModel()
Position errors from a timing error and an angle error, for a target at distance.
A timestamp off by dt places the target v dt along the travel and, while turning at omega, misorients the view by omega dt, which at range is d omega dt sideways. An angle error theta moves the target d theta sideways (calc_lever_arm_error, small angle).



engine.solvers.perception.VisibilityRangeModel()
Range at which fog with extinction beta drops a black target’s contrast to the threshold (Koschmieder).

title: engine.engine.Engine
text:
engine.engine.Engine()
The core analytical engine for single-node Roofline performance modeling.
Maps a (Workload, HardwareNode) pair to a PerformanceProfile by applying the Roofline model: the workload is “lowered” into a hardware-agnostic ComputationGraph, then bounded by the hardware’s compute ceiling and memory bandwidth ceiling.


Every solver in mlsysim ultimately decomposes into this equation:
Time = FLOPs / (N × Peak_FLOPS × MFU × η_scaling × Goodput)
where N is device count, MFU is Model FLOPs Utilization, η_scaling is scaling efficiency (communication overhead), and Goodput accounts for failures and checkpointing. This engine evaluates the single-node case (N=1, η_scaling=1, Goodput=1); DistributedModel handles the fleet case.
Source: Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Floating-Point Programs and Multicore Architectures.”

Description

Sweeps over hardware, batch sizes, and precisions to produce a list of PerformanceProfiles.

    precision='fp16',

title: physics.tool_calls
text:
physics.tool_calls
Tool calling: the equations behind a mediated call, its retry, and its catalog.
Pure arithmetic (added 2026-10-20). A call whose request or reply may be lost times out with one probability and, under one blind retry, executes twice with another; a model that polls a pending job makes one status call per interval before completion; a tool catalog staged on every call costs its descriptors, and selection pays once the descriptors it leaves out exceed its own overhead; a shared protocol turns pairwise adapters into one per party. The solvers in engine/solvers/tool_calls.py compose these.





Name
Description




calc_blind_retry_duplicate_probability
Probability that one blind retry after a timeout executes the effect a second time.


calc_bulkhead_admission
One burst of blocking calls against a capped dependency, before any completes.


calc_integration_adapters
Adapters needed to connect every host to every service: pairwise, and through one protocol.


calc_jitter_expected_arrivals
Expected retries inside a fixed window when each draws its arrival uniformly over the jitter span.


calc_layered_retry_attempts
Requests one failing logical operation sends when each layer retries on its own allowance.


calc_pending_polls
Status checks that find a job still pending.


calc_selection_break_even
Unused descriptors selection must leave out before it saves context.


calc_timeout_probability
Probability that one attempt times out when request and reply are lost independently.





physics.tool_calls.calc_blind_retry_duplicate_probability(
    request_loss,
    reply_loss,
)
Probability that one blind retry after a timeout executes the effect a second time.
The original request is delivered, its reply is lost, and the retry is delivered: Pr(dup) = (1 - q) r (1 - q). Losing the request alone leaves a harmless timeout; lost messages are taken never to arrive later.



physics.tool_calls.calc_bulkhead_admission(
    arrivals,
    workers,
    worker_cap,
    queue_cap,
)
One burst of blocking calls against a capped dependency, before any completes.
Up to worker_cap calls occupy workers, up to queue_cap wait without occupying one, and the rest are rejected at admission. Returns (occupied, queued, rejected, free_workers); without a cap, pass worker_cap = workers and queue_cap = 0.



physics.tool_calls.calc_integration_adapters(hosts, services)
Adapters needed to connect every host to every service: pairwise, and through one protocol.
Pairwise integration needs one adapter per pair (N x M); a shared protocol needs one client per host and one server per service (N + M).



physics.tool_calls.calc_jitter_expected_arrivals(retries, window, jitter_span)
Expected retries inside a fixed window when each draws its arrival uniformly over the jitter span.
E[n] = N w / J
An expectation only: the realized count in any one window can reach N.



physics.tool_calls.calc_layered_retry_attempts(attempts_per_layer, layers)
Requests one failing logical operation sends when each layer retries on its own allowance.
N = a^L
Every attempt of a layer drives a full set of attempts in the layer below, so independent allowances multiply; one owner with the same allowance sends a.



physics.tool_calls.calc_pending_polls(job_duration, poll_interval)
Status checks that find a job still pending.
Checks start one interval after dispatch and stop at completion; a check that lands exactly at completion already sees the result, so the pending checks are ceil(T / dt) - 1.



physics.tool_calls.calc_selection_break_even(
    selection_overhead,
    descriptor_tokens,
)
Unused descriptors selection must leave out before it saves context.
(N_reg - N_sel) s_desc > s_over   =>   break-even at s_over / s_desc



physics.tool_calls.calc_timeout_probability(request_loss, reply_loss)
Probability that one attempt times out when request and reply are lost independently.
Pr(timeout) = 1 - (1 - q)(1 - r)

title: API Reference
text: This reference is generated from the docstrings in the mlsysim package on every build, so it always matches the installed version. To browse the contents of a registry (every GPU, model, or fleet), use the Zoo.

title: API Reference
text:
Engine and scenarios
Entry points that turn a workload and a system into an estimate.



engine.engine.Engine
The core analytical engine for single-node Roofline performance modeling.


engine.scenarios.Scenario
Concrete executable case: a workload on a system with constraints.


engine.dse.DSE
Declarative Design Space Exploration (DSE) Engine.


engine.calibration
Parameters for analytical solvers and the roofline engine.

title: API Reference
text:
Workloads and systems
Typed objects that describe what runs and what it runs on.



models.types.Workload
Layer A (Workload Demand): Base representation of an ML model or task.


models.types.TransformerWorkload
Workload representation of an autoregressive Transformer (e.g., LLMs).


models.types.SparseTransformerWorkload
Workload representation of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformer.


models.types.CNNWorkload
Workload representation of a Convolutional Neural Network (e.g., Vision).


hardware.HardwareNode
Layer B (Hardware Supply): Represents a complete hardware accelerator.


systems.types.Node
Represents a physical server chassis containing multiple accelerators.


systems.types.Fleet
Layer D (Systems/Topology): The complete distributed cluster environment.

Registries
Vetted, sourced catalogs of hardware, models, fleets, and physical systems. Browse their contents in the Zoo.

Registry namespace for Hardware.

Registry namespace for Models.

Registry namespace for Systems.

Registry namespace for Infrastructure.

Deployment paradigms with latency, memory, and power envelopes.

Authoritative registry of embodied AI platforms, cyber-physical machines, and robotic embodiments.

Vetted cyber-physical machine platform (quadruped, humanoid, manipulator, drone, AMR, AV).


sensors.Sensors
Authoritative registry of robotics perception sensors.


sensors.Sensor
Base sensor type for cyber-physical perception systems.

Authoritative registry of robotic actuators and joint transmissions.


actuators.ActuatorJoint
Vetted robotic joint actuator (motor + transmission + driver).

Authoritative registry of agent system profiles and execution harnesses.

Vetted agent system profile (SWE-bench coding, deliberation tree search, multi-agent fleet, streaming).


agents.AgentWorkload
Recurring agent workload profile: task-level scenario inputs for one archetype.

title: API Reference
text:
Solvers
Analytical models, solvers, and optimizers. Import them from mlsysim.solvers.



solvers.SingleNodeModel
Resolves single-node hardware Roofline bounds and feasibility.


solvers.NetworkRooflineModel
Analyzes the Distributed Performance Bounds (The Network Wall).


solvers.EfficiencyModel
Models the gap between peak and achieved FLOPS (Wall 3: Software Efficiency).


solvers.ForwardModel
Forward-evaluating mechanistic engine (Y = f(X)).


solvers.ServingModel
Analyzes the two-phase LLM serving lifecycle: Pre-fill vs. Decoding.


solvers.TrainingMemoryModel
Decomposes per-accelerator training memory into teachable components.


solvers.ServingCapacityModel
Sizes an LLM serving deployment from a QPS and tail-latency target.


solvers.ContinuousBatchingModel
Compares static KV reservation with PagedAttention under continuous batching.


solvers.WeightStreamingModel
Analyzes Wafer-Scale inference (e.g., Cerebras CS-3) using Weight Streaming.


solvers.TailLatencyModel
Analyzes queueing delays and P99 tail latency for deployed inference models.


solvers.DataModel
Analyzes the ‘Data Wall’ — the throughput bottleneck between storage and compute.


solvers.TransformationModel
Quantifies the CPU preprocessing bottleneck (Wall 9: Transformation).


solvers.TopologyModel
Models bisection bandwidth for different network topologies (Wall 10).


solvers.ScalingModel
Analyzes the ‘Scaling Physics’ of model training (Chinchilla Laws).


solvers.InferenceScalingModel
Models inference-time compute scaling (Wall 12: Reasoning/CoT Cost).


solvers.CompressionModel
Analyzes model compression trade-offs (Accuracy vs. Efficiency).


solvers.DistributedModel
Resolves fleet-wide communication, synchronization, and pipelining constraints.


solvers.MoERoutingModel
Models first-order MoE routing imbalance and expert-parallel all-to-all cost.


solvers.ReliabilityModel
Calculates Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and optimal checkpointing intervals.


solvers.OrchestrationModel
Analyzes Cluster Orchestration and Queueing (Little’s Law).


solvers.EconomicsModel
Calculates Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) including Capex and Opex.


solvers.SustainabilityModel
Calculates Datacenter-scale Sustainability metrics.


solvers.CheckpointModel
Analyzes the storage constraints and I/O burst penalties of saving model states.


solvers.ResponsibleEngineeringModel
Models the computational cost of responsible AI practices (Wall 20: Safety).


solvers.SensitivitySolver
Identifies the binding constraint via numerical sensitivity analysis (Wall 21).


solvers.SynthesisSolver
Given an SLA, synthesizes the required hardware specs (Wall 22: Inverse Solve).


solvers.ParallelismOptimizer
Searches for the optimal 3D/4D parallelism split (DP, TP, PP, EP).


solvers.BatchingOptimizer
Finds the maximum batch size that satisfies a P99 latency SLA.


solvers.PlacementOptimizer
Finds the datacenter region that minimizes TCO plus a carbon tax.


solvers.FailureIntervalModel
Interval between failures across identical, independent components.


solvers.SeriesFailureModel
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.


solvers.ZeroFailureModel
Upper bound on the per-trial failure rate after a failure-free campaign.


solvers.FailureTriageModel
Failures that counterfactual probes remove below the weights, and the price of training on all of them.


solvers.ErrorFeedbackModel
A compressor that sends each value rounded to a whole unit, with error feedback.


solvers.TimingAttitudeErrorModel
Position errors from a timing error and an angle error, for a target at distance.


solvers.StereoDepthErrorModel
One-sigma stereo depth error against range, and where it spends each clearance.

title: engine.solvers.sustainability
text:
engine.solvers.sustainability
Sustainability solvers: facility power, run footprints, carbon placement, and demand.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__); kept per-domain so the logic stays reviewable. Added 2026-10-20.
Every model here works on a rated-power (TDP) basis unless a caller passes a measured power: these are upper-bound planning accounts, not meter readings. The power chain is accelerator power, times the rack’s IT-to-accelerator ratio (hosts, switches, conversion inside the IT boundary), times PUE (facility overhead, applied once at the facility boundary). Carbon is facility energy times a grid carbon intensity.





Name
Description




CarbonPricedPlacementModel
Placement of one run among regions with and without a carbon price.


CascadeEnergyModel
Edge-first cascade: every input runs a small edge model; a fraction


DataMovementEnergyModel
Modeled dynamic energy of using one weight: arithmetic against moving it.


DemandReboundModel
Fleet energy after a per-unit efficiency change and a volume change: e x v.


DevelopmentSweepModel
Final-run equivalents a development sweep consumes: candidates x relative cost.


DutyCycledPowerModel
Average power of stages each active a fraction of the time, against a reference always-on power.


EmbodiedPaybackModel
Time for a more efficient replacement to repay its manufacturing carbon.


FacilityPowerModel
The power chain from accelerators to the facility meter.


GridPlacementModel
One facility energy placed on several grids, optionally after an energy cut.


PueRetrofitModel
Energy and cost saved by lowering PUE under a fixed IT load over a period.


RepeatedWorkEnergyModel
Accelerator energy repeated when a fleet rolls back by each named interval.


RunFootprintModel
One training run’s energy, operational carbon, embodied carbon, and water.


ServiceLifeExtensionModel
Cut in embodied carbon charged per year when a service life grows: 1 - short / long.


ServingCrossoverModel
Days of serving at a request volume whose cumulative energy equals a one-time (training) energy.


WaterUseModel
Water consumed for an IT energy at a water usage effectiveness: W = E_IT x WUE.





engine.solvers.sustainability.CarbonPricedPlacementModel()
Placement of one run among regions with and without a carbon price.
The run’s duration is the days the fleet needs to spend it_energy at mfu (EconomicsModel’s IT energy per day is region-independent); the PlacementOptimizer then ranks regions by total cost, once with the carbon price and once without.



engine.solvers.sustainability.CascadeEnergyModel()
Edge-first cascade: every input runs a small edge model; a fraction escalation is sent (transmit) to a large cloud model. Mean energy per input E_edge + p (E_tx + E_cloud) against always sending to the cloud.



engine.solvers.sustainability.DataMovementEnergyModel()
Modeled dynamic energy of using one weight: arithmetic against moving it.
A weight of bytes_per_param read once for flops_per_param FLOPs costs bytes x E_byte to move and FLOPs x E_flop to compute. The energy crossover E_byte / E_flop is the arithmetic intensity at which the two match; operand_bytes prices one operand fetch against one FLOP.



engine.solvers.sustainability.DemandReboundModel()
Fleet energy after a per-unit efficiency change and a volume change: e x v.



engine.solvers.sustainability.DevelopmentSweepModel()
Final-run equivalents a development sweep consumes: candidates x relative cost.



engine.solvers.sustainability.DutyCycledPowerModel()
Average power of stages each active a fraction of the time, against a reference always-on power.



engine.solvers.sustainability.EmbodiedPaybackModel()
Time for a more efficient replacement to repay its manufacturing carbon.
The replacement does the old device’s work with saved_fraction less energy, running continuously at the old device’s power; the carbon it avoids per day is the saved energy times the grid intensity, and payback is the embodied carbon divided by that daily saving.



engine.solvers.sustainability.FacilityPowerModel()
The power chain from accelerators to the facility meter.
Accelerator power is devices x device_power; the IT load multiplies it by the rack’s IT-to-accelerator ratio (hosts, switches, network adapters, and conversion losses inside the IT boundary); the facility draws the IT load times PUE. The facility figure is what the grid connection must supply at every instant.



engine.solvers.sustainability.GridPlacementModel()
One facility energy placed on several grids, optionally after an energy cut.
Emissions are E x CI per grid; energy_cut is a fractional energy reduction applied before the grid factor (an algorithmic saving), so a placement and an efficiency gain can be compared at one energy.



engine.solvers.sustainability.PueRetrofitModel()
Energy and cost saved by lowering PUE under a fixed IT load over a period.



engine.solvers.sustainability.RepeatedWorkEnergyModel()
Accelerator energy repeated when a fleet rolls back by each named interval.



engine.solvers.sustainability.RunFootprintModel()
One training run’s energy, operational carbon, embodied carbon, and water.
Energy follows the power chain over the run’s device-hours: accelerator energy device_hours x device_power, IT energy times the rack ratio, facility energy times PUE. Operational carbon applies each named grid’s intensity to facility energy. Embodied carbon is devices x embodied_per_device at manufacture; the run is charged its time share, device_hours x embodied_per_device / service_life. Water applies each WUE to IT energy (WUE’s denominator is IT energy).



engine.solvers.sustainability.ServiceLifeExtensionModel()
Cut in embodied carbon charged per year when a service life grows: 1 - short / long.



engine.solvers.sustainability.ServingCrossoverModel()
Days of serving at a request volume whose cumulative energy equals a one-time (training) energy.



engine.solvers.sustainability.WaterUseModel()
Water consumed for an IT energy at a water usage effectiveness: W = E_IT x WUE.

title: engine.solvers.retrieval
text:
engine.solvers.retrieval
Retrieval solvers: what a read from long-term memory stages, ranks, streams, and maintains.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated counts: whole serialized records in a token allowance, one BM25 term in two documents, the bandwidth floor of an exact vector scan, the resident bytes of approximate indexes, an exact tree’s neighborhood against an allowance, the write-path cost of keeping an index current, the auxiliary bytes and re-index time of two stores, cost per accepted task with store upkeep, and the words two texts share. None models a tokenizer, a trained encoder, cache effects, or a real code graph’s cycles.





Name
Description




AnnFootprintModel
Resident bytes of two approximate indexes over the same vectors.


Bm25PairModel
One query term’s BM25 score in a short and a long document of one corpus.


ExactScanFloorModel
The time floor of an exact scan: every eligible vector streamed once.


GraphNeighborhoodModel
A typed traversal’s neighborhood, as an exact tree, against a token allowance.


IndexMaintenanceModel
Who pays to keep an index current after an edit.


RetrievalPayloadModel
Whole serialized records in the retrieval allowance of one model call.


StorageAmplificationModel
Auxiliary bytes and re-index time of a lexical-plus-graph store and a





engine.solvers.retrieval.AnnFootprintModel()
Resident bytes of two approximate indexes over the same vectors.
A navigable-small-world graph keeps every vector plus M links per node; product quantization replaces each vector with m codes of one byte and scores through a lookup table of m x centroids entries per query.



engine.solvers.retrieval.Bm25PairModel()
One query term’s BM25 score in a short and a long document of one corpus.
The same IDF multiplies both; term-frequency saturation (k1) and length normalization (b) decide the order. Lengths and frequencies are analyzer-term counts, not model tokens.



engine.solvers.retrieval.ExactScanFloorModel()
The time floor of an exact scan: every eligible vector streamed once.
N d b bytes cross memory and 2 N d FLOPs score them, so the intensity is 2 / b FLOP per byte at any corpus size. Below the host’s ridge point bandwidth sets the floor, t >= N d b / B. A floor, not a forecast: query encoding, record fetches, and caches are left out.



engine.solvers.retrieval.GraphNeighborhoodModel()
A typed traversal’s neighborhood, as an exact tree, against a token allowance.
Every node has c children and no node repeats, so depth d reaches (c^(d+1) - 1) / (c - 1) nodes; each serializes to a fixed size plus one envelope for edges. Real code graphs have cycles and hubs, so the count bounds distinct nodes from above.



engine.solvers.retrieval.IndexMaintenanceModel()
Who pays to keep an index current after an edit.
Synchronous re-indexing parses each changed file, updates postings per chunk, and embeds the chunks (in local batches, one remote request per batch, or one remote request per file) before the write returns. Exclusion records one entry per changed file and adds one lookup per candidate at query time. Durable commit and coordination, which both strategies share, are excluded.



engine.solvers.retrieval.RetrievalPayloadModel()
Whole serialized records in the retrieval allowance of one model call.
The allowance is what the window leaves after the output reserve and every other input role: S_max - K_max - S_other. The envelope is paid once; each record pays its body and its metadata, so the count is floor((allowance - envelope) / (body + metadata)). A count of bodies alone, floor(allowance / body), overshoots once serialized.



engine.solvers.retrieval.StorageAmplificationModel()
Auxiliary bytes and re-index time of a lexical-plus-graph store and a lexical-plus-dense store over the same files.
Both keep postings. The first adds structural edges per file and re-parses edited files; the second chunks the files, stores one vector and one set of graph-index links per chunk, and re-embeds edited chunks.

text:
physics.robotics.control
Action chunking, watchdog leases, real-time fieldbuses, and CBF safety.





Name
Description




calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization
Calculate a weight-stream lower bound and its amortized cost per waypoint.


calc_axi_fifo_contention
Compare a constructed FIFO backlog with priority bypass at AXI granularity.

Serialization time and bus occupancy of a cyclic CAN FD axis exchange.

Bit count of one CAN FD data frame, split by the bit rate each bit uses.

Project onto a supplied abstract half-space in Euclidean control coordinates.

Timing of a chunk policy that renews on a whole number of setpoint steps.

Longest pure delay a loop can absorb before its phase margin is gone (added 2026-10-20).


calc_ethercat_cycle_time
Calculate on-the-fly hardware processing latency and bus utilization for EtherCAT daisy chain.


calc_phase_lag_total
Total loop delay and the phase it removes at crossover (sample-and-hold,


calc_response_time_bound
Response-time bound of one periodic task: R = C + B + I.


calc_temporal_ensemble_weights
Normalized weights of a temporal ensemble over overlapping action chunks.

Calculate the ideal total delay budget before emergency braking begins.





physics.robotics.control.calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
    model_weight_memory,
    memory_bandwidth,
    chunk_horizon,
    bus_efficiency=0.7,
)
Calculate a weight-stream lower bound and its amortized cost per waypoint.
Under memory-bandwidth bound autoregressive weight streaming: t_stream = M_weights / (BW_peak * eta_bus) f_single = 1 / t_stream tau_step = t_stream / H f_waypoint_equivalent = 1 / tau_step = H * f_single
The waypoint-equivalent rate is an accounting ratio, not the rate at which the model observes the world or generates a fresh action chunk. Decoder work and other inference costs are excluded. f_effective is retained as a legacy alias for callers of this function.
Source: Zhao et al., “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware”, arXiv:2304.13705; Volume IV Chapter 3.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model_weight_memory
Quantity
Model parameter storage footprint (e.g. GB).
required


memory_bandwidth
Quantity
Peak memory bus bandwidth (e.g. GB/s).
required


chunk_horizon
int
Number of steps predicted per chunk H (>= 1).
required


bus_efficiency
float
Sustained DRAM efficiency factor eta (default 0.70).
0.7














Name
Type
Description





dict
t_stream, f_single, tau_step, f_waypoint_equivalent, f_effective (legacy alias), b_sustained.







physics.robotics.control.calc_axi_fifo_contention(
    tile_bytes,
    camera_bytes,
    telemetry_bytes,
    safety_read_bytes,
    transaction_bytes,
    bandwidth,
    bank_switches,
    bank_switch_time,
    compute_time,
)
Compare a constructed FIFO backlog with priority bypass at AXI granularity.
All transfers are aligned multiples of transaction_bytes. The FIFO scenario admits the entire tile, camera transfer, and telemetry transfer ahead of the safety read, then allows no new arrivals. The priority-bypass scenario waits only for one already in-flight transaction. These are controller-policy assumptions, not AXI timing guarantees. Peak bandwidth ignores arbitration, refresh, and protocol overhead, so times are floors.



physics.robotics.control.calc_canfd_bus_utilization(
    num_axes,
    payload_bytes=8,
    baud_arbitration=None,
    baud_data=None,
    cycle_time=None,
    frames_per_axis=2,
    extended_id=False,
    worst_case_stuffing=True,
)
Serialization time and bus occupancy of a cyclic CAN FD axis exchange.
Each axis exchanges frames_per_axis frames per cycle (default 2: one command frame from the controller and one feedback frame from the drive; CAN carries them separately, unlike a summation-frame bus such as EtherCAT). Frame bits come from calc_canfd_frame_bits:
t_frame   = bits_nominal / R_nom + bits_data / R_data
n_frames  = num_axes * frames_per_axis
t_total   = n_frames * t_frame
rho       = t_total / cycle_time
rho <= 1 is only a necessary condition: non-preemptive blocking, competing frames, and error retransmissions still need a response-time analysis.
Source: frame format per ISO 11898-1:2015 and Bosch CAN FD Specification 1.0 (2012), via calc_canfd_frame_bits.

Type
Description
Default

required

8

None

None

physics.robotics.control.calc_canfd_frame_bits(
    payload_bytes=8,
    extended_id=False,
    worst_case_stuffing=True,
)
Bit count of one CAN FD data frame, split by the bit rate each bit uses.
Frame layout (ISO 11898-1:2015 FD base format; extended format adds the SRR bit and the 18-bit identifier extension):
nominal rate, before the switch:  SOF 1, ID 11, RRS 1, IDE 1, FDF 1,
                                  res 1, BRS 1          (17 bits; 36 extended)
data rate, after BRS:             ESI 1, DLC 4, data 8n,
                                  stuff count 4, CRC 17 (n <= 16) or 21,
                                  fixed stuff bits 6 (CRC-17) or 7 (CRC-21)
nominal rate, after the switch:   CRC delimiter 1, ACK slot 1,
                                  ACK delimiter 1, EOF 7, intermission 3
                                                        (13 bits)
Dynamic stuff bits (one after five equal bits) apply from SOF through the end of the data field. The worst case over a stuffed run of L bits is floor((L - 1) / 4); the nominal-rate share is floor((L_nom - 1) / 4) and the rest fall in the data phase. The CRC field uses the fixed stuff bits above instead. BRS and the CRC delimiter straddle the rate switch; both are counted whole at the nominal rate, which slightly overstates the time.
Source: ISO 11898-1:2015, Road vehicles – Controller area network (CAN) – Part 1: Data link layer and physical signalling (FD frame format, stuff count, fixed stuff bits); Robert Bosch GmbH, CAN with Flexible Data-Rate, Specification Version 1.0, 2012 (dual bit rate, CRC-17/21, fixed CRC stuff bits).

Type
Description
Default

int
Application bytes to carry (0 to 64). Padded up to the next data-field size a DLC can encode.
8


extended_id
bool
29-bit identifier (extended format) instead of 11-bit.
False


worst_case_stuffing
bool
Include the worst-case dynamic stuff bits (the bound a response-time analysis needs). False gives the unstuffed length.
True














Name
Type
Description





dict
data_field_bytes, crc_bits, fixed_stuff_bits, stuff_bits_nominal, stuff_bits_data, bits_nominal, bits_data (all int).







physics.robotics.control.calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection(
    u_nom,
    a_vec,
    b_scalar,
)
Project onto a supplied abstract half-space in Euclidean control coordinates.
Solves the quadratic program: min 1/2 ||u - u_nom||^2 s.t. a^T u <= b
The caller must derive a and b from its plant and barrier. This arithmetic alone proves neither forward invariance nor a physical stop.



physics.robotics.control.calc_chunk_renewal_schedule(
    chunk_rate,
    chunk_step,
    chunk_horizon,
    inference_latency,
)
Timing of a chunk policy that renews on a whole number of setpoint steps.
A chunk policy begins a fresh evaluation every renewal period T_r = 1/f_r and emits H setpoints spaced Delta t apart. With the renewal on the setpoint grid (T_r = n Delta t for a whole number n), every renewal instant falls on a setpoint boundary, so a new chunk replaces its predecessor at a defined setpoint index and temporal ensembling can blend chunks step by step:
n          = T_r / Delta t                  (setpoints per renewal, integer)
T_open     = T_r + t_infer                  (worst evidence age at replacement)
h_min      = ceil(T_open / Delta t)         (setpoints that bridge one renewal)
T_span     = H * Delta t                    (motion one chunk supplies)
n_overlap  = floor(H / n)                   (chunks that cover one step)

    sample_period,
    compute_delay=None,
    transport_delay=None,
    phase_allowance=None,

Total loop delay and the phase it removes at crossover (sample-and-hold, compute, and transport terms together).
A zero-order hold behaves in the baseband like a pure delay of half a sample period. A controller that outputs its command some time after it samples adds that compute delay, and a command that reaches the actuator one bus cycle later adds the transport delay. A pure delay tau removes phase omega * tau at every frequency, so near crossover:
tau_total   = T_s / 2 + tau_comp + tau_bus

Given a phase allowance dphi_allow, the largest total delay the loop can absorb, and the highest crossover a given total delay supports, are
tau_allow   = dphi_allow / (2 * pi * f_c)
f_c,max     = dphi_allow / (2 * pi * tau_total)
Source: Franklin, G. F., Powell, J. D. and Workman, M. L., Digital Control of Dynamic Systems, 3rd ed., Addison-Wesley, 1998 (zero-order hold as a T/2 delay; phase of a pure delay). The half-sample approximation holds only well below the sampling frequency; it is a budget, not a stability proof.

)

All transfers are aligned multiples of transaction_bytes. The FIFO scenario admits the entire tile, camera transfer, and telemetry transfer ahead of the safety read, then allows no new arrivals.     payload_bytes=8,
    extended_id=False,
    worst_case_stuffing=True,
)
Bit count of one CAN FD data frame, split by the bit rate each bit uses.
Frame layout (ISO 11898-1:2015 FD base format; extended format adds the SRR bit and the 18-bit identifier extension):
nominal rate, before the switch:  SOF 1, ID 11, RRS 1, IDE 1, FDF 1,
                                  res 1, BRS 1          (17 bits; 36 extended)
data rate, after BRS:             ESI 1, DLC 4, data 8n,
                                  stuff count 4, CRC 17 (n <= 16) or 21,
                                  fixed stuff bits 6 (CRC-17) or 7 (CRC-21)
nominal rate, after the switch:   CRC delimiter 1, ACK slot 1,
                                  ACK delimiter 1, EOF 7, intermission 3
                                                        (13 bits)
Dynamic stuff bits (one after five equal bits) apply from SOF through the end of the data field. The worst case over a stuffed run of L bits is floor((L - 1) / 4); the nominal-rate share is floor((L_nom - 1) / 4) and the rest fall in the data phase. The CRC field uses the fixed stuff bits above instead. BRS and the CRC delimiter straddle the rate switch; both are counted whole at the nominal rate, which slightly overstates the time.
Source: ISO 11898-1:2015, Road vehicles – Controller area network (CAN) – Part 1: Data link layer and physical signalling (FD frame format, stuff count, fixed stuff bits); Robert Bosch GmbH, CAN with Flexible Data-Rate, Specification Version 1.0, 2012 (dual bit rate, CRC-17/21, fixed CRC stuff bits).

title: solvers.DistributedModel
text:
solvers.DistributedModel()
Resolves fleet-wide communication, synchronization, and pipelining constraints.
This model analyzes the constraints of distributed scale for distributed training. It decomposes a workload across a cluster using 3D Parallelism (DP, TP, PP) and calculates the resulting communication overheads and idle times (bubbles) that determine the Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU).
Literature Source: 1. Shoeybi et al. (2019), “Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism.” (3D Parallelism Framework) 2. Narayanan et al. (2019), “PipeDream: Efficient Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Models.” (1F1B Pipeline Bubble Model) 3. Patarasuk & Mueller (2009), “Bandwidth-Optimal All-Reduce Algorithms for Clusters of Workstations.” (Ring All-Reduce)
Formula contract: - split total accelerators into TP * PP * EP model-parallel groups and DP replicas; the split must be exact. - local step time is one model-parallel replica’s training step on the per-DP local batch (_replica_profile): step FLOPs shared across the replica’s TP * PP * EP accelerators, with per-accelerator sharded training state deciding feasibility. - exposed communication = DP gradient collective + TP activation collectives (4 AllReduces per layer per training step: 2 forward, 2 backward) + EP token all-to-all, optionally reduced by overlap. - total step latency = local compute + exposed communication + pipeline bubble, adjusted by explicit congestion and straggler multipliers.

Quantity-first formula helpers for LEGO cells — return Pint quantities, never strings.





Name
Description




carbon_from_energy
Carbon mass from energy and grid carbon intensity: m = E * CI.

Return duration for work divided by operation rate.

Energy for constant power applied over a duration: E = P * t.

Weight-memory footprint: bytes = params * bytes_per_param.

Return token rate from token count and duration.

Duration to move a payload at a sustained bandwidth: t = bytes / (bytes/s).





physics.quantities.carbon_from_energy(energy, carbon_intensity)
Carbon mass from energy and grid carbon intensity: m = E * CI.
energy must be energy-dimensioned (converted to kWh); carbon_intensity must be mass-per-energy (e.g. g/kWh, the unit grid operators publish; coerced if needed). Returns a Quantity in kilograms of CO2 (the CO2/CO2e distinction is the caller’s labeling concern).



physics.quantities.compute_time(work, throughput)
Return duration for work divided by operation rate.



physics.quantities.energy_from_power(power, duration)
Energy for constant power applied over a duration: E = P * t.
power must be power-dimensioned (W/kW/MW), duration time-dimensioned. Returns a Quantity in joules (use .to(kWh) for billing-scale display).



physics.quantities.memory_from_params(parameters, bytes_per_param)
Weight-memory footprint: bytes = params * bytes_per_param.
parameters must be param-dimensioned (e.g. 7 * Bparam); bytes_per_param is byte/param (2 for FP16/BF16, 4 for FP32, 1 for INT8/FP8). Weights only — excludes activations, gradients, optimizer state, and KV cache. Returns a Quantity in bytes.



physics.quantities.token_throughput(tokens, duration)
Return token rate from token count and duration.



physics.quantities.transfer_time(payload, bandwidth)
Duration to move a payload at a sustained bandwidth: t = bytes / (bytes/s).
Pure streaming model — no per-message latency or protocol overhead. payload must be byte-dimensioned, bandwidth byte-rate-dimensioned (any scale; Pint converts). Returns a Quantity in seconds.
