title: engine.solvers.security
text:
engine.solvers.security
Agent-security solvers: injection exposure and defense evaluation (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers. Each model is arithmetic on stated rates and episode counts: how often a task meets attacker text given how much untrusted content it reads, the same exposure counted in turns, and attack success against benign acceptance for two policies run on equal cohorts. None models an adaptive attacker or correlated payloads.





Name
Description




InjectionExposureModel
Per-task exposure to injected payloads across workloads that read different volumes.


PolicyComparisonModel
Two policies on equal, separate attacked and benign cohorts.





engine.solvers.security.InjectionExposureModel()
Per-task exposure to injected payloads across workloads that read different volumes.
Pr(exp) = 1 - (1 - q)^n,   linear estimate q n,
behind a screen that misses a fraction m:  1 - (1 - q m)^n
Reads are independent; a payload is counted once it is read, whatever it asks.



engine.solvers.security.PolicyComparisonModel()
Two policies on equal, separate attacked and benign cohorts.
lower = confirmed / attacked,  upper = (confirmed + unresolved) / attacked
reduction = 1 - candidate / baseline   (observed, both upper, least favorable)
p_acc = accepted benign / benign,  C_eff = C_attempt / p_acc
Unresolved episodes count as harm in the upper rate; the least favorable reduction sets the candidate’s upper rate against the baseline’s lower. At equal attempt cost, C_eff rises by p_acc(baseline) / p_acc(candidate) - 1.

title: physics.context
text:
physics.context
Context engineering: the equations behind what one agent request carries.
Pure arithmetic on serialized token counts (added 2026-10-20). A request is budgeted by role against the window, laid out in zones ordered by change rate so a serving engine can reuse its prefix, compacted between two watermarks, and edited when a write supersedes an observation. One attention head’s softmax gives the first-order cost of every admitted token. The solvers in engine/solvers/context.py compose these.





Name
Description




calc_compaction_cycle
Turns between compaction passes under two watermarks (hysteresis).


calc_equivalent_key_count
Keys at reference_logit that add as much to the normalizer as count keys at logit.


calc_observation_budget
Tokens left for observations once the reply and the fixed roles are reserved.


calc_softmax_target_weight
One attention head’s weight on a target key among fixed-logit competitors.


calc_turns_that_fit
Whole turns of appended observations that fit in observation_budget.


calc_zoned_prefill_tokens
Uncached input of a trajectory whose requests are ordered root, trunk, leaf.





physics.context.calc_compaction_cycle(trigger, target, tokens_per_turn)
Turns between compaction passes under two watermarks (hysteresis).
n_c = ceil((S_trigger - S_target) / delta)
A pass resets the request to target; it fires on the first turn whose appended observation brings the request to trigger or beyond.



physics.context.calc_equivalent_key_count(count, logit, reference_logit)
Keys at reference_logit that add as much to the normalizer as count keys at logit.



physics.context.calc_observation_budget(window, output_reserve, fixed_tokens)
Tokens left for observations once the reply and the fixed roles are reserved.
S_obs <= S_max - K_max - (S_system + S_tools + S_state)



physics.context.calc_softmax_target_weight(target_logit, competitors)
One attention head’s weight on a target key among fixed-logit competitors.
a = e^{z_t} / (e^{z_t} + sum_j n_j e^{z_j})
competitors is an iterable of (count, logit) pairs: count keys that each score logit. Every key adds a positive term to the shared normalizer, so more keys at fixed logits always lower the target’s weight.



physics.context.calc_turns_that_fit(observation_budget, tokens_per_turn)
Whole turns of appended observations that fit in observation_budget.



physics.context.calc_zoned_prefill_tokens(
    turns,
    root,
    trunk,
    leaf,
    trunk_rewrites,
)
Uncached input of a trajectory whose requests are ordered root, trunk, leaf.
The first call is cold (root + trunk + leaf); each of trunk_rewrites calls prefills trunk and leaf after the reused root; every other call prefills only the leaf after the reused root and trunk:
S + R (S_trunk + S_leaf) + (H - 1 - R) S_leaf
Assumes compatible cached state is retained for every matching prefix.

title: engine.solvers.deliberation
text:
engine.solvers.deliberation
Test-time deliberation solvers: spending more work on one decision with the weights fixed.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated token counts, pass rates, check error rates, and the per-token decode floor of a DecodeScenario: how one output ceiling turns into different latencies and bills as depth, breadth, or feedback; what a pool of independent candidates holds and what a fallible check lets through; how argmax selection concentrates scoring error; how a step check bounds a search tree; and what flat sampling, beam search, and feedback policies spend under one deadline. None models queueing, batching, prefill, or serving overhead unless a scenario states it.





Name
Description




AllocationAxesModel
One output ceiling spent three ways: depth, breadth, and feedback.


ArgmaxNoiseModel
Argmax over N equally good candidates whose scores carry independent noise.


BestOfNPoolModel
A parallel pool of N independent candidates against sequential retry.


DeadlinePolicyModel
Three deliberation policies for one task under one deadline.


ProbeVsAnswerModel
A generated explanation of K tokens against a prepared test of T_probe.


PrunedSearchTreeModel
Size of a search tree whose step check rejects each child with probability r.


ScopedRevisionModel
Output of regenerating a whole candidate plan against only its affected nodes.


SearchAccountsModel
Flat best-of-N against beam search, kept as separate accounts.


VerifiedPoolModel
First-passing selection from a fixed pool of n under a fallible check.





engine.solvers.deliberation.AllocationAxesModel()
One output ceiling spent three ways: depth, breadth, and feedback.
Depth generates the whole ceiling in one chain. Breadth runs N concurrent candidates, each billed its own copy of the S-token prompt, so it re-reads (N - 1) S tokens. Feedback runs H rounds of a candidate plus a check; each later request appends the earlier candidates and reports, so input is H S + (K + R) H (H - 1) / 2. Times are generation at the decode floor plus checks; bills count model tokens only.



engine.solvers.deliberation.ArgmaxNoiseModel()
Argmax over N equally good candidates whose scores carry independent noise.
The winner’s expected scoring error is the expected maximum of N standard normals (in units of the noise’s spread), below the large-N asymptote sqrt(2 ln N). A loophole present in a fraction g of single samples appears in a pool of N with 1 - (1 - g)^N.



engine.solvers.deliberation.BestOfNPoolModel()
A parallel pool of N independent candidates against sequential retry.
pass@N is 1 - (1 - p)^N. A parallel pool always generates N candidates; retrying one at a time and stopping at the first pass (capped at N) generates [1 - (1 - p)^N] / p on average, 1 / p per success. A mixed workload whose tasks pass at different rates must apply pass@N per task before averaging; averaging p first overstates it. The selector is assumed to return a passing member whenever one exists.



engine.solvers.deliberation.DeadlinePolicyModel()
Three deliberation policies for one task under one deadline.
A: one candidate and one check. B: N independent candidates generated and checked in parallel, pass@N. C: feedback; a failed first candidate plus its failure report feeds one revision that passes with the conditional rate, as many rounds as fit the deadline (the model assumes two). A round is a candidate at the decode floor plus a check. Bills count model tokens; per-pass figures divide by the pass probability.



engine.solvers.deliberation.ProbeVsAnswerModel()
A generated explanation of K tokens against a prepared test of T_probe.
Generation time is K * tau_decode at the weight-transfer floor; the charge is K output tokens at the output price. Prefill, queueing, and test preparation are excluded.



engine.solvers.deliberation.PrunedSearchTreeModel()
Size of a search tree whose step check rejects each child with probability r.
The effective branching factor is b (1 - r); above r = 1 - 1/b the expected frontier shrinks and the tree dies out on its own. Rejecting a parent removes its whole subtree, so the node saving exceeds r.



engine.solvers.deliberation.ScopedRevisionModel()
Output of regenerating a whole candidate plan against only its affected nodes.
Equal-sized nodes; only replaced nodes are generated. Input processing, checks, and physical effects are excluded.



engine.solvers.deliberation.SearchAccountsModel()
Flat best-of-N against beam search, kept as separate accounts.
Flat: N complete candidates of L segments of s tokens, each request billed the task prompt. Beam: each retained prefix proposes e extensions per stage and the best w survive; every extension request resends the prompt plus its prefix, and the scorer reads each full prefix. Generation runs in waves of the stated concurrency at the decode floor; scoring and final tests add fixed allowances. No prefix-reuse discount. The break-even input share is the input price fraction at which the beam’s output saving, net of scoring, pays for its repeated input.



engine.solvers.deliberation.VerifiedPoolModel()
First-passing selection from a fixed pool of n under a fallible check.
Each candidate is valid with rate v; the check rejects valid ones with eps_FR and passes invalid ones with eps_FA, so a candidate passes with q = v (1 - eps_FR) + (1 - v) eps_FA. Passing-set precision is v (1 - eps_FR) / q, one minus the Bayes posterior of a defect given a pass (CheckerPosteriorModel with defect_rate = 1 - v). The pool selects with 1 - (1 - q)^n and otherwise abstains; a selection is defective with 1 - precision. An incident loss prices each defective selection; the output bill prices the whole pool.

title: engine.solvers.deliberation
text:
Name
Description




AllocationAxesModel
One output ceiling spent three ways: depth, breadth, and feedback.


ArgmaxNoiseModel
Argmax over N equally good candidates whose scores carry independent noise.


BestOfNPoolModel
A parallel pool of N independent candidates against sequential retry.


DeadlinePolicyModel
Three deliberation policies for one task under one deadline.


ProbeVsAnswerModel
A generated explanation of K tokens against a prepared test of T_probe.


PrunedSearchTreeModel
Size of a search tree whose step check rejects each child with probability r.


ScopedRevisionModel
Output of regenerating a whole candidate plan against only its affected nodes.


SearchAccountsModel
Flat best-of-N against beam search, kept as separate accounts.


VerifiedPoolModel
First-passing selection from a fixed pool of n under a fallible check.





engine.solvers.deliberation.AllocationAxesModel()
One output ceiling spent three ways: depth, breadth, and feedback.
Depth generates the whole ceiling in one chain. Breadth runs N concurrent candidates, each billed its own copy of the S-token prompt, so it re-reads (N - 1) S tokens. Feedback runs H rounds of a candidate plus a check; each later request appends the earlier candidates and reports, so input is H S + (K + R) H (H - 1) / 2. Times are generation at the decode floor plus checks; bills count model tokens only.



engine.solvers.deliberation.ArgmaxNoiseModel()
Argmax over N equally good candidates whose scores carry independent noise.
The winner’s expected scoring error is the expected maximum of N standard normals (in units of the noise’s spread), below the large-N asymptote sqrt(2 ln N). A loophole present in a fraction g of single samples appears in a pool of N with 1 - (1 - g)^N.



engine.solvers.deliberation.BestOfNPoolModel()
A parallel pool of N independent candidates against sequential retry.
pass@N is 1 - (1 - p)^N. A parallel pool always generates N candidates; retrying one at a time and stopping at the first pass (capped at N) generates [1 - (1 - p)^N] / p on average, 1 / p per success. A mixed workload whose tasks pass at different rates must apply pass@N per task before averaging; averaging p first overstates it. The selector is assumed to return a passing member whenever one exists.



engine.solvers.deliberation.DeadlinePolicyModel()
Three deliberation policies for one task under one deadline.
A: one candidate and one check. B: N independent candidates generated and checked in parallel, pass@N. C: feedback; a failed first candidate plus its failure report feeds one revision that passes with the conditional rate, as many rounds as fit the deadline (the model assumes two). A round is a candidate at the decode floor plus a check. Bills count model tokens; per-pass figures divide by the pass probability.



engine.solvers.deliberation.ProbeVsAnswerModel()
A generated explanation of K tokens against a prepared test of T_probe.
Generation time is K * tau_decode at the weight-transfer floor; the charge is K output tokens at the output price. Prefill, queueing, and test preparation are excluded.



engine.solvers.deliberation.PrunedSearchTreeModel()
Size of a search tree whose step check rejects each child with probability r.
The effective branching factor is b (1 - r); above r = 1 - 1/b the expected frontier shrinks and the tree dies out on its own. Rejecting a parent removes its whole subtree, so the node saving exceeds r.



engine.solvers.deliberation.ScopedRevisionModel()
Output of regenerating a whole candidate plan against only its affected nodes.
Equal-sized nodes; only replaced nodes are generated. Input processing, checks, and physical effects are excluded.



engine.solvers.deliberation.SearchAccountsModel()
Flat best-of-N against beam search, kept as separate accounts.
Flat: N complete candidates of L segments of s tokens, each request billed the task prompt. Beam: each retained prefix proposes e extensions per stage and the best w survive; every extension request resends the prompt plus its prefix, and the scorer reads each full prefix. Generation runs in waves of the stated concurrency at the decode floor; scoring and final tests add fixed allowances. No prefix-reuse discount. The break-even input share is the input price fraction at which the beam’s output saving, net of scoring, pays for its repeated input.



engine.solvers.deliberation.VerifiedPoolModel()
First-passing selection from a fixed pool of n under a fallible check.
Each candidate is valid with rate v; the check rejects valid ones with eps_FR and passes invalid ones with eps_FA, so a candidate passes with q = v (1 - eps_FR) + (1 - v) eps_FA. Passing-set precision is v (1 - eps_FR) / q, one minus the Bayes posterior of a defect given a pass (CheckerPosteriorModel with defect_rate = 1 - v). The pool selects with 1 - (1 - q)^n and otherwise abstains; a selection is defective with 1 - precision. An incident loss prices each defective selection; the output bill prices the whole pool.

title: engine.solvers.tool_calls
text:
engine.solvers.tool_calls
Tool-calling solvers: what a retry duplicates, an observation carries, a poll costs, a catalog stages.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated probabilities, counts, and prices: duplicate effects under one blind retry with independent request and reply loss, a raw log against the shaped view later calls carry, the status calls a model makes while a job is pending, descriptor tokens staged per call with and without selection, cost per accepted task for structured tools against one shell tool, and adapters with and without a shared protocol. None models delayed packets, a tokenizer, cache eviction, or a provider’s price schedule.





Name
Description




BlindRetryModel
Timeouts and duplicate effects of calls mutating calls under one blind retry.


ModelPollingModel
Incremental cost of a model that checks a pending job every poll_interval.


ObservationCarryModel
A raw tool output in windows, and the input bill of a shaped view carried by later calls.


ToolCatalogSelectionModel
Descriptor tokens on every call: the whole catalog against a selected subset plus overhead.


ToolkitGranularityModel
Cost per accepted task for a structured toolkit against one general shell tool.





engine.solvers.tool_calls.BlindRetryModel()
Timeouts and duplicate effects of calls mutating calls under one blind retry.
Requests and replies are lost independently and never arrive later; every delivered request executes; each timeout triggers exactly one retry of a non-idempotent call with no deduplication.



engine.solvers.tool_calls.ModelPollingModel()
Incremental cost of a model that checks a pending job every poll_interval.
Checks start one interval after dispatch and stop at completion; each reads context_tokens (a cache_hit share billed at cached_fraction of the input price) and generates output_tokens. The worst detection delay is one interval. Useful calls common to every design are excluded.



engine.solvers.tool_calls.ObservationCarryModel()
A raw tool output in windows, and the input bill of a shaped view carried by later calls.
The raw byte count is converted at an assumed bytes-per-token ratio; the shaped observation is billed on each of carry_calls later requests, at the full input price or at cached_fraction of it.



engine.solvers.tool_calls.ToolCatalogSelectionModel()
Descriptor tokens on every call: the whole catalog against a selected subset plus overhead.
Other request content is held fixed; selection runs without an extra model call. Selection pays once the descriptors it leaves out exceed its overhead.



engine.solvers.tool_calls.ToolkitGranularityModel()
Cost per accepted task for a structured toolkit against one general shell tool.
The shell’s attempt is the structured attempt minus the descriptor tokens it saves over calls; each design then adds the expected loss of unconfined changes, p_change x change_cost, to its attempt cost.

title: physics.privacy
text:
physics.privacy
Differential privacy and information-leakage formulas (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




calc_basic_composition
Basic sequential composition: the budgets of releases on the same data add.


calc_laplace_scale
Scale b = sensitivity / epsilon of the Laplace mechanism.


calc_level_bits
Information carried by choosing one of levels equally likely values, in bits.


calc_membership_tpr_ceiling
Highest true-positive rate any membership test can reach at false-positive





physics.privacy.calc_basic_composition(epsilons)
Basic sequential composition: the budgets of releases on the same data add.



physics.privacy.calc_laplace_scale(sensitivity, epsilon)
Scale b = sensitivity / epsilon of the Laplace mechanism.
Adding Laplace(0, b) noise to a query whose value one protected contribution can change by at most sensitivity gives epsilon-differential privacy. The expected absolute error of one draw equals b. sensitivity may carry units (dollars, counts).



physics.privacy.calc_level_bits(levels)
Information carried by choosing one of levels equally likely values, in bits.



physics.privacy.calc_membership_tpr_ceiling(fpr, epsilon)
Highest true-positive rate any membership test can reach at false-positive rate fpr against a pure epsilon-DP release (delta = 0).
Applying the DP inequality to the event “test flags member” gives TPR <= e^eps FPR; applying it to the complement gives 1 - TPR >= e^-eps (1 - FPR).

title: Tutorial Slides

Module 1: Foundations & Architecture
Foundations: the iron law of ML systems, the roofline model, constraint-based systems engineering, dimensional strictness, and the Pydantic registry system.
Download Module 1 (PDF)

title: Tutorial Slides
text:

Bottlenecks: the data wall (ingestion vs transformation), LLM serving limits (pre-fill vs decoding), algorithmic optimizations (speculative decoding), and the reasoning wall (OpenAI o1 scaling).
Download Module 2 (PDF)

Source

cd mlsysim/tutorial

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text: MLSys·im produces quick, type-safe analytical estimates for capacity planning, hardware selection, cost modeling, and sustainability analysis, in seconds and from specifications alone. Equations are documented and tied to the relevant literature; hardware registry specs come from datasheets where available.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Why Use Analytical Models
Before running expensive benchmarks or provisioning cloud instances, an engineer needs directional answers:

Will this model fit in GPU memory? Check before renting the GPU
Why does training fail when inference fits? Separate weights, gradients, optimizer state, and activations
What is the expected TTFT for my LLM? Estimate before building the serving stack
How many replicas do I need for a P99 target? Size serving capacity before benchmarking
What is the MoE routing tax? Sweep expert imbalance before choosing EP topology
How many H100s do I actually need? Model scaling efficiency before buying the cluster
What will this cost per year? TCO analysis before signing the contract
How often will my training job crash? Reliability modeling before committing to a 30-day run
What is the carbon footprint of this deployment? Quantify before the sustainability review

MLSys·im answers these in microseconds using first-order equations. It does not replace profiling, but it shows where to start profiling.






TipTheory Behind the Tools



Each solver implements equations from the Math Foundations page. For the full conceptual framework, see the companion slide decks linked in the Solver-to-Slides Map below.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Quick Start: Roofline Analysis
The Engine implements the Roofline Performance Model (Williams et al. 2009) to classify workloads as compute-bound or memory-bound.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

# Single-node: Is ResNet-50 memory-bound on A100?
profile = Engine.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100,
    batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)
print(f"{profile.bottleneck}, {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"MFU: {profile.mfu:.1%}, Arithmetic Intensity: {profile.arithmetic_intensity:~.2f}")

Compute, 0.57 ms
MFU: 4.6%, Arithmetic Intensity: 145.84 flop / B


The returned PerformanceProfile reports latency, throughput, bottleneck classification, Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU), arithmetic intensity, energy, and a feasibility flag, which together support a first-pass hardware assessment.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
LLM Serving Analysis
The ServingModel models the two-phase LLM inference lifecycle: compute-bound pre-fill and memory-bound decoding.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

serving = ServingModel()
result = serving.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=4096, batch_size=1
)
print(f"TTFT:       {result.ttft.to('ms'):~.1f}")
print(f"ITL:        {result.itl.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"KV-cache:   {result.kv_cache_size.to('GB'):~.1f}")
print(f"Feasible:   {result.feasible}")
print(f"Mem util:   {result.memory_utilization:.0%}")

TTFT:       1258.5 ms
ITL:        43.35 ms
KV-cache:   1.3 GB
Feasible:   False
Mem util:   166%


The feasibility check shows immediately whether the model plus its KV-cache fit in device memory, before an out-of-memory error appears in production.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Hardware Sweep Pattern
Compare devices programmatically instead of reading datasheets:

import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

model = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50

for hw in [mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
           mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100,
           mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.T4,
           mlsysim.Hardware.Edge.JetsonOrinNX]:
    p = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=hw, batch_size=32, precision="fp16")
    print(f"{hw.name:22s}  {p.bottleneck:10s}  {p.latency.to('ms'):>8.2f~}  {p.throughput.to('1/s').magnitude:>8.0f} img/s")

NVIDIA H100             Compute         1.04 ms     30750 img/s
NVIDIA A100             Compute         2.20 ms     14565 img/s
NVIDIA T4               Compute         8.60 ms      3719 img/s
NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX   Compute        21.69 ms      1475 img/s

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Distributed Training Analysis
The DistributedModel models 3D parallelism (data, tensor, pipeline) with communication overhead from ring all-reduce and pipeline bubbles.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel

dist = DistributedModel()
result = dist.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    batch_size=512, precision="fp16",
    tp_size=8, pp_size=4, microbatch_count=16
)
print(f"Scaling efficiency:  {result.scaling_efficiency:.1%}")
print(f"DP all-reduce:       {result.dp_communication_latency.to('ms'):~.1f}")
print(f"TP overhead:         {result.tp_communication_latency.to('ms'):~.1f}")
print(f"Pipeline bubble:     {result.bubble_fraction:.1%}")
print(f"Step latency:        {result.step_latency_total.to('ms'):~.1f}")

Scaling efficiency:  64.3%
DP all-reduce:       618.5 ms
TP overhead:         668.7 ms
Pipeline bubble:     15.8%
Step latency:        5456.6 ms


Tune tp_size, pp_size, and microbatch_count to find the parallelism configuration that maximizes scaling efficiency for a given cluster topology.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Composing Solvers for Real Questions
The core solvers are designed to chain. Three common engineering workflows follow.

Serving Llama-70B on H100s within budget

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel, EconomicsModel

# Step 1: Does it fit and what's the latency?
serving = ServingModel()
result = serving.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=4096, batch_size=1
)

# Step 2: What does that fleet cost?
econ = EconomicsModel()
cost = econ.solve(
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    duration_days=365,
    kwh_price=0.08
)
print(f"Annual TCO: ${cost.tco_usd:,.0f}")
print(f"  CapEx:    ${cost.capex_usd:,.0f}")
print(f"  OpEx:     ${cost.total_opex_usd:,.0f}")

Annual TCO: $2,593,987
  CapEx:    $2,133,333
  OpEx:     $460,653




Choosing a training region to minimize carbon

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import SustainabilityModel

sustain = SustainabilityModel()
for grid in [mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec, mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg,
             mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland]:
    r = sustain.solve(
        fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
        duration_days=30,
        datacenter=grid
    )
    carbon_tons = r.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
    print(f"{grid.name:16s}  {carbon_tons:8.1f} tCO2e  "
          f"PUE={r.pue:.2f}  Water={r.water_usage_liters:,.0f} L")

Quebec (Hydro)         2.7 tCO2e  PUE=1.06  Water=0 L
US Average            62.0 tCO2e  PUE=1.12  Water=260,112 L
Poland (Coal)        167.2 tCO2e  PUE=1.58  Water=366,944 L


For the theory behind PUE, carbon intensity, and the energy hierarchy, see the Sustainable AI slide deck.


Reliability of a 30-day training run on 256 GPUs

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ReliabilityModel

rel = ReliabilityModel()
result = rel.solve(
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    job_duration_hours=720,       # 30 days
    checkpoint_time_s=120.0       # 2 minutes per checkpoint
)
print(f"Fleet MTBF:              {result.fleet_mtbf.to('hour'):~.1f}")
print(f"P(failure before done):  {result.failure_probability:.1%}")
print(f"Optimal ckpt interval:   {result.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('minute'):~.1f}")
print(f"Expected failures:       {result.expected_failures:.1f}")

Fleet MTBF:              146.5 h
P(failure before done):  99.3%
Optimal ckpt interval:   187.5 min
Expected failures:       4.9


This solver implements the Young-Daly checkpoint model, which sets the checkpoint interval for long training jobs.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Type Safety
All quantities are pint.Quantity objects. Unit conversions are explicit, and dimensional errors are caught at runtime:

import mlsysim
hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
print(hw.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s"))
print(hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s"))
try:
    hw.memory.bandwidth.to("second")
except Exception as err:
    print(f"{type(err).__name__}: bytes per second can never become seconds")

312.0 TFLOPs/s
2.039 TB/s
DimensionalityError: bytes per second can never become seconds


Pint catches physical-dimension mismatches (bytes per second can never become seconds). Since 2026-06, compute work also has its own pint dimension, so a bare .to("flop/s") on a bandwidth raises DimensionalityError directly, as does adding a FLOP rate to a memory bandwidth:

for label, attempt in [
    ("FLOP rate + bandwidth", lambda: hw.compute.peak_flops + hw.memory.bandwidth),
    ("bandwidth -> TFLOPs/s", lambda: hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TFLOPs/s")),
]:
    try:
        attempt()
        print(f"{label}: accepted (unexpected)")
    except Exception as err:
        print(f"{label}: {type(err).__name__}")

FLOP rate + bandwidth: DimensionalityError
bandwidth -> TFLOPs/s: DimensionalityError


Bytes, counts, parameters, and dollars remain dimensionless aliases, so MLSys·im additionally enforces unit-family checks at every schema boundary (require_unit_family in mlsysim.core.types) to keep those distinct. A field declared as memory bandwidth rejects a count rate, and vice versa.

title: The Sensor Zoo
text: The Sensor Zoo lists every sensor in the mlsysim.Sensors registry. Each entry carries units and a provenance record, so the timing and bandwidth numbers that feed information-age and ingestion budgets trace back to a datasheet.

title: The Sensor Zoo
text:
Where these numbers are used
Sensor timing sets the floor on how stale an observation is by the time the system acts on it. The Volume IV chapters use these entries for information-age budgets (half the exposure plus readout, transport, and processing) and for multi-camera ingestion bandwidth. The underlying formulas are in physics.robotics.perception.

title: The Infrastructure Zoo
text: The Infrastructure Zoo provides the Environmental Context for ML deployments: the carbon intensity of regional electricity grids and datacenter efficiency profiles. Every value is sourced from published government energy data and IEA reporting.

title: The Infrastructure Zoo
section: How to Read the Infrastructure Zoo
text:
How to Read the Infrastructure Zoo

Carbon Intensity: The Biggest Lever
The single most impactful decision for ML sustainability is where a model is trained. Carbon intensity varies by 41× across the grids above. Quebec’s hydro-dominated grid produces 20 gCO₂/kWh, while Poland’s coal-dominated grid produces 820 gCO₂/kWh. The same model on the same hardware therefore carries a vastly different environmental cost.


PUE: The Hidden Multiplier
Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) measures how much energy the datacenter wastes on cooling and overhead. Quebec’s typical PUE of 1.06 means 6% facility overhead, whereas Poland’s typical PUE of 1.58 means 58% of IT energy is added for cooling and power delivery. Modern liquid-cooled facilities (1.06) are substantially more efficient than older air-cooled ones (1.58).


Connecting to TCO
Infrastructure specifications feed directly into both the SustainabilityModel (carbon and water footprint) and the EconomicsModel (electricity costs in TCO). Regional electricity prices vary as much as carbon intensity, a factor the TCO model accounts for.


Cloud and storage pricing anchors
Illustrative list-price anchors for TCO analyses live under Infrastructure.Pricing:

gpu_hr = mlsysim.Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.GpuTrainingPerHour
egress = mlsysim.Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.EgressPerGB
s3 = mlsysim.Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.S3StandardPerTbMonth

print(f"{gpu_hr.name}: {gpu_hr.rate:~P}")
print(f"{egress.name}: {egress.rate:~P}")
print(f"{s3.name}: {s3.rate:~P}")

Cloud GPU training: 4.0 dollar/h
Cloud egress: 0.09 dollar/GB
S3 standard: 23.0 dollar/TB/month


Each PricePoint carries metadata.provenance pointing at the book economics appendix.


Textbook Connection
The Sustainable AI chapter uses these grid profiles to quantify the carbon footprint of training runs. The Compute Infrastructure chapter connects PUE to total facility cost. Try the Geography Tutorial to explore these tradeoffs interactively.

Note: For carbon and water usage formulas, see the SustainabilityModel API Reference.

title: The Model Zoo
section: How to Read the Model Zoo
text:
How to Read the Model Zoo

Parameters vs. Inference FLOPs
These two numbers measure different things:

Parameters determine memory footprint: at fp16, each parameter is 2 bytes. Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters) needs 141.2 GB for the weights alone, more than a single 80 GiB (85.9 GB) A100 holds.
Inference FLOPs determine compute time: the total floating-point operations for one forward pass. Higher FLOPs means more work for the GPU’s compute cores.

The ratio of FLOPs to memory accessed (the arithmetic intensity) determines whether a workload is compute-bound or memory-bound. At small batch sizes, most models are memory-bound because the weights must be loaded regardless of batch size.


Matching Models to Hardware
As a rough guide:

TinyML MCUs (192 KiB–4 MiB memory): only Tiny models fit (DS-CNN, MicroSpeech, WakeVision)
Edge devices (Jetson, 8–64 GiB): small Vision and Language models at int8
Single Cloud GPU (80–141 GiB): models up to ~30B parameters at fp16 on an 80 GiB GPU
Multi-GPU clusters: 70.6B+ models in fp16 require distributed serving or training



Textbook Connection
The Model Training and Model Serving chapters use these workload profiles to demonstrate roofline analysis and serving cost estimation. The Model Compression chapter shows how quantization reduces both parameter memory and inference FLOPs.







NoteAdding a custom model



Custom workloads are straightforward to define: extend the registry, or define a TransformerWorkload (or CNNWorkload, SSMWorkload, DiffusionWorkload) object directly in code. Learn more in the Contributing Guide and the Models API Reference.








TipCLI Access



Browse the Model Zoo from the terminal: mlsysim zoo models


For dynamic memory footprint and KV-cache calculations, see the API Reference.

title: The Agents Zoo
text: The Agents Zoo is the authoritative registry for autonomous agent system configurations in mlsysim. It captures operational execution boundaries, context window allocations, deliberation search profiles, and tool-use execution environments across Volume III (Agentic ML Systems).

title: The Agents Zoo
text:
Agentic Systems Architecture (Volume III)
Agent systems turn foundation models from static advisory oracles into active processors:

Coding & Software Engineering Agents (Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner)

ReAct and Plan-and-Solve execution patterns executing inside isolated, hermetic microVM sandboxes (Firecracker CoW fork latency \(\le 5\text{ ms}\), snapshot restore \(\le 15\text{ ms}\), \(512\text{ MiB}\) memory footprint).
Served on high-density execution nodes (Systems.Nodes.HGX_H100_EPYC) with 192 AMD EPYC CPU cores (Dual AMD EPYC 9654) to prevent host core contention during parallel microVM execution.
Bounded by token context limits (\(128\text{k}\) tokens) and deterministic AST / unit-test verification oracles across trajectory steps (\(\le 30\) steps).

Developer Workstation Baseline (Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Workstation)

Local unified memory developer baseline running on Systems.Nodes.Workstation_M3Max (16-core CPU, 128 GiB unified LPDDR5X @ 400 GB/s) paired with Models.Language.Llama3_8B (Llama-3.1-8B).

Reference Platforms (Agents.Platforms / AgentPlatforms)

Canonical whole-system envelopes binding compute nodes, foundation models, and sandboxes: Agents.Platforms.Cloud_DGX_H100 for enterprise clusters and Agents.Platforms.Workstation_Apple for local developer iteration.

Deliberative Reasoning Agents (Agents.Deliberation.TreeSearch)

Allocates test-time inference compute through tree search / MCTS (\(N=8\) branches) scored by Process Reward Models (PRMs) with verifier cost ratio \(0\.15\).
Multiplies branch capacity via PagedAttention Copy-on-Write KV-cache page sharing across shared prompt prefixes.

Multi-Agent Fleets (Agents.MultiAgent.SupervisorWorker)

Coordinates specialized workers (Coder, Reviewer, Tester) via asynchronous message buses with bounded coordination overhead (\(\beta = 0\.030\)).

Real-Time Interactive Agents (Agents.Interactive.StreamingVoice)

Streaming speech-to-speech pipelines with \(8\text{k}\)-token context window and \(2\text{k}\)-token active working memory bound by human conversational latency budgets.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text: MLSys·im avoids “black box” heuristics. Every output traces back to one of the equations below. Read this page before the code to understand what the solvers compute and why.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
1. The Roofline Model (Single-Node Performance)
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.SingleNodeModel. Slide Deck: Hardware Acceleration (Vol I, Ch 11)






Intuition: Hardware has two speed limits: how fast it can compute (FLOP/s) and how fast it can feed data to the compute units (bytes/s). Actual throughput is set by whichever limit is reached first. This is why we take the maximum of two terms, not their sum.




1.1 Latency Equation
\[
T = \max \left( \underbrace{\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta}}_{\text{compute time}},\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{Memory\_BW}}}_{\text{memory time}} \right) + \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
\]



Symbol
Meaning
Typical Range




\(\eta\)
Achieved compute efficiency
0.25–0.55 (training); ~0.35 (inference). See Accuracy & Validation.


Dispatch_Tax
Kernel-launch overhead (CUDA, driver)
0.01–0.1 ms





1.2 Arithmetic Intensity and the Ridge Point
The key diagnostic ratio is arithmetic intensity:
\[
I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes Transferred}}
\]
The ridge point is the hardware’s crossover intensity:
\[
I^* = \frac{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s}}{\text{Memory\_BW}}
\]








If…
Regime
Action




\(I > I^*\)
Compute-bound
Faster math units, lower precision, or fewer FLOPs


\(I < I^*\)
Memory-bound
Larger batch size, operator fusion, or higher memory bandwidth









TipWorked Example: Dense Layer on H100





A dense layer with 2048→512, FP16, batch=1:

FLOPs: \(2 \times 2048 \times 512 = 2.1\text{M}\)
Bytes: \(2048 \times 512 \times 2 = 2.1\text{MB}\)
Arithmetic Intensity: \(2.1\text{M} / 2.1\text{MB} = 1\) FLOP/byte
H100 Ridge Point: \(989\text{ TF} / 3\.35\text{ TB/s} \approx 295\) FLOP/byte (vs. \(312\text{ TF} / 2\.04\text{ TB/s} \approx 153\) FLOP/byte on A100)

At \(I = 1 \ll 295 = I^*\), this workload is deeply memory-bound. The H100 achieves <1% of peak compute. Increasing to batch=64 raises \(I\) to ~64, recovering significant throughput.
Source: Slide deck worked example, Vol I Ch 11.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
2. Distributed Training (3D/4D Parallelism)
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.DistributedModel. Slide Decks: Distributed Training (Vol II, Ch 6) | Collective Communication (Vol II, Ch 5)
Real distributed training involves complex interactions between computation, communication, and scheduling. Empirical profiling requires access to expensive multi-GPU clusters and takes hours per configuration. MLSys·im decomposes the problem into independent overheads, each governed by a closed-form equation, so thousands of parallelism configurations can be evaluated in seconds.

2.1 Parallelism Decomposition
MLSys·im supports 4D parallelism. Given a cluster of \(N\) total GPUs:
\[
\text{DP} = \frac{N}{\text{TP} \times \text{PP} \times \text{EP}}
\]








Dimension
What It Splits
Communication Pattern




Data Parallelism (DP)
Batch across replicas
AllReduce (gradients)


Tensor Parallelism (TP)
Individual layers across GPUs
Point-to-point (intra-node NVLink)


Pipeline Parallelism (PP)
Layer groups across stages
Forward/backward activations


Expert Parallelism (EP)
MoE experts across GPUs
All-to-All (token routing)





2.2 Scaling Efficiency
The solver computes an overall scaling efficiency, the fraction of ideal linear speedup actually achieved:
\[
\eta_{\text{scale}} = \frac{T_{\text{compute}}}{T_{\text{compute}} + T_{\text{dp}} + T_{\text{tp}} + T_{\text{ep}} + T_{\text{bubble}}}
\]
An efficiency of 80% on 256 GPUs delivers the throughput of ~205 GPUs; the rest is lost to communication and pipeline bubbles. For the GPT-3 175B reference job (eight-way tensor and eight-way pipeline parallelism on HDR InfiniBand, fixed GPT-3 batch of 1,536 sequences), the solver predicts about 93% at 64 GPUs, 92% at 256, 86% at 1,024, and 55% at 8,192, where the pipeline bubble dominates. Production systems with larger batches and interleaved pipelines retain more. MegaScale’s 175B MFU falls only from 59.1% to 55.2% between 3,072 and 12,288 GPUs [1].


2.3 Ring All-Reduce (Data Parallelism)
Slide Deck: Collective Communication (Vol II, Ch 5)
After each training step, every GPU must synchronize gradients. The standard algorithm is ring all-reduce, which arranges \(N\) GPUs in a logical ring and passes gradient chunks in two phases (scatter-reduce, then all-gather).
Using the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) communication model (\(\alpha\) = per-message latency, \(\beta\) = bandwidth):
\[
T_{\text{ring}} = 2(N-1) \cdot \alpha \;+\; \frac{2(N-1)}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(M\)
Total gradient size in bytes


\(N\)
Number of GPUs in the ring


\(\alpha\)
Per-message startup latency


\(\beta\)
Per-link bandwidth (bytes/s)



Why ring all-reduce scales well: The bandwidth term \(\frac{2(N-1)}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}\) approaches \(\frac{2M}{\beta}\) as \(N\) grows, so it is asymptotically constant in the number of GPUs. Total data transferred per GPU is always ~\(2M\), regardless of cluster size. The latency term \(2(N-1) \cdot \alpha\) grows linearly, but is negligible for large messages.
MLSys·im also implements tree all-reduce (latency-optimal for small messages):
\[
T_{\text{tree}} = 2 \log_2(N) \cdot \alpha \;+\; 2 \log_2(N) \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
\]
The crossover point between ring and tree is approximately \(M_{\text{cross}} \approx N \cdot \alpha \cdot \beta\). Below this size, tree wins (latency dominates); above it, ring wins (bandwidth dominates).






TipWorked Example: 140 GB Gradient Sync





A 70B-parameter model in FP16 produces a 140 GB gradient. On a 1,024-GPU cluster with InfiniBand NDR (\(\beta = 50\) GB/s, \(\alpha = 2\;\mu\)s):

Bandwidth term: \(\frac{2 \times 1023}{1024} \times \frac{140}{50} \approx 5\.6\) s
Latency term: \(2 \times 1023 \times 2\;\mu\text{s} \approx 4\) ms (negligible)
Total: ~5.6 s, bandwidth-dominated as expected for large messages.

Upgrading from 100 Gb Ethernet (~12.5 GB/s) to NDR (~50 GB/s) recovers 10–30% scaling efficiency.





2.4 Pipeline Parallelism Bubble
Slide Deck: Distributed Training (Vol II, Ch 6)
Pipeline parallelism splits a model’s layers across \(P\) stages. At the start of each batch, downstream stages sit idle while upstream stages produce output. This idle time is the pipeline bubble.






Intuition: The speed of light is fixed, but the software schedule can change. Assigning multiple virtual stages (\(V\)) to each GPU interleaves execution: while a GPU waits for one virtual stage’s next microbatch, it computes a different virtual stage’s microbatch, hiding latency behind useful work.



With \(P\) pipeline stages, \(M\) microbatches, and \(V\) virtual stages per GPU:
\[
\text{Bubble Fraction} = \frac{P - 1}{V \times M + P - 1}
\]



Configuration
Bubble Fraction




\(P=4, M=16, V=1\)
\(3/19 = 15\.8\%\)


\(P=4, M=16, V=2\)
\(3/35 = 8\.6\%\)


\(P=8, M=32, V=1\)
\(7/39 = 17\.9\%\)


\(P=16, M=16, V=1\)
\(15/31 = 48\.4\%\) (unacceptable)



Keeping the bubble below 5% with standard 1F1B (\(V=1\)) requires \(M \geq 19 \times (P - 1)\) microbatches. Interleaved schedules (\(V \geq 2\)) cut this requirement proportionally.


2.5 Expert Parallelism (Mixture of Experts)






Intuition: Dense Transformers obey a strict “Iron Law”: doubling parameters doubles both memory and compute. Mixture of Experts (MoE) breaks this law by routing tokens to specific expert subnetworks. The memory bound is set by the total parameters, but the compute bound is set by the much smaller active parameters. The physical tradeoff is a network bandwidth tax (All-to-All communication) to route tokens across the cluster.



When \(\text{EP} > 1\), the solver adds an All-to-All communication penalty for token routing:
\[
T_{\text{all-to-all}} = (N-1) \cdot \alpha \;+\; \frac{N-1}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
\]
where \(N\) is the EP degree. Compared to AllReduce, All-to-All creates \(O(N^2)\) point-to-point connections, making it latency-sensitive. A 4 KB token routing message is latency-bound, while a 140 GB gradient sync is bandwidth-bound.
MoE routing is rarely perfectly balanced. MLSys·im exposes a single routing-imbalance factor \(\gamma \ge 1\):
\[
E_{\text{active,eff}} = \min(E_{\text{total}}, \gamma \cdot E_{\text{top-k}})
\]
\[
P_{\text{active,eff}} = P_{\text{active}} \cdot \frac{E_{\text{active,eff}}}{E_{\text{top-k}}}
\]
MoERoutingModel reports the effective active experts, effective active parameters, routed bytes, and optional expert-parallel all-to-all latency. This is a first-order hot-expert proxy, not a router simulation; it is intended to capture the load-balancing concern surfaced by sparsely-gated MoE, GShard, and Switch-style systems [2], [3], [4].

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
3. Training Scaling Laws
Used by mlsysim.physics.calc_transformer_training_flops. Slide Deck: Training (Vol I, Ch 8)
The 6PD rule estimates total training FLOPs for a Transformer:
\[
C \approx 6 \times P \times D
\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(C\)
Total training FLOPs


\(P\)
Number of model parameters


\(D\)
Number of training tokens



The factor of 6 is 2 FLOPs per parameter per token (forward pass multiply-accumulate) × 3 passes (forward + backward for weights + backward for activations). Combined with the roofline model (Section 1), this gives training time:
\[
T_{\text{train}} = \frac{6PD}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta}
\]






TipWorked Example: GPT-3 Training Time





GPT-3 175B trained on 300B tokens:

Total FLOPs: \(6 \times 175 \times 10^9 \times 300 \times 10^9 = 3\.15 \times 10^{23}\)
On 1,024 A100s (\(312\text{ TF each} \times 0.5\) MFU): \(3\.15 \times 10^{23} / (1024 \times 312 \times 10^{12} \times 0.5) \approx 1\.97 \times 10^6\text{ s} \approx 23\text{ days}\)

Narayanan et al. estimate about 34 days for this configuration [5]. The gap from 23 days is not a scaling loss. Their estimate counts 8 FLOPs per parameter per token, because activation recomputation repeats the forward pass, and it uses a measured 140 TFLOP/s per GPU (about 45% of peak), which already includes communication and pipeline losses.




3.1 Training Memory Accounting
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.TrainingMemoryModel.
Inference memory is mostly weights plus KV cache. Training memory adds gradients, optimizer state, saved activations, and communication buffers:
\[
M_{\text{train}} =
M_{\text{weights}} + M_{\text{grad}} + M_{\text{opt}} +
M_{\text{act}} + M_{\text{comm}}
\]
For mixed-precision Adam training, the default per-parameter state is:



Component
Default bytes / parameter
ZeRO sharding




Weights
2
Stage 3


Gradients
2
Stage 2+


Adam optimizer state
12
Stage 1+



Tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism first shard the model states across model-parallel ranks. ZeRO then shards data-parallel states [6]. Activation memory scales with local microbatch size, sequence length, hidden dimension, and the chosen activation-checkpointing strategy [7].

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
4. LLM Serving Lifecycle
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.ServingModel. Slide Decks: Model Serving (Vol I, Ch 13) | Inference at Scale (Vol II, Ch 10)
LLM autoregressive inference has two physically distinct phases. Capacity planning depends on knowing which phase dominates.

4.1 Pre-fill Phase (Compute-Bound)
The initial forward pass processes all prompt tokens in parallel:
\[
\text{TTFT} = \frac{2 \times P \times S \times B}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta} + \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(P\)
Number of model parameters


\(S\)
Input sequence length


\(B\)
Batch size



The factor of 2 counts both the multiply and the add in each multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation.


4.2 Decoding Phase (Memory-Bound)
Each decode step loads the entire model weight matrix plus the accumulated KV-cache:
\[
\text{ITL} = \frac{\text{Model\_Bytes} + \text{KV\_Cache\_Bytes}}{\text{Memory\_BW}}
\]
This phase is almost always memory-bound because generating one token requires loading the full weight matrix but performs far fewer FLOPs (a single matrix-vector product per layer). On an H100 at batch=1, compute takes ~3% of the time; memory loading takes ~97%.






TipWorked Example: Llama-3 70B Decode on H100





Single-token decode, batch=1 (70.6B parameters, 141.2 GB in FP16):

Compute: \(2 \times 70\.6\text{B} / 989\text{ TF} = 0\.14\text{ ms}\) (0.3% of memory time)
Memory: \(141\.2\text{ GB} / 3\.35\text{ TB/s} = 42\.1\text{ ms}\)
Total: ~42 ms/token → ~24 tokens/s

The decode phase is so memory-bound that a hypothetical 2× compute upgrade yields zero speedup. Only higher memory bandwidth (or batching) helps.
Source: Compute Infrastructure slides (Vol II, Ch 2).





4.3 KV-Cache Size
\[
\text{KV\_Bytes} = 2 \times L \times H_{\text{kv}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times S \times B \times b_{\text{elem}}
\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(L\)
Number of Transformer layers


\(H_{\text{kv}}\)
Number of KV attention heads (equals \(H\) for MHA; smaller for GQA/MQA)


\(d_{\text{head}}\)
Dimension per head


\(S\)
Sequence length


\(B\)
Batch size


\(b_{\text{elem}}\)
Bytes per element (2 for FP16/BF16)



The factor of 2 accounts for both the K and V tensors. With Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), \(H_{\text{kv}} < H\), which reduces cache size. Llama-3 70B uses 8 KV heads vs. 64 query heads, an 8× reduction.






TipWorked Example: KV-Cache Capacity Planning





Llama-3 70B: 80 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), \(d_{\text{head}} = 128\), FP16:

Per-token: \(2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327\.7\text{ KB}\)
Batch=16, seq=4096: \(327\.7\text{K} \times 16 \times 4096 = 21\.5\text{ GB}\)
Batch=32, seq=4096: \(327\.7\text{K} \times 32 \times 4096 = 42\.9\text{ GB}\)

Weights (35.3 GB at INT4) + KV-cache (42.9 GB at FP16) = 78.2 GB, which barely fits on an 80 GiB H100. At batch=64 or longer contexts, the model must be sharded across multiple GPUs.
Source: Inference at Scale slides (Vol II, Ch 10).





4.4 Chunked Prefill and Decode Interference
Production serving systems often mix new prefill work with ongoing decode iterations. Long prefills can stall decode unless the scheduler bounds the amount of prefill work admitted per iteration. MLSys·im models this with an optional prefill chunk size. Let \(S_{\text{new}} = S - S_{\text{cache}}\), with \(0 \le S_{\text{cache}} < S\) and \(S_{\text{chunk}} > 0\):
\[
C = \left\lceil \frac{S_{\text{new}}}{S_{\text{chunk}}} \right\rceil
\]
\[
\text{TTFT}_{\text{chunked}} =
\text{TTFT}_{\text{compute}} + C \times \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
\]
\[
\text{Decode\_Stall}_{\max} \approx
\max_i\left(T_{\text{chunk},i}\right)
\]
Here \(T_{\text{chunk},i}\) is the compute time for chunk \(i\) plus one dispatch tax.







Symbol
Meaning




\(C\)
Number of prefill chunks


\(S_{\text{new}}\)
Prompt tokens that still require prefill computation


\(S_{\text{cache}}\)
Prompt tokens already covered by prefix caching


\(S_{\text{chunk}}\)
Maximum prefill tokens admitted per scheduler iteration



This estimates a coarse scheduling proxy used by chunked-prefill systems: smaller chunks do not reduce total prefill compute, but they reduce the largest decode stall caused by a co-scheduled prefill. MLSys·im does not implement Sarathi-Serve’s full scheduler. Disaggregated systems such as Splitwise and DistServe mitigate prefill/decode interference by assigning the phases to separate resources, trading scheduler interference for KV-cache transfer and resource-partitioning costs [8], [9], [10].


4.5 KV Allocation and Batch Capacity
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.ContinuousBatchingModel.
Decode is memory-bound, so the number of requests sharing a step is the throughput lever, and the KV-cache allocator decides how many fit. Let \(M_{\text{KV}}\) be the HBM left after the weights and \(k\) the KV bytes per token (KV-Cache Size). A static allocator reserves the maximum sequence length \(S_{\max}\) for every request. A paged allocator divides the budget into blocks of \(p\) tokens and hands a request of \(S\) tokens \(\lceil S/p \rceil\) of them on demand:
\[
N_{\text{static}} = \left\lfloor \frac{M_{\text{KV}}}{k\,S_{\max}} \right\rfloor
\qquad
N_{\text{paged}} = \left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor M_{\text{KV}} / (k\,p) \rfloor}{\mathbb{E}\left[\lceil S/p \rceil\right]} \right\rfloor
\]
The scheduler’s maximum batch size caps both. Request lengths are \(S = \min(X, S_{\max})\) with \(X\) exponential, scaled so that \(\mathbb{E}[S] = \bar{S}\): most requests are short, and the rare long one is cut off at the context window. Summing tail probabilities gives the expected block count in closed form
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\lceil S/p \rceil\right] = \sum_{j=0}^{K-1} P(S > jp) = \frac{1 - r^{K}}{1 - r},
\qquad r = e^{-p/\mu},\quad K = \lceil S_{\max}/p \rceil
\]
The unused share of each allocation (internal fragmentation) is \(1 - \bar{S}/S_{\max}\) for static reservation and \(1 - \bar{S}/\left(p\,\mathbb{E}[\lceil S/p \rceil]\right)\) for paging. The paged tail averages about \(p/2\) tokens per request, so page size matters even when \(S_{\max}\) divides evenly by \(p\). Memory-bound decode streams only the tokens requests have filled, so for either allocator
\[
t_{\text{step}} = \frac{|W| + N\,\bar{S}\,k}{\text{Memory\_BW}},
\qquad R_{\text{tok}} = \frac{N}{t_{\text{step}}}
\]
and speedup_vs_static is \(R_{\text{tok}}\) at \(N_{\text{paged}}\) divided by \(R_{\text{tok}}\) at \(N_{\text{static}}\).







Symbol
Meaning




\(M_{\text{KV}}\)
HBM capacity left for the KV cache after the weights


\(k\)
KV bytes per token


\(S_{\max}\)
Longest context a request may reach (max_seq_len)


\(\bar{S}\)
Mean tokens a request fills (mean_request_tokens; defaults to \(S_{\max}\))


\(p\)
Block (page) size in tokens (page_size)


\(\mu\)
Exponential scale chosen so that \(\mathbb{E}[\min(X, S_{\max})] = \bar{S}\)









TipWorked Example: Llama-3 8B on H100 with an 8K Context





FP16 KV costs \(k = 131\,072\) bytes per token, so the H100’s KV budget holds about 532,831 tokens. With \(S_{\max} = 8192\) and \(\bar{S} = 2048\):

Static reservation: \(\lfloor 532\,831 / 8192 \rfloor = 65\) requests, with 75% of every reservation unused
Paged, \(p = 16\): about 128.5 blocks per request, so 259 requests with 0.4% unused
Paged, \(p = 2048\): 165 requests with 36% unused
Decode throughput: paged at \(p = 16\) runs about 1.56× static

Allocation policy matters only when memory binds. If the scheduler caps the batch below 65, both allocators admit the same requests and the speedup is 1.
Source: ContinuousBatchingModel. The Monte Carlo allocators in the KV-cache tutorial admit the same 65 and 259 requests; the tutorial’s throughput ratio is lower because its single random draw happens to give the first 65 requests a below-average length.



Kwon et al. profile contiguous pre-allocation and find that only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV-cache memory holds token states. The rest is reserved slots for future tokens, internal fragmentation from over-provisioning for the maximum length, and external fragmentation from the allocator. PagedAttention limits each request’s waste to one block [11]. The static baseline here is max-length reservation, which captures the first two kinds of waste and is modeled without external fragmentation. Exact-size and power-of-two contiguous allocators, which trade reservation waste for external fragmentation, are not modeled. Sizing both allocators with every request at its full length is a peak-occupancy view: a request mid-generation holds fewer paged blocks, so paged capacity is conservative.


4.6 Serving Capacity Planning
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.ServingCapacityModel.
Capacity planning composes three first-order quantities:

base request latency from ServingModel;
per-replica token throughput from ContinuousBatchingModel;
queueing delay from TailLatencyModel.

For an average response length \(G\) tokens and per-replica decode throughput \(R_{\text{tok}}\), the first-order request capacity is:
\[
Q_{\text{replica}} = \frac{R_{\text{tok}}}{G}
\]
The required replica count is the smallest \(c\) such that traffic intensity remains stable and:
\[
P99_{\text{request}} \approx T_{\text{base}} + P99_{\text{queue}}(Q, Q_{\text{replica}}, c)
\le T_{\text{target}}
\]
Per-replica throughput \(R_{\text{tok}}\) comes from paged allocation in KV Allocation and Batch Capacity, so passing mean_request_tokens below max_seq_len raises the batch each replica can hold. Base latency is then evaluated at the mean request length. This is deliberately a capacity model. It does not simulate request arrivals, preemption, or scheduler internals.


4.7 Serving Cost Dominance
At production scale, serving costs dominate training:
\[
C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{training}} + C_{\text{serving}} \times T_{\text{deploy}} \times Q_{\text{rate}}
\]
A 70B model costing $2M to train, serving 1M daily users at 50 requests/day, costs ~$18M/year in inference, 9× the training cost in year one. This is why inference optimization (batching, quantization, speculative decoding) has outsized economic impact.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
5. Datacenter Sustainability
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.SustainabilityModel. Slide Deck: Sustainable AI (Vol II, Ch 15)

5.1 Total Energy
\[
E = \text{IT\_Power} \times \text{Hours} \times \text{PUE}
\]
Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) accounts for cooling and facility overhead. A PUE of 1.0 is theoretical perfect efficiency; hyperscale datacenters achieve 1.05–1.10 (liquid-cooled) to 1.4–1.6 (air-cooled). The industry average is 1.58, meaning 37% of energy goes to cooling and power distribution, not computation.


5.2 Carbon Footprint
\[
C = E \times \text{Carbon\_Intensity}
\]
Where \(C\) is in kg CO₂e and Carbon_Intensity is in g CO₂e/kWh, sourced from regional grid data.






TipWorked Example: Training Carbon Footprint





64 GPUs × 400W × 336 hours = 8,602 kWh. With PUE 1.2 = 10,322 kWh.



Grid Region
Carbon Intensity
CO₂ Emissions




Quebec (hydro)
20 g/kWh
206 kg


US Average
429 g/kWh
4,428 kg


Poland (coal)
820 g/kWh
8,464 kg



Geographic choice alone creates a ~41× difference for identical workloads. Combined with hardware choice (5×) and quantization (4×), the total optimization lever is up to 800×.
Source: Sustainable AI slides (Vol II, Ch 15).

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
6. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.EconomicsModel. Slide Deck: Compute Infrastructure (Vol II, Ch 2)
\[
\text{TCO} = \underbrace{\frac{\text{Hardware\_Cost}}{\text{Depreciation\_Years}}}_{\text{CapEx (amortized)}} + \underbrace{E \times \text{Electricity\_Rate}}_{\text{OpEx (power)}} + \text{OpEx}_{\text{maintenance}}
\]






TipWorked Example: On-Prem vs. Cloud








Metric
On-Prem (H100 Node)
Cloud On-Demand




Unit cost
$350K (amortize over 3 yr)
N/A


Annual cost (80% util)
~$122K/node/yr
~$224K/node/yr


Effective GPU-hour rate
~$2.40
~$4.00



Break-even occupancy: ~55%. Below 55% sustained occupancy, cloud is cheaper. At 20% occupancy, on-prem costs ~$6/GPU-hour, which is more expensive than cloud on-demand.
The right metric is cost per useful TFLOP-hour, not cost per GPU-hour. An H100 delivers 3.2× the FP16 TFLOP/s of an A100 (or 6.3× comparing H100 FP8 to A100 FP16), so a higher sticker price may yield a lower effective cost.
Source: Compute Infrastructure slides (Vol II, Ch 2).

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
7. Cluster Reliability (The Young-Daly Model)
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.ReliabilityModel. Slide Deck: Fault Tolerance (Vol II, Ch 7)






Intuition: When training on thousands of GPUs for months, hardware failures are a statistical certainty. If a node fails, the job loses all progress since the last checkpoint. Checkpointing too often wastes time writing; checkpointing too rarely wastes time recomputing. The Young-Daly model finds the optimal balance.




7.1 Cluster MTBF
Individual component reliability degrades linearly with scale:
\[
\text{MTBF}_{\text{cluster}} = \frac{\text{MTBF}_{\text{component}}}{N}
\]



Cluster Size (\(N\))
System MTBF (50,000 hr/GPU)




8 GPUs
~8 months


1,000 GPUs
50 hours


10,000 GPUs
5 hours


16,000 GPUs
~3 hours (Llama-3 scale: 419 failures in 54 days)





7.2 Optimal Checkpoint Interval
\[
\tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \times \delta \times M}
\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(\delta\)
Time to write one checkpoint


\(M\)
Mean Time Between Failures (cluster MTBF)





7.3 Wasted Compute Fraction
The total overhead from checkpointing has two components:
\[
\text{Waste} = \underbrace{\frac{\delta}{2\tau}}_{\text{checkpoint writes}} + \underbrace{\frac{\tau}{2M}}_{\text{lost work on failure}}
\]
At the optimal \(\tau_{\text{opt}}\), both terms are equal, and waste is minimized.






TipWorked Example: Llama-3 Scale Checkpointing





16,384 GPUs, \(\delta = 2\) min, cluster MTBF \(M = 180\) min:
\[\tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \times 2 \times 180} = \sqrt{720} \approx 27\text{ min}\]



Checkpoint Interval
Overhead




10 min (too frequent)
17%


27 min (optimal)
7%


60 min (too rare)
15%



On a cluster costing $10M/month, 7% overhead = $700K/month. Async checkpointing (overlapping writes with computation) can reduce this to ~3%.
Source: Fault Tolerance slides (Vol II, Ch 7).

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
8. Failure Probability
Implemented in mlsysim.physics.calc_failure_probability.
The probability of at least one failure during a job of duration \(T\) follows an exponential model:
\[
P(\geq 1\text{ failure}) = 1 - e^{-T / \text{MTBF}}
\]
For a 30-day training run on a cluster with MTBF of 5 hours: \(P = 1 - e^{-720/5} \approx 1\.0\), so failure is virtually certain. This is why checkpointing (Section 7) is not optional at scale.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
9. Effective FLOPS (Fleet Goodput)
Implemented in mlsysim.physics.calc_effective_flops. Slide Deck: Performance Engineering (Vol II, Ch 9)
The actual useful computation delivered by a fleet after all overheads:
\[
\text{Effective\_FLOP/s} = \text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \underbrace{\text{MFU}}_{\text{per-GPU}} \times \underbrace{\eta_{\text{scale}}}_{\text{comm overhead}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{Goodput}}{\text{Rawput}}}_{\text{failure waste}}
\]
Each factor in the cascade represents a distinct loss mechanism. Typical values for large-scale training: MFU ≈ 0.3–0.5, \(\eta_{\text{scale}}\) ≈ 0.4–0.85, Goodput/Rawput ≈ 0.85–0.97. The compound effect means a fleet may deliver only 10–35% of its theoretical peak.







NoteLimitations of First-Order Models



These equations are first-order analytical models. They assume: (1) uniform memory access patterns, (2) no cache hierarchy effects, (3) no network contention under heavy load, and (4) linear scaling of throughput with batch size.
Real systems deviate from these assumptions. Trust MLSys·im for bottleneck classification and relative comparisons. Absolute latency is workload-dependent; well-calibrated cases are often within ±15–30%, while production serving can be 1.5–2× slower than idealized roofline bounds. See Accuracy & Validation for detailed comparisons against MLPerf benchmarks.

title: Hello, Roofline
text:
An engineer has a model and a GPU. Before writing any code, training anything, or renting any cloud instance, which hardware resource will be the bottleneck?
This tutorial teaches the single most important skill in ML systems: using the roofline model to answer that question in under a second.






NotePrerequisites



None. This is the starting point for all MLSys·im tutorials.








TipKey Terms for These Tutorials



Readers new to ML will meet the following terms throughout this tutorial series:







Term
Meaning




Model
A mathematical function with learned parameters (weights) that maps inputs to outputs (e.g., an image to a label)


Parameters
The numbers a model learns during training. A “25M parameter” model stores 25 million numbers


Inference
Running a trained model on new input to get a prediction (as opposed to training, which learns the parameters)


CNN
Convolutional Neural Network, a model architecture for images (e.g., ResNet-50)


LLM
Large Language Model, a model that generates text one token (roughly one word) at a time (e.g., GPT-4, Llama-3)


FP16
16-bit floating point (“half precision”), which uses 2 bytes per parameter. ML often uses reduced precision for speed


FLOP/s
Floating-point operations per second, a measure of compute speed. TFLOP/s = trillion FLOP/s


HBM
High Bandwidth Memory, the fast DRAM attached to a GPU (e.g., HBM2e on A100, HBM3 on H100)


Batch size
How many inputs are processed together in one pass. Larger batches amortize the cost of loading weights



See the Glossary for a complete list of terms.








NoteLearning Objectives




Identify the performance bottleneck (memory-bound vs. compute-bound) for any model-hardware pair
Predict how batch size shifts the operating point along the roofline
Interpret the ridge point as the boundary between two performance regimes
Use Engine.solve as the foundational API for all MLSys·im analyses









TipBackground: The Roofline Model



The roofline model (Williams, Waterman, and Patterson, 2009) is the foundational analytical tool for predicting hardware bottlenecks. Every accelerator has two speed limits:

Compute ceiling: how fast it can do arithmetic (measured in FLOP/s)
Memory bandwidth ceiling: how fast it can load data from memory (measured in bytes/s)

The roofline model reduces to four lines of algebra:
\[T_{\text{compute}} = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak FLOP/s}}
\qquad
T_{\text{memory}} = \frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{Peak BW}}\]
\[T = \max(T_{\text{compute}},\; T_{\text{memory}})\]
\[\text{Ridge point} = \frac{\text{Peak FLOP/s}}{\text{Peak BW}} \quad [\text{FLOP/byte}]\]
A model’s arithmetic intensity (FLOPs ÷ Bytes) determines which ceiling it hits. Below the ridge point, the workload is memory-bound (starved for data). Above it, the workload is compute-bound (saturating the arithmetic units). This single classification drives every optimization decision downstream.
Caveat: The roofline is an upper bound. Real performance is always below it because of scheduling overhead, memory access patterns, and imperfect utilization. Achieving 40–60% of the roofline ceiling is considered good in practice. The model’s value lies not in predicting exact latency but in identifying the binding constraint (the resource that limits performance).








NoteConventions Used in These Tutorials




FLOP counting: Both the MLSys Zoo and vendor datasheets count one multiply-accumulate (MAC) as 2 FLOPs (one multiply plus one add). Some academic papers count 1 MAC = 1 FLOP, which halves both model FLOPs and hardware peak FLOP/s. Check which convention a paper uses before comparing raw numbers.
Peak vs. sustained specs: Passing efficiency=1.0 to Engine.solve evaluates the theoretical roofline ceiling using vendor-published peak Tensor Core throughput and peak HBM bandwidth. Real workloads typically sustain 40–70% of peak (Engine.solve defaults to efficiency=0.5 when efficiency is omitted).
Units: Q_ creates physical quantities with units (e.g., Q_("2 TB/s")). The ~ in format strings like :~.2f formats abbreviated unit symbols.

title: Hello, Roofline
text:
1. Setup
After pip install mlsysim, the import is two lines:
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

title: Hello, Roofline
section: 2. Pick a Model and a GPU
text:
2. Pick a Model and a GPU
Pull vetted specifications from the MLSys Zoo instead of searching datasheets.

from mlsysim.show import table, info

model = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100

info("Model",
     Name=f"{model.name} ({model.architecture})",
     Parameters=model.parameters,
     FLOPs_per_inf=model.inference_flops)

info("Hardware",
     Name=hardware.name,
     Peak_FP16=hardware.compute.peak_flops.to('TFLOPs/s'),
     HBM_BW=hardware.memory.bandwidth.to('TB/s'))

── Model ───────────────────────────────────
Name:           ResNet-50 (CNN)
Parameters:     25,557,032 param
FLOPs per inf:  8,200,000,000 flop
── Hardware ────────────────────────────────
Name:       NVIDIA A100
Peak FP16:  312 TFLOPs/s
HBM BW:     2.04 TB/s


In the Zoo, ResNet-50 has 25.6M parameters and 8.2 GFLOP per single-image forward pass, while the NVIDIA A100 provides 312 TFLOP/s of FP16 Tensor Core throughput, 2.04 TB/s (2039 GB/s) of HBM2e bandwidth, and 80 GiB of capacity.

title: Hello, Roofline
text:
3. Solve: One Line, One Answer
The Engine.solve method applies the roofline model. It calculates which of the two speed limits the workload hits first and returns latency, throughput, and the bottleneck classification.

# One line: model + hardware + config → theoretical roofline prediction
profile = Engine.solve(
    model=model,
    hardware=hardware,
    batch_size=1,          # Single image inference
    precision="fp16",      # Half-precision (16-bit floating point)
    efficiency=1.0         # Theoretical roofline ceiling
)

info(Bottleneck=profile.bottleneck,
     Arithmetic_Intensity=f"{profile.arithmetic_intensity.to('flop/byte'):~.1f}",
     Latency=profile.latency.to('ms'),
     Throughput=f"{profile.throughput.to('1/s').magnitude:.0f} images/sec")

Bottleneck:            Memory
Arithmetic Intensity:  145.8 flop / B
Latency:               0.543 ms
Throughput:            1843 images/sec


At batch size 1, ResNet-50 performs 8.2 GFLOP and transfers both model weights (51.1 MB at 2 bytes per parameter) and intermediate activations, yielding an arithmetic intensity of 145.8 FLOP/byte. That sits just below the A100’s theoretical ridge point of 153.0 FLOP/byte, making batch-1 inference memory-bound.
Sanity check: The weight-transfer and compute bounds from the Background equations confirm why the two ceilings are nearly balanced at batch size 1:

\(T_{\text{memory (weights)}} = 51\.1\;\text{MB} \div 2\.04\;\text{TB/s} = 0\.025\;\text{ms}\)
\(T_{\text{compute}} = 8\.2\;\text{GFLOP} \div 312\;\text{TFLOP/s} = 0\.026\;\text{ms}\)
Including activation traffic brings total memory time to \(0\.543\;\text{ms} > T_{\text{compute}}\), placing the operating point just on the memory-bound side of the ridge.

ResNet-50 at batch 1 sits right next to the ridge point. When \(T_{\text{compute}} \approx T_{\text{memory}}\), the operating point is near the boundary between the two regimes.
Computing arithmetic intensity from first principles: This ratio extends the analysis to any model, not only those in the Zoo. The formula is FLOPs ÷ Bytes. Compare two different workloads at batch size 1:

ResNet-50 (batch 1): 8.2 GFLOP across weights and activations = 145.8 FLOP/byte → just below the A100 ridge (153.0 FLOP/byte), near the crossover
LLM decode (batch 1): Each token performs 2 FLOPs per parameter and loads 2 bytes per parameter = 1.0 FLOP/byte → deeply memory-bound (explored in Tutorial 2)

For an unfamiliar model, compute this ratio first. It reveals the regime before any code runs.

title: Hello, Roofline
section: 4. Sweep Batch Size: Watch the Regime Shift
text:
4. Sweep Batch Size: Watch the Regime Shift
Increasing the batch size shows when the bottleneck changes. More images per batch means more computation per weight load, which increases arithmetic intensity past the 153.0 FLOP/byte ridge point.

rows = []
for batch in [1, 4, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]:
    p = Engine.solve(
        model=model,
        hardware=hardware,
        batch_size=batch,
        precision="fp16",
        efficiency=1.0
    )
    rows.append([
        batch,
        p.bottleneck,
        f"{p.arithmetic_intensity.to('flop/byte'):~.1f}",
        f"{p.throughput.to('1/s').magnitude:.0f}/s",
        p.latency.to('ms'),
    ])

table(["Batch", "Bottleneck", "Arithmetic Intensity", "Throughput", "Latency"], rows)

Batch  Bottleneck  Arithmetic Intensity  Throughput   Latency
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1          Memory        145.8 flop / B      1843/s  0.543 ms
4         Compute        458.4 flop / B      6450/s  0.620 ms
16        Compute        987.2 flop / B     17103/s  0.936 ms
32        Compute       1222.3 flop / B     23598/s   1.36 ms
64        Compute       1387.5 flop / B     29130/s   2.20 ms
128       Compute       1488.0 flop / B     32997/s   3.88 ms
256       Compute       1543.9 flop / B     35343/s   7.24 ms


The roofline plot below shows where batch-1 ResNet-50 sits relative to the ridge point (the crossover between memory-bound and compute-bound regimes).

from mlsysim.viz.plots import plot_roofline

# The plot_roofline function takes the hardware node and a list of workloads
fig, ax = plot_roofline(hardware, workloads=[model])














ImportantKey Insight



The roofline model predicts performance without running a single experiment. The answer is determined by two ratios: the workload’s arithmetic intensity and the hardware’s ridge point. Batch size is the primary knob that moves a workload along the roofline. At small batches the workload is memory-bound, and at large batches it is compute-bound. The ridge point is the most efficient operating point. Every optimization decision starts with knowing which side of the ridge the workload is on.








WarningPitfall: Assuming Peak FLOP/s Determines Inference Speed



A common mistake is selecting hardware based on peak FLOP/s alone. LLM decode at batch size 1 performs about 1 FLOP per byte loaded, so it is deeply memory-bound, and the 312 TFLOP/s compute ceiling is irrelevant. A GPU with half the FLOP/s but the same bandwidth would deliver identical decode latency. Always check the regime before comparing specs.

title: Two Phases, One Request
text:
A CNN processes one image in one pass. An LLM generates text one token at a time, yet the first token and the hundredth token are bottlenecked by completely different hardware resources. Why does the same model on the same GPU have two different speed limits?
Understanding this two-phase structure is what separates a systems engineer who can predict serving costs from one who has to discover them in production.






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline and Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall. This tutorial assumes familiarity with memory-bound vs. compute-bound regimes and the roofline model.








NoteLearning Objectives




Distinguish the two phases of LLM inference: prefill (TTFT) and decode (ITL)
Explain why prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound
Predict which hardware spec (FLOP/s or bandwidth) matters for each phase
Compare GPUs based on their serving characteristics, not only peak specs









TipBackground: How LLM Inference Works



Unlike a CNN that processes a fixed input in one forward pass, an LLM generates output autoregressively, one token at a time:

Prefill (Time to First Token, TTFT): The model processes the entire input prompt in a single forward pass. All prompt tokens are processed in parallel, saturating the GPU’s compute units. This phase is compute-bound, so optimizing TTFT means getting more TFLOP/s.
Decode (Inter-Token Latency, ITL): Each subsequent token requires a full forward pass through the model but processes only one token of new input. The model weights (8.03 billion parameters × 2 bytes per FP16 parameter = 16.06 GB for Llama-3.1-8B) must be loaded from HBM for each token, yet only a small amount of arithmetic is performed. This phase is memory-bound, so optimizing ITL means getting more GB/s of HBM bandwidth.

The same GPU and the same model face two completely different bottlenecks.
