title: Two Phases, One Request
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel
The previous tutorials used Engine.solve, which models inference as a single forward pass. LLM serving, however, is not a single pass; it has two distinct phases with different bottlenecks. The ServingModel models each phase separately and reports TTFT (time to first token) and ITL (inter-token latency) instead of a single latency number.

title: Two Phases, One Request
text:
2. First Serving Prediction
Load Llama-3.1-8B (8.03B parameters, 32 layers, hidden dimension 4096) and the NVIDIA H100 (989 TFLOP/s FP16, 3.35 TB/s HBM3, 80 GiB / 85.9 GB capacity) from the Zoo:

from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100

solver = ServingModel()
result = solver.solve(
    model=model,
    hardware=hardware,
    seq_len=2048,       # 2K token context window
    batch_size=1,       # single user
    precision="fp16"
)

from mlsysim.show import table, info

info("Phase Analysis",
     TTFT_prefill=result.ttft.to('ms'),
     ITL_per_token=result.itl.to('ms'))

info("Memory Budget",
     Model_weights=result.model_weights_size,
     KV_cache=result.kv_cache_size,
     Memory_utilization=f"{result.memory_utilization:.1%}")

── Phase Analysis ──────────────────────────
TTFT prefill:   70.97 ms
ITL per token:  5.19 ms
── Memory Budget ───────────────────────────
Model weights:       16.06 GB
KV cache:            0.268 GB
Memory utilization:  19.0%


The two numbers tell different stories:

TTFT is 71.0 ms, governed by the 989 TFLOP/s compute ceiling (evaluated at ServingModel’s default 50% compute efficiency)
ITL is 5.19 ms, governed by the 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth ceiling

The asymmetry comes from parallelism. Prefill processes all 2048 prompt tokens in parallel, performing 2048× more linear arithmetic per weight load than decode, which processes one token at a time. Across the linear layers, prefill’s arithmetic intensity is 2048 FLOP/byte, well above the H100’s 295.2 FLOP/byte ridge point. Decode’s linear intensity is 1.0 FLOP/byte, far below that ridge point. The weights (16.06 GB) are the same and are loaded the same way, yet the two phases operate in completely different regimes.

title: Two Phases, One Request
section: 3. Why They Respond to Different Optimizations
text:
3. Why They Respond to Different Optimizations
The same asymmetry appears across GPU generations. Because TTFT and ITL operate in different regimes, they respond to different hardware specs:

gpus = [
    ("A100",  mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100),
    ("H100",  mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100),
    ("H200",  mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H200),
]

rows = []
for name, hw in gpus:
    r = solver.solve(model=model, hardware=hw, seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")
    rows.append([
        name,
        hw.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s"),
        hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s"),
        r.ttft.to('ms'),
        r.itl.to('ms'),
    ])

table(["GPU", "TFLOP/s", "BW (TB/s)", "TTFT (ms)", "ITL (ms)"], rows)

GPU        TFLOP/s  BW (TB/s)  TTFT (ms)  ITL (ms)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
A100  312 TFLOPs/s  2.04 TB/s   225.0 ms   8.33 ms
H100  989 TFLOPs/s  3.35 TB/s   70.97 ms   5.19 ms
H200  989 TFLOPs/s  4.80 TB/s   70.97 ms   3.72 ms


Compare the ratios:

A100 → H100: FLOP/s increases 3.2× (312 to 989 TFLOP/s), and TTFT improves 3.2× (225.0 ms to 71.0 ms). Bandwidth increases 1.6× (2.04 to 3.35 TB/s), and ITL improves 1.6× (8.33 ms to 5.19 ms).
H100 → H200: FLOP/s stays at 989 TFLOP/s, and TTFT stays at 71.0 ms. Bandwidth increases 1.4× (3.35 to 4.80 TB/s), and ITL improves 1.4× (5.19 ms to 3.72 ms).

Each metric tracks its own ceiling. TTFT scales with compute. ITL scales with bandwidth.

title: Two Phases, One Request
text:
4. The Asymmetry: Where Quantization Helps
Quantization (reducing numerical precision) shrinks the model weights from 16.06 GB (FP16) to 8.03 GB (INT8) and 4.02 GB (INT4). Because decode must load all weights from HBM at every step, fewer bytes directly reduce ITL (from 5.19 ms in FP16 to 2.76 ms in INT8 and 1.54 ms in INT4). Weight-only INT4 quantization, which dequantizes weights to FP16 in registers, leaves prefill TTFT unchanged at 71.0 ms, whereas native INT8 Tensor Cores on the H100 also double prefill compute throughput (35.5 ms):

rows = []
for prec in ["fp16", "int8", "int4"]:
    r = solver.solve(model=model, hardware=hardware, seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, precision=prec)
    rows.append([prec, r.ttft.to('ms'), r.itl.to('ms'), r.model_weights_size])

table(["Precision", "TTFT (ms)", "ITL (ms)", "Weights"], rows)

Precision  TTFT (ms)  ITL (ms)   Weights
────────────────────────────────────────
fp16        70.97 ms   5.19 ms  16.06 GB
int8        35.47 ms   2.76 ms   8.03 GB
int4        70.97 ms   1.54 ms   4.02 GB








ImportantKey Insight



LLM serving is not one problem but two problems in sequence. Prefill (TTFT) is compute-bound and scales with FLOP/s. Decode (ITL) is memory-bound and scales with bandwidth. Three consequences follow:

Quantization is a decode optimization (reduces bytes loaded per step)
More TFLOP/s is a prefill optimization (processes prompt tokens faster)
The right GPU depends on which phase dominates the latency budget

A chatbot (short prompts, long responses) is ITL-dominated → buy bandwidth. A summarization service (long documents, short outputs) is TTFT-dominated → buy compute.








TipGoing Further: Speculative Decoding



This two-phase asymmetry also explains why speculative decoding works: a small draft model generates candidate tokens cheaply, then the large model verifies them in a single parallel pass (like prefill). It converts the large model’s spare compute into reduced memory loads, attacking the decode bottleneck at the algorithmic level.

title: Two Phases, One Request
section: 5. Putting It Together: SLA-Based Hardware Selection
text:
5. Putting It Together: SLA-Based Hardware Selection
Suppose the production SLA is TTFT < 200 ms and ITL < 50 ms/token at a 4096-token context. The sweep below shows which GPUs qualify:

gpus_all = [
    ("T4",    mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.T4),
    ("A100",  mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100),
    ("H100",  mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100),
    ("H200",  mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H200),
]

TTFT_SLA = 200   # ms
ITL_SLA = 50     # ms

rows = []
for name, hw in gpus_all:
    r = solver.solve(model=model, hardware=hw, seq_len=4096, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")
    ttft = r.ttft.to("ms").magnitude
    itl = r.itl.to("ms").magnitude
    ttft_ok = ttft <= TTFT_SLA
    itl_ok = itl <= ITL_SLA
    rows.append([
        name,
        f"{ttft:.1f} ms",
        f"{itl:.2f} ms",
        "✓" if ttft_ok else "✗",
        "✓" if itl_ok else "✗",
        "PASS" if ttft_ok and itl_ok else "FAIL",
    ])

table(["GPU", "TTFT", "ITL", "TTFT OK?", "ITL OK?", "Verdict"], rows)

GPU        TTFT       ITL  TTFT OK?  ITL OK?  Verdict
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T4    2294.7 ms  52.19 ms         ✗        ✗     FAIL
A100   478.1 ms   8.46 ms         ✗        ✓     FAIL
H100   150.8 ms   5.27 ms         ✓        ✓     PASS
H200   150.8 ms   3.78 ms         ✓        ✓     PASS


This is the analysis every ML engineer should run before choosing serving infrastructure. The answer depends not only on the GPU but on the model size, context length, batch size, and precision, all of which the ServingModel captures analytically.

title: The Differential Explainer
text:
1. Setup
Import the necessary modules. The tutorial uses the standard Engine to get the baseline and proposed profiles, and the DifferentialExplainer to compare them.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.engine.engine import Engine
from mlsysim.engine.explainers import DifferentialExplainer

title: The Differential Explainer
text:
2. A Memory-Bound Upgrade (The Disappointment)
The classic scenario is a hardware upgrade for LLM inference at a low batch size. For Llama-3.1-8B at batch size 1, both GPUs sit in the memory-bound regime, so the 1.61× speedup tracks the 1.64× HBM bandwidth ratio rather than the 3.2× compute ratio:

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B

# Get the two profiles
prof_a100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100, batch_size=1)
prof_h100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100, batch_size=1)

# Ask the explainer what happened
explanation = DifferentialExplainer.compare_performance(
    baseline=prof_a100,
    proposal=prof_h100
)

print(explanation)

📊 Differential Analysis: Proposal vs. Baseline
• Speedup: 1.61x
• Baseline Regime: Memory
• Proposal Regime: Memory

Analysis: The workload remained Memory Bound. The speedup is constrained strictly by the ratio of HBM bandwidth between the two configurations. Any additional compute capacity (FLOP/s) in the proposal was left unutilized.

title: The Differential Explainer
text:
3. Compute-Bound Scaling and Regime Shifts
For a high-intensity workload such as ResNet-50 at batch size 256, both GPUs operate in the compute-bound regime, giving a 2.94× speedup that approaches the 3.2× peak compute ratio:

cnn = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50

# At batch size 256, both GPUs are compute-bound
prof_a100_batch = Engine.solve(model=cnn, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100, batch_size=256)
prof_h100_batch = Engine.solve(model=cnn, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100, batch_size=256)

explanation_batch = DifferentialExplainer.compare_performance(
    baseline=prof_a100_batch,
    proposal=prof_h100_batch
)

print(explanation_batch)

📊 Differential Analysis: Proposal vs. Baseline
• Speedup: 2.94x
• Baseline Regime: Compute
• Proposal Regime: Compute

Analysis: The workload remained Compute Bound. The speedup is constrained strictly by the ratio of peak arithmetic throughput (FLOP/s) between the two configurations. Additional memory bandwidth was not the limiting factor.


When an upgrade crosses the ridge point—such as ResNet-50 at batch size 1, where the NVIDIA A100 is Compute-bound (0.57 ms) and the NVIDIA H100’s 3.2× higher compute ceiling shifts the bottleneck to Memory (0.53 ms, a 1.08× speedup)—DifferentialExplainer flags the Regime Shift automatically:

prof_a100_b1 = Engine.solve(model=cnn, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100, batch_size=1)
prof_h100_b1 = Engine.solve(model=cnn, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100, batch_size=1)

print(DifferentialExplainer.compare_performance(baseline=prof_a100_b1, proposal=prof_h100_b1))

📊 Differential Analysis: Proposal vs. Baseline
• Speedup: 1.08x
• Baseline Regime: Compute
• Proposal Regime: Memory

Analysis: Regime Shift. The proposed hardware provided enough compute capacity to lift the compute wall, exposing a memory bandwidth bottleneck. The speedup is a blended result of higher compute and the new memory ceiling.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
A team has Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters) and a budget for 1024 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Communication overhead (AllReduce, pipeline bubbles) will consume some of the scaling efficiency, as every distributed-training engineer expects. How do communication overhead and cluster reliability evolve as the fleet scales from 8 to 1024 GPUs over a 30-day training run?






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline and Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall. This tutorial assumes familiarity with memory-bound vs. compute-bound regimes and the roofline model.








NoteLearning Objectives




Calculate scaling efficiency across GPU counts from 8 to 1024
Predict cluster Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) using the reliability model
Compare communication overhead vs. checkpoint overhead over a 30-day training run
Explain how checkpoint I/O and failure rollbacks scale with cluster size









TipBackground: Cluster Reliability and the Young-Daly Formula



At scale, hardware failures are not rare events; they are routine. In the MLSys Zoo, a single GPU has a Mean Time To Failure (MTTF) of 50,000 hours, a NIC has an MTTF of 150,000 hours, and a PSU has an MTTF of 100,000 hours. A cluster of \(N\) GPUs alone has a collective MTBF of \(\text{MTTF} / N\) (97.7 hours at 512 GPUs). Including all node components (8 GPUs, 8 NICs, and 0 non-redundant PSUs per DGX H100 node) lowers the cluster MTBF to 73.2 hours at 512 GPUs and 36.6 hours at 1024 GPUs.
To survive failures, training jobs checkpoint periodically: save the full model state (weights + optimizer) to storage. The Young-Daly formula gives the optimal checkpoint interval that minimizes total wasted time:
\[T_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot \delta \cdot M}\]
where \(\delta\) is the time to write one checkpoint and \(M\) is the cluster MTBF. This assumes failures arrive as a Poisson process (exponentially distributed inter-arrival times) and that on failure, work since the last checkpoint is lost (on average, half the checkpoint interval). The cost of checkpointing is therefore not only the write time but also this rollback time.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
2. Single-Node Baseline
The simplest case is 8 GPUs in a single DGX H100 node (450 GB/s intra-node NVLink per direction), with no cross-node data-parallel traffic. This configuration sets the ceiling for scaling efficiency.

from mlsysim import Models, Systems
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet, Node, NetworkFabric
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
from mlsysim.show import table, info

model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
solver = DistributedModel()

# Single DGX H100 node: 8 GPUs, NVLink interconnect
single_node = Fleet(
    name="Single Node",
    node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
    count=1,
    fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
)

baseline = solver.solve(
    model=model, fleet=single_node,
    batch_size=64, precision="fp16", tp_size=8, pp_size=1
)

info("Single-Node Baseline",
     GPUs=single_node.total_accelerators,
     Compute_latency=baseline.node_profile.latency.to('ms'),
     Communication=baseline.communication_latency.to('ms'),
     Scaling_efficiency=f"{baseline.scaling_efficiency:.1%}")

── Single-Node Baseline ────────────────────
GPUs:                8
Compute latency:     14,037.3 ms
Communication:       2,674.7 ms
Scaling efficiency:  84.0%


With 8 GPUs on a single node at batch size 64, compute takes 14,037.3 ms and intra-node tensor-parallel AllReduce over NVLink takes 2,674.7 ms, yielding a baseline scaling efficiency of 84.0%.
This tutorial uses the three dimensions of 3D parallelism:

TP (Tensor Parallelism) = 8: splits each layer’s weight matrices across 8 GPUs within a node, communicating via NVLink (450 GB/s)
PP (Pipeline Parallelism) = 1: no pipeline stages (the model is not split across sequential stages), so no pipeline bubbles
DP (Data Parallelism) = \(N / 8\): each node processes different data batches, synchronizing gradients via AllReduce over IB NDR (400 Gbps)

Setting PP=1 isolates the communication vs. reliability comparison cleanly. Real production systems often use PP > 1 for models too large to fit on one node with TP alone, which introduces pipeline bubble overhead (idle time proportional to \(1/\text{PP}\) stages).

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
3. Scale Sweep: 8 to 1024 GPUs
The sweep below covers cluster sizes from 8 to 1024 GPUs. At each scale, it measures communication overhead (intra-node TP AllReduce plus inter-node DP AllReduce) and scaling efficiency.

gpu_counts = [8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024]

rows = []
results = {}
for n_gpus in gpu_counts:
    n_nodes = n_gpus // 8
    fleet = Fleet(
        name=f"{n_gpus}-GPU Cluster",
        node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
        count=n_nodes,
        fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
    )
    # Use TP=8 within node, DP across nodes
    r = solver.solve(
        model=model, fleet=fleet,
        batch_size=max(64, n_gpus),
        precision="fp16", tp_size=8, pp_size=1
    )
    results[n_gpus] = r
    rows.append([
        n_gpus, n_nodes,
        f"{r.communication_latency.to('ms').magnitude:.1f}",
        f"{r.pipeline_bubble_latency.to('ms').magnitude:.1f}",
        f"{r.scaling_efficiency:.1%}"
    ])

GPUs  Nodes  Comm (ms)  Bubble (ms)  Efficiency
───────────────────────────────────────────────
8         1     2674.7          0.0       84.0%
32        4     1199.9          0.0       74.5%
64        8      954.1          0.0       64.8%
128      16      998.3          0.0       63.8%
256      32     1020.5          0.0       63.3%
512      64     1031.9          0.0       63.0%
1024    128     1038.0          0.0       62.9%


Once the global batch scales linearly with GPU count from 64 GPUs (954.1 ms AllReduce, 64.8% scaling efficiency) to 1024 GPUs (1,038.0 ms AllReduce, 62.9% scaling efficiency), ring AllReduce bandwidth utilization stabilizes and scaling efficiency degrades gradually. This is Amdahl’s Law in action: if the serial fraction (communication) is \(f\), the maximum speedup at \(N\) GPUs is \(1 / (f + (1-f)/N)\).
This communication analysis, however, assumes that every node stays healthy for the entire 30-day training run. Communication is not the whole story.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
4. The Reliability Reveal
A separate question is how often a 64-GPU, 512-GPU, or 1024-GPU cluster experiences a hardware failure. The ReliabilityModel computes cluster-level MTBF, expected failures, optimal checkpoint intervals, and steady-state goodput.

from mlsysim.solvers import ReliabilityModel

rel_solver = ReliabilityModel()

rows = []
rel_results = {}
for n_gpus in gpu_counts:
    n_nodes = n_gpus // 8
    fleet = Fleet(
        name=f"{n_gpus}-GPU",
        node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
        count=n_nodes,
        fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
    )
    # 30-day training run, 60-second checkpoint write time
    r = rel_solver.solve(fleet=fleet, job_duration_hours=30*24, checkpoint_time_s=60.0)
    rel_results[n_gpus] = r
    mtbf_h = r.fleet_mtbf.to("hour").magnitude
    rows.append([
        n_gpus, n_nodes,
        f"{mtbf_h:.1f} h",
        f"{r.expected_failures:.1f}",
        f"{r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h",
        f"{r.goodput_ratio:.1%}"
    ])

table(["GPUs", "Nodes", "Cluster MTBF", "Failures/30d", "Optimal Ckpt", "Goodput"], rows)

GPUs  Nodes  Cluster MTBF  Failures/30d  Optimal Ckpt  Goodput
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8         1      4687.5 h           0.2        12.5 h    99.9%
32        4      1171.9 h           0.6         6.2 h    99.7%
64        8       585.9 h           1.2         4.4 h    99.6%
128      16       293.0 h           2.5         3.1 h    99.4%
256      32       146.5 h           4.9         2.2 h    99.2%
512      64        73.2 h           9.8         1.6 h    98.8%
1024    128        36.6 h          19.7         1.1 h    98.3%


At 64 GPUs, the cluster MTBF is 585.9 h (1.2 expected failures over 30 days, 4.4 h optimal checkpoint interval, 99.6% steady-state goodput). At 512 GPUs, the cluster MTBF drops to 73.2 h (9.8 failures over 30 days, 1.6 h optimal checkpoint interval, 98.8% goodput). At 1024 GPUs, MTBF reaches 36.6 h, with 19.7 expected failures in 30 days, an optimal checkpoint interval of 1.1 h, and 98.3% steady-state goodput. Every checkpoint pauses training, and every failure rolls back to the last checkpoint, discarding all work in between.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
section: 5. The Hidden Cost: Communication vs. Checkpoints
text:
5. The Hidden Cost: Communication vs. Checkpoints
The comparison below tracks how total time lost over a 30-day (720-hour) training run evolves across cluster sizes for both unoverlapped communication overhead and synchronous checkpoint plus rollback overhead.

from mlsysim.solvers import CheckpointModel

ckpt_solver = CheckpointModel()
job_hours = 30 * 24  # 30 days

rows = []
for n_gpus in [64, 256, 512, 1024]:
    dist_r = results[n_gpus]
    rel_r = rel_results[n_gpus]

    # Communication overhead per step as fraction of step time
    comm_fraction = 1.0 - dist_r.scaling_efficiency
    comm_loss_hours = comm_fraction * job_hours

    # Checkpoint overhead: write time per checkpoint + rollback from failures
    ckpt_r = ckpt_solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerator,
        optimizer="adam", checkpoint_interval_hours=rel_r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to("hour").magnitude
    )
    ckpt_write_s = ckpt_r.write_time_seconds.to("second").magnitude
    ckpt_interval_h = rel_r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to("hour").magnitude

    # Number of checkpoints in 30 days
    n_checkpoints = job_hours / ckpt_interval_h if ckpt_interval_h > 0 else 0
    total_ckpt_write_h = n_checkpoints * ckpt_write_s / 3600

    # Rollback cost: each failure loses ~half the checkpoint interval on average
    avg_rollback_h = ckpt_interval_h / 2
    total_rollback_h = rel_r.expected_failures * avg_rollback_h

    total_ckpt_loss_h = total_ckpt_write_h + total_rollback_h
    ratio = total_ckpt_loss_h / comm_loss_hours if comm_loss_hours > 0 else 0

    rows.append([n_gpus, f"{comm_loss_hours:.1f}", f"{total_ckpt_loss_h:.1f}", f"{ratio:.2f}x"])

table(["GPUs", "Comm Loss (h)", "Ckpt Loss (h)", "Ckpt/Comm"], rows)

GPUs  Comm Loss (h)  Ckpt Loss (h)  Ckpt/Comm
─────────────────────────────────────────────
64            253.4            9.1      0.04x
256           264.6           18.2      0.07x
512           266.4           25.8      0.10x
1024          267.4           36.4      0.14x








ImportantKey Insight



While ring AllReduce overhead plateaus with cluster size, reliability overhead grows as \(\sqrt{N}\). Between 64 and 1024 GPUs, unoverlapped communication loss changes by only 5.5% (from 253.4 h to 267.4 h over 720 hours), whereas synchronous checkpoint I/O and failure rollback losses grow 4.0× (from 9.1 h at 64 GPUs to 36.4 h at 1024 GPUs, or 14% of the unoverlapped communication loss). When DP communication is overlapped with backward computation, checkpoint I/O and failure recovery become the primary scaling bottleneck.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
6. The Checkpoint Size Problem
Checkpoint overhead is costly because modern models produce large checkpoint files. The cell below computes the checkpoint size for Llama-3.1-70B with the Adam optimizer:

ckpt_result = ckpt_solver.solve(
    model=model,
    hardware=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerator,
    optimizer="adam",
    checkpoint_interval_hours=1.0
)

info("Checkpoint Analysis",
     Model=model.name,
     Checkpoint_size=ckpt_result.checkpoint_size.to('GB'),
     Write_time=ckpt_result.write_time_seconds.to('second'),
     MFU_penalty_1h=f"{ckpt_result.mfu_penalty_pct:.2%}",
     Storage_bottleneck=ckpt_result.storage_bottleneck)

── Checkpoint Analysis ─────────────────────
Model:               Llama-3.1-70B
Checkpoint size:     988.4 GB
Write time:          141.2 s
MFU penalty 1h:      3.92%
Storage bottleneck:  True


A single mixed-precision Adam checkpoint for Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters at 14 bytes per parameter) is 988.4 GB and requires 141.2 s of synchronous storage write time. At a 1-hour interval, checkpoint I/O alone imposes a 3.92% MFU penalty.

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
A fundamentally different architecture can change which wall binds. GPUs are weight-stationary: weights live in HBM (80 GiB at 3.35 TB/s on NVIDIA H100), and the bottleneck is HBM capacity and bandwidth. The Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3) takes the opposite approach: it is activation-stationary, holding activations on 44 GiB of on-wafer SRAM (21 PB/s) and streaming weights from external MemoryX nodes (1.2 TB/s). Does this eliminate the memory wall, or does it move the wall somewhere else?






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline, Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall, and Tutorial 9: Sensitivity Analysis. This tutorial assumes familiarity with roofline analysis, binding constraints, and sensitivity-based investment decisions.








NoteLearning Objectives




Compare GPU and Cerebras architectures on the same workload using different solvers
Identify that the binding constraint shifts from HBM bandwidth to injection bandwidth
Compute the optimal batch size \(B^*\) where injection and compute overlap perfectly
Explain why this is a qualitative regime change, not only a quantitative speedup









TipBackground: Two Philosophies of Memory



Conventional GPUs use a two-level memory hierarchy: fast but small on-chip SRAM (registers, L1/L2 cache) and large but slower off-chip HBM. The central idea of wafer-scale computing is to make the chip large enough that SRAM alone can hold the working set. The Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3) is an entire silicon wafer (46,225 \(\text{mm}^2\) vs. ~800 \(\text{mm}^2\) for an NVIDIA H100 die) with 44 GiB of on-wafer SRAM delivering 21 PB/s of bandwidth and 125 PFLOP/s of peak compute across 900,000 cores.
GPU (weight-stationary): Model weights live in HBM (80 GiB at 3.35 TB/s on NVIDIA H100). At each decode step, the entire model streams from HBM to the compute units. Activations are small and transient. Bottleneck: HBM capacity and bandwidth.
Cerebras WSE-3 (activation-stationary): Activations and KV-cache live on the 44 GiB of on-wafer SRAM. However, 44 GiB cannot hold a 350 GB model (GPT-3 (175B) at FP16), so weights must stream in layer-by-layer from external MemoryX nodes, dedicated memory boxes connected to the wafer via the SwarmX / MemoryX interconnect (1.2 TB/s). Bottleneck: injection bandwidth from MemoryX.
Same model, same math, completely different performance physics.

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import SingleNodeModel
from mlsysim.solvers import WeightStreamingModel, SensitivitySolver

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
2. GPU Baseline: H100 Inference
The workload is GPT-3 (175B) (175B parameters across 96 layers), a model large enough that architectural differences in how weights reach compute become the dominant factor. At batch size 1, each decode step must stream all 350 GB of FP16 weights.

from mlsysim.solvers import SingleNodeModel
from mlsysim.solvers import WeightStreamingModel, SensitivitySolver
from mlsysim.show import table, info, banner

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.GPT3
gpu_hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100

gpu_solver = SingleNodeModel()
gpu_result = gpu_solver.solve(
    model=model, hardware=gpu_hw,
    batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)

info("GPU Baseline",
     Model=f"{model.name} ({model.parameters.to('Bparam').magnitude:.0f}B)",
     Hardware=gpu_hw.name,
     Bottleneck=gpu_result.bottleneck,
     Latency=gpu_result.latency.to('ms'),
     HBM_BW=gpu_hw.memory.bandwidth.to('TB/s'),
     Peak_FLOPS=gpu_hw.compute.peak_flops.to('TFLOPs/s'))

── GPU Baseline ────────────────────────────
Model:       GPT-3 (175B) (175B)
Hardware:    NVIDIA H100
Bottleneck:  Memory
Latency:     6,016.6 ms
HBM BW:      3.35 TB/s
Peak FLOPS:  989 TFLOPs/s


At batch size 1, GPT-3 (175B) performs 2 FLOPs per parameter per token and must stream 175B parameters (350 GB at FP16). Its arithmetic intensity is 0.91 FLOP/byte, far below the NVIDIA H100 ridge point of 295.2 FLOP/byte. Because 350 GB exceeds a single NVIDIA H100’s 80 GiB HBM capacity, single-device execution spills over PCIe (64 GB/s) for a latency of 6,016.6 ms, and even across a multi-GPU node where weights fit in 3.35 TB/s HBM, pure weight transfer requires 104.5 ms while the 989 TFLOP/s compute units take 0.71 ms.

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
section: 3. Cerebras Path: Weight Streaming on WSE-3
text:
3. Cerebras Path: Weight Streaming on WSE-3
The next cell analyzes the same model on the Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3). Instead of loading weights from HBM, the WSE-3 streams them from MemoryX nodes over the 1.2 TB/s SwarmX / MemoryX interconnect.

ws_hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.Cerebras_CS3
ws_solver = WeightStreamingModel()

ws_result = ws_solver.solve(
    model=model, hardware=ws_hw,
    seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)

info("Cerebras WSE-3",
     Hardware=ws_hw.name,
     Feasible=ws_result.feasible,
     Bottleneck=ws_result.bottleneck,
     Throughput=f"{ws_result.throughput_tokens_per_sec:.1f} tokens/sec",
     Layer_compute_time=ws_result.layer_compute_time.to('ms'),
     Layer_injection_time=ws_result.layer_injection_time.to('ms'),
     Optimal_batch_size=ws_result.optimal_batch_size,
     SRAM_utilization=f"{ws_result.wafer_memory_utilization:.1%}")

── Cerebras WSE-3 ──────────────────────────
Hardware:              Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3)
Feasible:              True
Bottleneck:            Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound
Throughput:            3.4 tokens/sec
Layer compute time:    1.06e-03 ms
Layer injection time:  3.04 ms
Optimal batch size:    52083
SRAM utilization:      22.5%


The WSE-3 reports two times per layer: how long the wafer takes to compute one layer (1.06 µs at 125 PFLOP/s), and how long it takes to inject that layer’s weights from MemoryX (3.04 ms at 1.2 TB/s). The bottleneck is whichever is slower: at batch size 1, injection takes 2,871× longer than compute.

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
4. Side-by-Side: Where the Wall Shifts

gpu_lat_ms = gpu_result.latency.to('ms').magnitude
# Cerebras total decode: max(inject, compute) per layer * num_layers
ws_layer_time = max(
    ws_result.layer_injection_time.to('ms').magnitude,
    ws_result.layer_compute_time.to('ms').magnitude
)
ws_total_ms = ws_layer_time * model.layers
speedup = gpu_lat_ms / ws_total_ms if ws_total_ms > 0 else 0

table(
    ["Metric", "H100 (GPU)", "CS-3 (WSE)"],
    [
        ["Bottleneck", gpu_result.bottleneck, ws_result.bottleneck],
        ["Total decode time (ms)", f"{gpu_lat_ms:.2f}", f"{ws_total_ms:.2f}"],
        ["Speedup", "1.0x", f"{speedup:.1f}x"],
        ["Optimal batch B*", "N/A", ws_result.optimal_batch_size],
    ]
)

Metric                  H100 (GPU)                    CS-3 (WSE)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Bottleneck                  Memory  Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound
Total decode time (ms)     6016.60                        291.67
Speedup                       1.0x                         20.6x
Optimal batch B*               N/A                         52083


The GPU and WSE-3 hit fundamentally different walls:

GPU (NVIDIA H100): Limited by HBM capacity (80 GiB) and HBM bandwidth (3.35 TB/s)
WSE-3 (Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3)): Limited by MemoryX injection bandwidth (1.2 TB/s, requiring 291.67 ms across 96 layers)

The optimization strategies therefore differ completely. On the GPU, optimization reduces the bytes loaded (quantization, smaller models, tensor parallelism). On the WSE-3, it overlaps injection with compute by increasing batch size toward \(B^* = 52\,083\).






ImportantKey Insight



The binding constraint is not a property of the model but a property of the model-architecture pair. GPUs are bound by HBM capacity and bandwidth (3.35 TB/s on NVIDIA H100). Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3) eliminates the HBM wall entirely (activations stay in 44 GiB of 21 PB/s on-wafer SRAM) and replaces it with an injection bandwidth wall (1.2 TB/s from MemoryX). This is a qualitative regime change: the wall shifted, it did not disappear. When evaluating any novel architecture, the question is not “is it faster?” but “which wall does it move, and what new wall does it create?”

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
5. The SRAM Ceiling: Finding B*
The WSE-3 has a distinct optimization knob: batch size controls how much compute is performed per weight injection. At the theoretical balance point \(B^* = 52\,083\), per-layer compute time matches the 3.04 ms injection time. Activations and KV-cache, however, must fit in 44 GiB of on-wafer SRAM, and that limit is the SRAM ceiling.

rows = []
for batch in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]:
    r = ws_solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=ws_hw,
        seq_len=2048, batch_size=batch, precision="fp16"
    )
    rows.append([
        batch, r.bottleneck,
        f"{r.throughput_tokens_per_sec:.1f}/s",
        f"{r.wafer_memory_utilization:.1%}",
        "YES" if r.feasible else "OOM"
    ])

table(["Batch", "Bottleneck", "Throughput", "SRAM Util", "Feasible"], rows)

Batch                    Bottleneck  Throughput  SRAM Util  Feasible
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1      Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       3.4/s      22.5%       YES
2      Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       6.9/s      45.0%       YES
4      Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound      13.7/s      90.0%       YES
8      Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s     180.0%       OOM
16     Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s     360.0%       OOM
32     Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s     720.0%       OOM
64     Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s    1440.0%       OOM
128    Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s    2880.0%       OOM


At sequence length 2048, a single request consumes 22.5% of the 44 GiB on-wafer SRAM (3.4 tokens/s). Increasing batch size to 4 raises throughput to 13.7 tokens/s at 90.0% SRAM utilization, and at batch size 8 the KV-cache demand reaches 180.0% of wafer SRAM (OOM), long before reaching \(B^* = 52\,083\).

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
section: 6. Sensitivity Confirmation: Different Walls, Different Levers
text:
6. Sensitivity Confirmation: Different Walls, Different Levers
Running SensitivitySolver on NVIDIA H100 confirms how the GPU walls behave: for GPT-3 (175B) (350 GB), single-device execution binds on memory_capacity, and for an HBM-resident model (Llama-3.1-8B), it binds on memory_bandwidth (-0.0856).

sens_solver = SensitivitySolver()
gpu_sens = sens_solver.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B, hardware=gpu_hw, precision="fp16"
)

banner(f"GPU Sensitivity ({gpu_hw.name}, HBM-Resident {mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B.name})")
info(Baseline_latency=gpu_sens.baseline_latency.to('ms'),
     Binding_constraint=gpu_sens.binding_constraint)

sens_rows = [[param, f"{val:+.4f}"] for param, val in gpu_sens.sensitivities.items()]
table(["Parameter", "Sensitivity"], sens_rows)

banner("Cerebras WSE-3")
info(Binding_constraint="injection bandwidth (MemoryX -> wafer)",
     Optimization_lever="increase batch size within on-wafer SRAM capacity")

print()
print("Different architectures -> different walls -> different strategies.")


=== GPU Sensitivity (NVIDIA H100, HBM-Resident Llama-3.1-8B) ===
Baseline latency:    5.60 ms
Binding constraint:  memory_bandwidth
Parameter         Sensitivity
─────────────────────────────
peak_flops            +0.0000
memory_bandwidth      -0.0856
memory_capacity       +0.0000

=== Cerebras WSE-3 ===
Binding constraint:  injection bandwidth (MemoryX -> wafer)
Optimization lever:  increase batch size within on-wafer SRAM capacity

Different architectures -> different walls -> different strategies.








WarningThe Deeper Lesson



When evaluating novel architectures (wafer-scale, photonic, analog, neuromorphic), the diagnostic question is not “Is it faster?” but “Which wall does it move, and what new wall does it create?” Every architecture eliminates one bottleneck by introducing another.

title: Tutorial Template — MLSys·im
text:
This document defines the canonical structure for all MLSys·im tutorials. Every tutorial follows this template exactly. Consistency is pedagogical.




One tutorial = one core question. The title IS the question. Every cell exists to answer it.
Predict → Compute → Reflect. Before showing code output, tell the reader what to expect. After showing it, explain what it means. This is the learning cycle.
The central finding is the point of the tutorial. Every tutorial has exactly ONE insight that changes how the reader thinks. Frame it, build to it, land it in the Key Insight callout.
Real hardware, real models. No toy examples. Every tutorial uses published specs from the Zoo.
Code-first, prose-second. Keep prose tight. The insight comes from the numbers, not from reading paragraphs. Explanations serve the code, not the other way around.
Sub-30-second runtime. Every tutorial runs on a laptop in under 30 seconds. No GPU needed.





Every tutorial has exactly these sections, in this order:
---
title: "<Core Question as Statement>"
subtitle: "<One-sentence hook — what makes this surprising or important>"
description: "<2-sentence summary for search/SEO>"
---

## The Question                          ← 2-3 sentences framing WHY this matters
                                          No code. Pure motivation.

::: {.callout-note}

<What tutorials must be completed first. Link them.>
:::

::: {.callout-note}

<Exactly 3–4 bullet points. Each starts with a verb. Measurable outcomes.>
:::

::: {.callout-tip}

<Define key terms needed for THIS tutorial. Keep it to one concept.>
:::

---

   - Code cell (3–8 lines, heavily commented)
   - Brief prose interpreting the output

## 3. <Second Analysis Step>             ← The sweep / comparison / composition
   - Code cell
   - Prose or callout interpreting the pattern

## 4. <The Reveal>                       ← Where the aha moment lands
   - Code cell showing the surprising result
   - KEY INSIGHT callout (see below)

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Insight
<1–3 sentences. The ONE thing the reader should remember from this tutorial.
This is the "tweet-length" summary. Bold the core claim.>
:::

## 5. <Extension / Composition>          ← OPTIONAL: chain another solver
   - Shows how this connects to the broader system

title: Where to Invest: Sensitivity Analysis
text:
A team has budget for one hardware upgrade. Should it buy more FLOP/s or more memory bandwidth? Intuition suggests that more compute is always better, yet for single-stream Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters) inference on an NVIDIA A100, a 10% bandwidth upgrade changes latency by -8.90% (an elasticity of \(\frac{\Delta T / T}{\Delta \text{BW} / \text{BW}} = \-0\.89\)), whereas a 10% compute upgrade changes latency by +0.00% (memory transfer takes 84× longer than compute). This tutorial computes those sensitivities analytically and then inverts the Roofline to derive minimum hardware specifications from an SLA.






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline and Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall. This tutorial assumes familiarity with memory-bound vs. compute-bound regimes and the ridge point concept.








NoteLearning Objectives




Compute numerical sensitivities of latency with respect to each hardware parameter
Identify the binding constraint for any model-hardware pair
Quantify the asymmetry between bandwidth and FLOP/s sensitivity
Derive minimum hardware specs from a latency SLA using inverse Roofline synthesis









TipBackground: Sensitivity Analysis



In optimization, the binding constraint is the resource that actually limits performance, the one holding with equality at the solution. SensitivitySolver perturbs each hardware parameter (peak_flops, memory_bandwidth, memory_capacity) by a fixed percentage (\(\Delta x / x = 10%\)) and measures the normalized latency response \(\Delta T / T = (T_{\text{perturbed}} - T_{\text{base}}) / T_{\text{base}}\) (with corresponding elasticity \(\frac{\Delta T / T}{\Delta x / x}\)). The parameter with the largest absolute response is the binding constraint and the lever most worth investing in.

title: Where to Invest: Sensitivity Analysis
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel
from mlsysim.solvers import SensitivitySolver, SynthesisSolver
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_

title: Where to Invest: Sensitivity Analysis
text:
2. Sensitivity Analysis: Llama-3 70B on A100
The analysis targets Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters) inference on a single NVIDIA A100 (80 GiB / 85.9 GB HBM2e). At FP16 (141.2 GB of weights), the model exceeds a single 80 GiB GPU and binds on memory_capacity; quantizing to INT8 (70.6 GB of weights) fits within HBM and exposes the steady-state hardware sensitivities.

from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel
from mlsysim.solvers import SensitivitySolver, SynthesisSolver
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
from mlsysim.show import table, info

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100

# Compute normalized latency response to a 10% upgrade in each hardware parameter
solver = SensitivitySolver()
res = solver.solve(model=model, hardware=hardware, precision="int8")

info("Configuration",
     Model=model.name,
     Hardware=hardware.name,
     Baseline_latency=res.baseline_latency.to('ms'),
     Perturbation=f"{res.perturbation_pct}%")

rows = [[param, f"{sensitivity:+.4f}"] for param, sensitivity in res.sensitivities.items()]
table(["Parameter", "Sensitivity"], rows)

── Configuration ───────────────────────────
Model:             Llama-3.1-70B
Hardware:          NVIDIA A100
Baseline latency:  38.90 ms
Perturbation:      10.0%
Parameter         Sensitivity
─────────────────────────────
peak_flops            +0.0000
memory_bandwidth      -0.0890
memory_capacity       +0.0000


Each reported sensitivity is the fractional latency change \(\Delta T / T\) for a 10% parameter increase. A sensitivity of -0.0890 on memory_bandwidth (elasticity \(\frac{\Delta T / T}{\Delta \text{BW} / \text{BW}} = \-0\.89\)) means a 10% bandwidth increase yields an 8.9% latency reduction (from 38.90 ms to 35.44 ms). A sensitivity of +0.0000 on peak_flops means additional compute produces zero latency reduction.

title: Where to Invest: Sensitivity Analysis
text:
3. The Binding Constraint

info("Binding Constraint",
     Constraint=res.binding_constraint,
     Interpretation=f"{res.binding_constraint} is the hardware knob most worth turning for {model.name} on {hardware.name}")

── Binding Constraint ──────────────────────
Constraint:      memory_bandwidth
Interpretation:  memory_bandwidth is the hardware knob most worth turning for Llama-3.1-70B on NVIDIA A100


For Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters) at batch size 1, every decode step streams 70.6 GB of INT8 weights (plus activations) from HBM. The arithmetic intensity is 1.82 FLOP/byte, far below the NVIDIA A100 ridge point of 153.0 FLOP/byte. Memory transfer takes 38.09 ms while compute takes only 0.45 ms, confirming quantitatively that the workload is deeply memory-bound.

title: Where to Invest: Sensitivity Analysis
text:
4. The Bandwidth vs. Compute Asymmetry
The asymmetry between memory bandwidth and compute throughput appears directly in the sensitivity comparison:

sens_bw = abs(res.sensitivities.get("memory_bandwidth", 0))
sens_flops = abs(res.sensitivities.get("peak_flops", 0))

if sens_flops > 0:
    ratio = sens_bw / sens_flops
    info("Sensitivity Asymmetry",
         Bandwidth_sensitivity=f"{sens_bw:.4f}",
         FLOPS_sensitivity=f"{sens_flops:.4f}",
         Ratio=f"{ratio:.1f}x",
         Verdict=f"A dollar spent on bandwidth improvement is ~{ratio:.0f}x more impactful than the same dollar spent on more FLOP/s")
else:
    info("Sensitivity Asymmetry",
         Bandwidth_sensitivity=f"{sens_bw:.4f}",
         FLOPS_sensitivity=f"{sens_flops:.4f}",
         Verdict="FLOPS has zero sensitivity --- purely memory-bound")

── Sensitivity Asymmetry ───────────────────
Bandwidth sensitivity:  0.0890
FLOPS sensitivity:      0.0000
Verdict:                FLOPS has zero sensitivity --- purely memory-bound








ImportantKey Insight



Sensitivity analysis quantifies why bandwidth dominates single-stream LLM inference. Under the Roofline model \(T = \max(T_{\text{compute}}, T_{\text{memory}}) + T_{\text{overhead}}\), memory transfer for Llama-3.1-70B on NVIDIA A100 takes 38.09 ms versus 0.45 ms for compute (an 84× gap). Consequently, a 10% bandwidth increase reduces latency by 8.90% (\(\Delta T / T = \-0\.0890\), elasticity \(\-0\.89\)), whereas a 10% compute increase yields 0.00% improvement (\(\Delta T / T = \+0\.0000\)). The binding constraint, not the headline spec, determines where a hardware budget creates value.








WarningFallacy: Investing in the Highest-Spec Number Maximizes Performance



GPU vendors advertise peak FLOP/s prominently (312 TFLOP/s on NVIDIA A100, 989 TFLOP/s on NVIDIA H100) because the number is large. For memory-bound workloads where \(T_{\text{memory}}\) exceeds \(T_{\text{compute}}\) by 84×, a 10% bandwidth increase cuts latency by 8.9% while a 10% compute increase yields 0.0%. The datasheet headline and the binding constraint are often different parameters, and sensitivity analysis shows which one actually matters.

title: Where to Invest: Sensitivity Analysis
section: 5. Inverse Roofline: From SLA to Hardware
text:
5. Inverse Roofline: From SLA to Hardware
Sensitivity analysis identifies which parameter is worth improving. The natural follow-up is how much improvement a given performance target requires.
The SynthesisSolver inverts the Roofline model. Instead of “given hardware, what is the latency?”, it asks: “given a latency SLA, what hardware do I need?”
Suppose a deployment requires an FP16 inter-token latency (ITL) of 50 ms or less:

synth = SynthesisSolver()
specs = synth.solve(
    model=model,
    target_latency=Q_("50 ms"),
    precision="fp16"
)

info("Inverse Roofline: Required Hardware",
     Target_SLA="50 ms ITL",
     Min_memory_BW=specs.required_bw.to('TB/s'),
     Min_compute=specs.required_flops.to('TFLOPs/s'),
     Min_memory=specs.required_memory.to('GB'))

── Inverse Roofline: Required Hardware ─────
Target SLA:     50 ms ITL
Min memory BW:  2.82 TB/s
Min compute:    5.65 TFLOPs/s
Min memory:     141.2 GB


Meeting a 50 ms FP16 SLA for Llama-3.1-70B requires 2.82 TB/s of memory bandwidth (1.38× what NVIDIA A100’s 2.04 TB/s provides), at least 5.65 TFLOP/s of effective compute, and 141.2 GB of HBM capacity. This immediately explains why single-GPU FP16 exceeded the 80 GiB (85.9 GB) NVIDIA A100 and narrows the single-device search to high-capacity H100/H200/B200-class accelerators or multi-GPU tensor parallelism.

title: Where to Invest: Sensitivity Analysis
section: 6. Generational Comparison: Whether the Binding Constraint Shifts
text:
6. Generational Comparison: Whether the Binding Constraint Shifts
Sensitivity analysis also reveals whether hardware upgrades shift the binding constraint. The comparison below spans three GPU generations for INT8 single-GPU inference:

gpus = [
    ("A100", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100),
    ("H100", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100),
    ("H200", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H200),
]

rows = []
for name, hw in gpus:
    r = solver.solve(model=model, hardware=hw, precision="int8")
    s_bw = r.sensitivities.get("memory_bandwidth", 0)
    s_fl = r.sensitivities.get("peak_flops", 0)
    lat = r.baseline_latency.to("ms").magnitude
    rows.append([name, f"{s_bw:+.4f}", f"{s_fl:+.4f}", r.binding_constraint, f"{lat:.2f}ms"])

table(["GPU", "BW Sens", "FLOPS Sens", "Binding", "Latency"], rows)

GPU   BW Sens  FLOPS Sens           Binding  Latency
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A100  -0.0890     +0.0000  memory_bandwidth  38.90ms
H100  -0.0878     +0.0000  memory_bandwidth  23.99ms
H200  -0.0866     +0.0000  memory_bandwidth  16.99ms


Across all three generations (NVIDIA A100 at 38.90 ms, NVIDIA H100 at 23.99 ms, and NVIDIA H200 at 16.99 ms), memory_bandwidth remains the binding constraint (-0.0890, -0.0878, and -0.0866). In FP16 (141.2 GB required), by contrast, NVIDIA A100 and NVIDIA H100 (85.9 GB capacity) bind on memory_capacity, NVIDIA H200 (151.4 GB capacity) exhibits a memory_capacity sensitivity of +0.0000 because a 10% capacity increase crosses the 141.2 GB fit threshold, and NVIDIA B200 (193.3 GB capacity) shifts the binding constraint from memory_capacity to memory_bandwidth (-0.0873 at 20.22 ms).

text:

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
A 256-GPU cluster (32 DGX H100 nodes) trains a model for 30 days. Where that cluster is located makes no difference to latency or throughput, which the hardware fixes. For carbon emissions, water usage, and total cost of ownership, does geography matter, and if so, by how much?






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall. No other prerequisites are required; this tutorial can be completed independently.








NoteLearning Objectives




Calculate the carbon footprint of identical training runs in different regions
Quantify the gap between the cleanest and dirtiest electricity grids
Compare geography vs. training duration as levers for sustainability
Apply the EconomicsModel to show how carbon pricing changes the cheapest option









TipBackground: Grid Carbon Intensity



Every kilowatt-hour of electricity has a carbon cost, measured in grams of \(\text{CO}_2\) per kWh (\(\text{gCO}_2/\text{kWh}\)). This number depends entirely on how the electricity is generated. Representative profiles from mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids span nearly two orders of magnitude:

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
2. Two-Region Comparison
The first comparison runs the same training job in two locations: Quebec (Hydro) (20 gCO2/kWh, PUE 1.06) and Poland (Coal) (820 gCO2/kWh, PUE 1.58). The 256-GPU fleet, the model, and the 30-day duration are identical. The only variable is where the electricity comes from.

from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.solvers import SustainabilityModel
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet, Node, NetworkFabric
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
from mlsysim.show import table, info

# 256-GPU cluster: 32 DGX H100 nodes
fleet = Fleet(
    name="256-GPU Training Cluster",
    node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
    count=32,
    fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
)

solver = SustainabilityModel()

# Quebec: hydroelectric grid
res_quebec = solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet, duration_days=30,
    datacenter=mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec
)

# Poland: coal-heavy grid
res_poland = solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet, duration_days=30,
    datacenter=mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland
)

carbon_q = res_quebec.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude  # tonnes
carbon_p = res_poland.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
ratio = carbon_p / carbon_q if carbon_q > 0 else 0

table(
    ["Region", "Carbon (tonnes CO2)"],
    [
        ["Quebec (Hydro)", f"{carbon_q:.1f}"],
        ["Poland (Coal)", f"{carbon_p:.1f}"],
    ]
)
info(Ratio=f"{ratio:.0f}x")

Region          Carbon (tonnes CO2)
───────────────────────────────────
Quebec (Hydro)                  2.7
Poland (Coal)                 167.2
Ratio:  61x


Same cluster. Same model. Same 30-day duration. Because Poland’s grid carbon intensity is 41× higher than Quebec’s (820 vs. 20 gCO2/kWh) and its facility PUE is 1.49× higher (1.58 vs. 1.06), the total carbon footprint differs by 61× (167.2 tonnes vs. 2.7 tonnes \(\text{CO}_2\)). The difference comes from a location decision, not from an algorithmic optimization.

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
3. All-Region Sweep
The next sweep expands the comparison to four grid regions in the Infrastructure Zoo, adding energy consumption, water usage, and PUE to the picture.

grids = [
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec,
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Norway,
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg,
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland,
]

region_results = {}
rows = []
for grid in grids:
    r = solver.solve(fleet=fleet, duration_days=30, datacenter=grid)
    energy_mwh = r.total_energy_kwh.magnitude / 1000
    carbon_t = r.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
    water_kl = r.water_usage_liters / 1000
    region_results[r.region_name] = r
    rows.append([r.region_name, f"{energy_mwh:,.1f}", f"{carbon_t:,.1f}", f"{water_kl:,.1f}", f"{r.pue:.2f}"])

table(["Region", "Energy (MWh)", "Carbon (t)", "Water (kL)", "PUE"], rows)

Region          Energy (MWh)  Carbon (t)  Water (kL)   PUE
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Quebec (Hydro)         136.8         2.7         0.0  1.06
Norway (Hydro)         136.8         1.4         0.0  1.06
US Average             144.5        62.0       260.1  1.12
Poland (Coal)          203.9       167.2       366.9  1.58


Total facility energy varies across regions from 136.8 MWh in Quebec (Hydro) and Norway (Hydro) (PUE 1.06) to 203.9 MWh in Poland (Coal) (PUE 1.58). Water consumption ranges from 0.0 kL in closed-loop cold-climate hydro facilities to 260.1 kL (US Average) and 366.9 kL (Poland (Coal)). Combined with grid carbon intensity, emissions span 1.4 t in Norway (Hydro) and 2.7 t in Quebec (Hydro) up to 167.2 t in Poland (Coal) (61× vs. Quebec and 122× vs. Norway).

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
4. Geography vs. Training Duration
The trade-off between training longer in a clean region and shorter in a dirty region shows up in a comparison of 30 days in Quebec (Hydro) against 10 days in Poland (Coal).

# 30 days in Quebec
res_30d_quebec = solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet, duration_days=30,
    datacenter=mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec
)

# 10 days in Poland (1/3 the training time)
res_10d_poland = solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet, duration_days=10,
    datacenter=mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland
)

c_q = res_30d_quebec.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
c_p = res_10d_poland.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude

table(
    ["Scenario", "Carbon (tonnes CO2)"],
    [
        ["30 days in Quebec", f"{c_q:.1f}"],
        ["10 days in Poland", f"{c_p:.1f}"],
    ]
)
info(Ratio=f"{c_p/c_q:.1f}x")

Scenario           Carbon (tonnes CO2)
──────────────────────────────────────
30 days in Quebec                  2.7
10 days in Poland                 55.7
Ratio:  20.4x








ImportantKey Insight



Geography is a larger lever than training duration for carbon footprint. Even training for one-third the time (10 days vs. 30 days) in Poland (Coal) emits 55.7 tonnes of \(\text{CO}_2\), which is 20.4× more than the full 30-day run in Quebec (Hydro) (2.7 tonnes). Because grid carbon intensity differs by 41× and total facility emissions per day differ by 61×, no plausible reduction in training time can compensate for a coal-heavy grid. For any organization serious about sustainable AI, datacenter location is not a logistics detail but a first-order systems design decision.

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
section: 5. Economic Angle: When Carbon Has a Price
text:
5. Economic Angle: When Carbon Has a Price
Carbon pricing (through taxes or cap-and-trade) gives emissions a financial cost and changes the economics of datacenter location. The cell below computes TCO with a carbon price of $50/tonne.

from mlsysim.solvers import EconomicsModel

econ = EconomicsModel()
carbon_price = 50  # USD per tonne CO2

rows = []
for grid in grids:
    tco = econ.solve(fleet=fleet, duration_days=30, grid=grid)
    carbon_cost = (tco.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude) * carbon_price
    total = tco.tco_usd + carbon_cost
    rows.append([tco.region_name, f"${tco.tco_usd:,.0f}", f"${carbon_cost:,.0f}", f"${total:,.0f}"])

table(["Region", "TCO ($)", "Carbon Cost ($)", "Total ($)"], rows)

Region           TCO ($)  Carbon Cost ($)  Total ($)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Quebec (Hydro)  $218,056             $137   $218,192
Norway (Hydro)  $218,056              $68   $218,124
US Average      $218,985           $3,100   $222,084
Poland (Coal)   $226,107           $8,358   $234,465


At $50/tonne, carbon pricing adds $137 to the 30-day run in Quebec (Hydro) (bringing total cost from $218,056 to $218,192) versus $8,358 in Poland (Coal) (bringing total cost from $226,107 to $234,465, a $16,273 spread). At higher carbon prices, this location differential grows proportionally.

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
1. Setup
First, import the necessary modules. This tutorial uses the Pipeline orchestrator directly instead of relying on the high-level Engine.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.engine.pipeline import Pipeline
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel, EconomicsModel

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
2. The Composable Pipeline
The Pipeline object accepts a list of resolvers. Calling .run() executes them in order, and the output of an early solver is automatically made available as input to later solvers.
A standard evaluation pipeline looks like this:

# 1. Define the execution graph
pipe = Pipeline([
    DistributedModel(),
    EconomicsModel()
])

# 2. Provide the initial inputs (Demand & Supply)
results = pipe.run(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Frontier_8K,
    batch_size=32,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.45,
    duration_days=30
)

# 3. Access results by stage name
tco = results["EconomicsModel"].tco_usd
print(f"Total Cost of Ownership: ${tco:,.2f}")

Total Cost of Ownership: $7,007,509.16


For Llama-3.1-8B on the 8,192-GPU Frontier Cluster (8192 GPUs) cluster over 30 days, DistributedModel computes a scaling efficiency of 64.4% and feeds into EconomicsModel, which reports a 30-day TCO of $7,007,509.16.

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
3. Injecting Custom Solvers
Because the pipeline is dynamic, it accepts custom analytical solvers. Suppose a custom plugin called PowerEfficiencyModel has been written (as described in the Extending the Engine guide).
It slots directly into the DAG:
# Assuming a custom ForwardModel subclass is defined:
# class PowerEfficiencyModel(ForwardModel): ...

custom_pipe = Pipeline([
    DistributedModel(),
    PowerEfficiencyModel(), # Injected right into the middle
    EconomicsModel()
])

# Use it just like before
# custom_pipe.run(...)

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
4. Callbacks (Middleware)
MLSys·im supports middleware hooks. To log metrics to an external platform (like a database, MLflow, or Weights & Biases), write a Callback class with an on_stage_end method.
The pipeline will trigger this method every time a solver finishes.

class WandbLogger:
    def on_stage_end(self, stage_name: str, result):
        print(f"[W&B Callback] Logging data for {stage_name}...")

        # If the result is a Pydantic model, dump it to a dict
        if hasattr(result, "model_dump"):
            metrics = result.model_dump(exclude_none=True)

            # Example: wandb.log({f"{stage_name}/{k}": v for k, v in metrics.items()})
            print(f"  -> Logged {len(metrics)} keys")

# Attach the logger
pipe.register_callback(WandbLogger())

# Run the pipeline again to see the callback fire
print("Running Pipeline with Callback:")
_ = pipe.run(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Frontier_8K,
    batch_size=32,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.45,
    duration_days=30
)

Running Pipeline with Callback:
[W&B Callback] Logging data for DistributedModel...
  -> Logged 12 keys
[W&B Callback] Logging data for EconomicsModel...
  -> Logged 11 keys

title: For Students
text: For a student taking a first ML systems course or preparing for industry interviews, MLSys·im offers a way to experiment with real hardware specifications and see why systems behave the way they do. Hardware registry specs come from datasheets where available; outputs are derived from documented equations.

title: For Students
text:
Learning Objectives
Students who work through the MLSys·im tutorials learn to:

Identify bottlenecks: Determine whether a workload is memory-bound or compute-bound on any hardware, and understand why
Reason quantitatively: Use real datasheet numbers (not made-up examples) to calculate latency, throughput, and cost
Build systems intuition: See how batch size, precision, parallelism strategy, and datacenter location each affect performance
Think across the stack: Connect workload characteristics to hardware specs to infrastructure constraints

title: For Students
text:
Prerequisites

Python: Comfortable with functions, loops, and f-strings
Math: Basic algebra (no calculus required; all solver equations are arithmetic)
ML: Familiarity with terms like “model parameters,” “inference,” and “training” (the Glossary defines everything else)

No GPU, no cloud account, and no special hardware are required. Installation is one command:
pip install mlsysim
See the Getting Started guide for development installs. Local install is the supported path; Colab works by running pip install mlsysim in the first cell, but one-click Colab/Binder launch buttons are not available yet.

title: For Students
text:
Quick Start

import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

# Load a model and hardware from the vetted registry
model = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
gpu   = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100

# Solve: is this workload memory-bound or compute-bound?
profile = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=gpu, batch_size=1, precision="fp16", efficiency=1.0)

print(f"Bottleneck: {profile.bottleneck}")
print(f"Latency:    {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")

Bottleneck: Memory
Latency:    0.54 ms

Composing Resolvers
Real-world questions require chaining multiple tiers. Here are three common patterns:

Serving Llama-70B on 4 H100s within budget

from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

serving = ServingModel().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=2048, batch_size=4
)
print(f"TTFT: {serving.ttft.to('ms'):~.1f}, ITL: {serving.itl.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"KV-Cache: {serving.kv_cache_size.to('GB'):~.2f}")

TTFT: 2428.1 ms, ITL: 43.75 ms
KV-Cache: 2.68 GB




The parameter that matters most for Llama-8B latency

from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.solvers import SensitivitySolver

sensitivity = SensitivitySolver().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    precision="fp16",
    perturbation_pct=10.0
)
print(f"Binding constraint: {sensitivity.binding_constraint}")
print(f"BW sensitivity:     {sensitivity.sensitivities['memory_bandwidth']:+.3f}")
print(f"FLOPS sensitivity:  {sensitivity.sensitivities['peak_flops']:+.3f}")

Binding constraint: memory_bandwidth
BW sensitivity:     -0.086
FLOPS sensitivity:  +0.000




The hardware a 50ms SLA requires

from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.solvers import SynthesisSolver
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_

synthesis = SynthesisSolver().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    target_latency=Q_("50 ms"),
    precision="fp16"
)
print(f"Required bandwidth: {synthesis.required_bw.to('TB/s'):~.2f}")
print(f"Required FLOPS:     {synthesis.required_flops.to('TFLOPs/s'):~.1f}")

Required bandwidth: 0.32 TB / s

title: API Stability Promise
text:
Applies to: mlsysim v0.1.x

This document defines which parts of the mlsysim API are stable, which are experimental, and what guarantees code built on top of the framework can rely on.



mlsysim follows Semantic Versioning with one important caveat: we are pre-1.0. Under semver, this means:







Version bump
What it means




0.1.x -> 0.1.y (patch)
Bug fixes only. No API changes. Safe to upgrade.


0.1.x -> 0.2.0 (minor)
Breaking changes allowed. Read the changelog before upgrading.


1.0.0
Full stability guarantee begins. Breaking changes require a major bump.



In practice: code pinned to mlsysim ~= 0.1.0 (any 0.1.x) will not break. Upgrading to 0.2.0 means updating imports and possibly adjusting call signatures.




These interfaces are locked for the entire 0.1.x series. Bug fixes may change return values (e.g., correcting a formula), but signatures and field names will not change.


from mlsysim import Engine

result = Engine.solve(
    model=...,        # ModelSpec or registry name
    hardware=...,     # HardwareSpec or registry name
    batch_size=32,    # int
    precision="fp16", # str: "fp32", "fp16", "bf16", "int8", "int4"
    efficiency=0.45,  # float: 0.0-1.0
)
All five parameters to Engine.solve() are stable. Their names, types, and positions will not change.



from mlsysim import Hardware

gpu = Hardware.Cloud.H100            # All current entries are stable
gpu = Hardware.Cloud.A100
gpu = Hardware.Edge.JetsonOrinNX
# ... every entry shipping in 0.1.x
New entries may be added in patch releases, but existing entries will not be removed or renamed.



from mlsysim import Models

model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B      # All current entries are stable
model = Models.Language.GPT2
# ... every entry shipping in 0.1.x
Same guarantee as Hardware: additions are allowed, removals are not.



Use nested canonical paths in Python:
mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100
mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B
mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
Flat aliases at the registry root (for example bare H100 or ResNet50 leaf names) were removed in the registry migration. The CLI still resolves short names (mlsysim eval Llama3_8B H100) for convenience.
Solvers not listed in mlsysim.__init__ (for example CompressionModel, MoERoutingModel) import from mlsysim.solvers. Workload types import from mlsysim.models.types.



from mlsysim import ReferenceStats, Scenarios
Scenarios.* is the executable scenario registry: each entry composes an existing Models.* workload, a Hardware.* or Systems.* target, and scenario-local constraints such as latency or power budget. ReferenceStats.* holds non-executable sourced anchors, such as mobile power envelopes, Waymo data-rate ranges, and TinyML case-study measurements.
There are no compatibility aliases between these namespaces. Use Scenarios.SmartDoorbell for an executable case and ReferenceStats.MobilePower for sourced non-executable anchors.



The following fields on the result object returned by Engine.solve() are stable:



Field
Type
Description




latency
pint.Quantity
Wall-clock time for one forward pass


throughput
pint.Quantity
Tokens/sec or samples/sec


bottleneck
str
"Compute" or "Memory"


mfu
float
Model FLOPs Utilization (0.0-1.0)


feasible
bool
Whether the workload fits in memory


energy
pint.Quantity
Energy consumption per forward pass






from mlsysim import ureg
The Pint unit registry instance is stable. All quantities returned by the engine use this registry.





These interfaces work today but are not yet finalized. Use them freely for exploration, but do not build production tooling against them without pinning to an exact version.


from mlsysim.solvers import ForwardModel, DistributedModel, ServingModel
The solver class hierarchy, their constructors, and their method signatures may change. The Engine.solve() facade insulates calling code from these changes, so prefer it over direct solver instantiation.
Solver classes are exported from mlsysim.solvers, not the package root. Use from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel so solver-specific dependencies stay explicit and the root namespace remains reserved for registries, units, and formatting helpers.



Engine.solve(..., is_training=True)  # experimental
The is_training flag will likely be replaced by separate Engine.train() and Engine.infer() methods in v0.2.0, or by a more expressive workload specification.



The API for composing multiple solver stages into a pipeline (e.g., prefill + decode, or TP + PP) is experimental. The abstraction is correct but the interface is still being refined.



The search/sweep API for exploring hardware-model combinations is experimental. Parameter names and result formats may change.



All mlsysim CLI command names, subcommands, and flags are experimental. Shell scripts that call the CLI should pin to an exact version.



Fields on specialized result types (DistributedResult, ServingResult, etc.) beyond the six stable PerformanceProfile fields listed above are experimental. They may be renamed, reorganized, or moved to nested objects.





These interfaces still work in v0.1.x but emit deprecation warnings and will be removed in the next minor release.
No public import path is deprecated in 0.1.2. Deprecations will be listed here and in the changelog before the next minor release.





Pin the dependency: mlsysim ~= 0.1.0 (allows 0.1.x patches, blocks 0.2.0).
Use Engine.solve() as the primary interface. It is the most stable entry point.
Use mlsysim.solvers only when solver-specific features are needed. The engine facade covers most use cases.
Run with warnings enabled (python3 -W default) to catch deprecation notices early.
Read the changelog before any minor version upgrade.

title: API Stability Promise
text:
These interfaces work today but are not yet finalized. Use them freely for exploration, but do not build production tooling against them without pinning to an exact version.


from mlsysim.solvers import ForwardModel, DistributedModel, ServingModel
The solver class hierarchy, their constructors, and their method signatures may change. The Engine.solve() facade insulates calling code from these changes, so prefer it over direct solver instantiation.
Solver classes are exported from mlsysim.solvers, not the package root. Use from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel so solver-specific dependencies stay explicit and the root namespace remains reserved for registries, units, and formatting helpers.



Engine.solve(..., is_training=True)  # experimental
The is_training flag will likely be replaced by separate Engine.train() and Engine.infer() methods in v0.2.0, or by a more expressive workload specification.



The API for composing multiple solver stages into a pipeline (e.g., prefill + decode, or TP + PP) is experimental. The abstraction is correct but the interface is still being refined.



The search/sweep API for exploring hardware-model combinations is experimental. Parameter names and result formats may change.



All mlsysim CLI command names, subcommands, and flags are experimental. Shell scripts that call the CLI should pin to an exact version.



Fields on specialized result types (DistributedResult, ServingResult, etc.) beyond the six stable PerformanceProfile fields listed above are experimental. They may be renamed, reorganized, or moved to nested objects.

text:
