title: Glossary
text: This page defines every technical term used across the MLSys·im documentation. When a term is first used on any page, it either links here or is defined inline. Terms marked with slide links point to the relevant lecture deck for deeper coverage.

title: Glossary
text:
A

AllReduce

A collective communication primitive in which every device contributes a local tensor and receives the globally reduced (typically summed) result. The dominant synchronization pattern in data-parallel training. Ring-AllReduce and tree-AllReduce are common algorithms; performance is modeled by the Alpha-Beta Model. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training, Vol II Ch 5: Collective Communication

Alpha-Beta Model (\(\alpha\)-\(\beta\))

An analytical model for communication cost: \(T_\text{comm} = \alpha + n\beta\), where \(\alpha\) is the per-message latency (seconds), \(n\) is the message size (bytes), and \(\beta\) is the inverse bandwidth (seconds/byte). Used throughout MLSys·im to estimate collective communication overhead in distributed training. Slides: Vol II Ch 3: Network Fabrics, Vol II Ch 5: Collective Communication

Arithmetic Intensity (AI)

The ratio of floating-point operations to bytes of memory accessed: \(I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{Bytes}\). High arithmetic intensity means the workload reuses data extensively (compute-bound); low arithmetic intensity means it streams data without reuse (memory-bound). Units: FLOP/byte. Determines which side of the Ridge Point a workload falls on in the Roofline Model. Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

title: Glossary
text:
B

Bandwidth (Memory Bandwidth)

The rate at which data can be transferred between memory (DRAM/HBM) and compute units. Measured in GB/s or TB/s. The A100, for example, provides 2.04 TB/s of HBM bandwidth (and the H100 provides 3.35 TB/s). Not to be confused with network bandwidth (inter-node communication rate) or bisection bandwidth (aggregate cross-section throughput of a network fabric). Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure, Vol II Ch 3: Network Fabrics

Batch Size

The number of inputs processed simultaneously in one forward pass. Larger batch sizes increase Arithmetic Intensity, shifting workloads from memory-bound toward compute-bound. In distributed training, the global batch size equals the per-device batch size multiplied by the number of data-parallel replicas. Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 8: Model Training

Bottleneck

The hardware resource that limits performance. For a given workload-hardware pair, either compute or memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, determined by comparing the workload’s Arithmetic Intensity to the hardware’s Ridge Point. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

title: Glossary
text:
C

CapEx (Capital Expenditure)

The upfront cost of purchasing hardware. In TCO analysis, CapEx is amortized over the hardware’s useful lifetime (typically 3–5 years). Slides: Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

Carbon Intensity

The mass of CO2-equivalent emissions per unit of electricity consumed, measured in gCO2e/kWh. Varies widely by region: 20 gCO2e/kWh (Quebec hydro) to 820 gCO2e/kWh (Poland coal). MLSys·im uses per-region carbon intensity values from the sustainability registry to estimate training and inference emissions. Slides: Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

Compute-Bound

A workload whose performance is limited by the hardware’s peak FLOP/s rate rather than memory bandwidth. Occurs when Arithmetic Intensity exceeds the Ridge Point. Remedies include using tensor cores, upgrading to a faster accelerator, or reducing precision. Contrast with Memory-Bound. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

Continuous Batching

A serving optimization that dynamically inserts and retires requests from a running batch, rather than waiting for all sequences in a static batch to finish before starting new ones. Improves GPU occupancy substantially for LLM inference, where sequence lengths vary widely. Also called iteration-level batching. Slides: Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture)

NVIDIA’s programming platform for writing GPU-accelerated programs. A “CUDA kernel” is a function that runs in parallel across thousands of GPU threads. Dispatch Tax is the per-kernel launch overhead inherent to this model. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

title: Glossary
text:
D

Data Parallelism (DP)

A distributed training strategy where the full model is replicated across \(N\) devices, each processing a different shard of the batch. Requires an AllReduce synchronization step after each backward pass to average gradients. Scales well for models that fit in a single device’s memory. See also Tensor Parallelism, Pipeline Parallelism, and 3D Parallelism. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

Dispatch Tax

The constant per-operation overhead of launching a GPU kernel (typically 0.01–0.1 ms for CUDA kernel launch). Becomes significant at small batch sizes where kernel launch time dominates actual compute time. Captured as the additive term in the Iron Law. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking

title: Glossary
text:
F

FLOP/s (Floating-Point Operations per Second)

The rate at which a device can perform floating-point arithmetic. The A100 achieves 312 TFLOP/s (and the H100 achieves 989 TFLOP/s) at FP16 via its Tensor Cores. Also written as TFLOP/s (tera-) or PFLOP/s (peta-). Not to be confused with FLOPs (a count, not a rate). Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking

FLOPs (Floating-Point Operations)

A count of arithmetic operations (multiplies, adds, etc.) required to execute a single inference or training step. A ResNet-50 (25.6M parameters) inference requires 8.2 GFLOPs; a GPT-3 (175B parameters) forward pass requires 350 GFLOPs per token. Not the same as FLOP/s (the rate). Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation

Forward Pass / Backward Pass

In neural network training, the forward pass runs input data through the model to produce a prediction. The backward pass (backpropagation) computes gradients, the direction and magnitude of change needed for each parameter to reduce error. In distributed systems, gradients must be synchronized across all devices after each backward pass via AllReduce. Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 8: Model Training

title: Glossary
text:
G

GQA (Grouped Query Attention)

A transformer attention variant where multiple query heads share a single key-value head, reducing KV-Cache memory by a factor equal to the group size without significantly affecting model quality. Used in Llama 3 (for example, Llama-3 70B uses 8 KV heads for 64 query heads, an 8× reduction) and other modern LLMs. See also KV-Cache. Slides: Vol I Ch 6: Network Architectures, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

title: Glossary
text:
H

HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory)

Stacked DRAM technology used in modern AI accelerators. Provides far higher bandwidth than GDDR (e.g., 2.04 TB/s on A100, 3.35 TB/s on H100) at the cost of limited capacity (80 GiB, or 85.9 GB, per A100/H100 device). The bandwidth ceiling in the Roofline Model is set by HBM. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure

title: Glossary
text:
I

InfiniBand

A high-throughput, low-latency network fabric commonly used in GPU clusters for distributed training. Supports RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) for zero-copy data transfer that bypasses the CPU. NDR InfiniBand provides 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) per port. See also NVLink (intra-node) vs. InfiniBand (inter-node). Slides: Vol II Ch 3: Network Fabrics

Iron Law of ML Systems

The fundamental performance equation: \[T = \max\!\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak} \times \eta},\; \frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{BW}}\right) + \text{Dispatch\_Tax}\] The \(\max\) captures the Roofline Model insight that performance is limited by whichever resource (compute or memory bandwidth) is the bottleneck. Named by analogy with the Iron Law of processor performance in computer architecture. Slides: Vol I Ch 8: Model Training, Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

ITL (Inter-Token Latency)

The time to generate each successive token after the first during LLM autoregressive decoding. Almost always Memory-Bound; each decode step loads the full model weights plus the KV-Cache. Measured in ms/token. See also TTFT. Slides: Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

title: Glossary
text:
K

Knowledge Distillation

A model compression technique where a smaller “student” model is trained to match the output distribution of a larger “teacher” model. Reduces model size and inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s accuracy. See also Quantization and Pruning. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression

KV-Cache

The cached Key and Value matrices from the transformer attention mechanism, retained across decoding steps to avoid recomputation. Memory footprint grows linearly with sequence length and batch size: \(\text{Bytes} = 2 \times L \times B \times d \times \text{layers} \times \text{bytes\_per\_param}\). GQA reduces KV-Cache size; PagedAttention manages it more efficiently. Slides: Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

title: Glossary
text:
L

Latency

The wall-clock time to complete one inference or training step. In MLSys·im, latency is the primary output of the Iron Law equation. Measured in ms or \(\mu\)s. Maximizing Throughput often conflicts with minimizing latency. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking, Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving

LLM (Large Language Model)

A transformer-based model trained on large text corpora, typically with billions of parameters. Examples: GPT-4, Llama 3 (8.0B, 70.6B, and 405B parameters), Gemini. Key serving metrics: TTFT and ITL. Key memory bottleneck: KV-Cache. Slides: Vol I Ch 6: Network Architectures

title: Glossary
text:
M

Memory-Bound

A workload whose performance is limited by the hardware’s memory Bandwidth, not its peak FLOP/s. Occurs when Arithmetic Intensity falls below the Ridge Point. Remedies include lower Precision, Operator Fusion, or faster memory (e.g., HBM3). Contrast with Compute-Bound. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

MFU (Model FLOP Utilization)

The fraction of theoretical peak FLOP/s actually achieved: \(\text{MFU} = \text{Achieved FLOP/s} / \text{Peak FLOP/s}\). Well-optimized training achieves 30–50% MFU; poorly optimized code may fall below 10%. MFU is the single most important efficiency metric for large-scale training runs. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

Microbatch

A subdivision of the training batch used in Pipeline Parallelism. Increasing the number of microbatches \(M\) reduces the Pipeline Bubble fraction: \(\text{Bubble} = (P{-}1) / (P{-}1{+}M)\), where \(P\) is the pipeline depth. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)

The average time a component operates before failing. For a fleet of \(N\) identical nodes, \(\text{MTBF}_\text{fleet} = \text{MTBF}_\text{node} / N\). A 1,024-node cluster with 100,000-hour node MTBF has a fleet MTBF of ~98 hours. Input to the Young-Daly Formula. Slides: Vol II Ch 7: Fault Tolerance

title: Glossary
text:
N

NVLink

NVIDIA’s high-bandwidth interconnect for GPU-to-GPU communication within a server. Provides 900 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth per GPU in DGX H100 systems. Required for Tensor Parallelism, where low-latency intra-node communication is critical. Contrast with InfiniBand for inter-node communication. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure, Vol II Ch 3: Network Fabrics

title: Glossary
text:
O

OpEx (Operational Expenditure)

The ongoing costs of running hardware: electricity, networking, cooling, labor. In cloud pricing, OpEx dominates over a 3-year period by 2–5x over CapEx. Slides: Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

Operator Fusion

Combining multiple small GPU kernels into a single larger one to reduce memory transfers between operations. For example, fusing a matrix multiply followed by an activation function avoids writing and re-reading the intermediate result from HBM. A key optimization for reducing Memory-Bound overhead. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

title: Glossary
text:
P

Pipeline Bubble

The fraction of time a pipeline-parallel system spends idle waiting for the first Microbatch to propagate through all stages: \(\text{Bubble} = (P{-}1) / (P{-}1{+}M)\), where \(P\) is pipeline depth and \(M\) is microbatch count. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

Pipeline Parallelism (PP)

A distributed training strategy that splits the model’s layers across devices, each device processing a different “stage.” Introduces a Pipeline Bubble of idle time. Complementary to Data Parallelism and Tensor Parallelism in 3D Parallelism. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

Precision

The numerical format used to represent weights and activations. fp32 (32-bit float) is most accurate; fp16/bf16 (16-bit) halves memory and doubles throughput on Tensor Cores; int8 and int4 further reduce memory at the cost of accuracy. Lower precision increases Arithmetic Intensity by reducing bytes per operation. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression

Progressive Lowering

MLSys·im’s architectural principle: workload specifications (demand) are progressively mapped onto hardware specifications (supply) through a chain of analytical transformations. The reverse of how hardware is typically specified: it starts from the algorithm, not the chip.

Pruning

A model compression technique that removes redundant weights or entire structures (channels, attention heads) from a trained model. Unstructured pruning zeros out individual weights; structured pruning removes whole rows/columns for hardware-friendly speedups. See also Quantization and Knowledge Distillation. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression

PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness)

\(\text{PUE} = \text{Total Facility Power} / \text{IT Equipment Power}\). A PUE of 1.0 is theoretical perfection; hyperscale datacenters achieve 1.1–1.4. Higher PUE means more energy wasted on cooling and facility overhead. Used in MLSys·im’s sustainability solver alongside Carbon Intensity and WUE. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure, Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

title: Glossary
text:
Q

Quantization

Reducing the numerical Precision of model weights and/or activations (e.g., FP32 to INT8 or INT4) to shrink memory footprint and increase throughput. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) converts a pre-trained model without retraining; Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) simulates low-precision during training for higher accuracy. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression

title: Glossary
text:
R

Ridge Point

The Arithmetic Intensity at which a workload transitions from Memory-Bound to Compute-Bound on a given hardware platform: \(I^* = \text{Peak FLOP/s} / \text{Memory BW}\). For the A100 at FP16: \(I^* = 312 \text{ TFLOP/s} / 2\.04 \text{ TB/s} \approx 153 \text{ FLOP/byte}\) (and for the H100 at FP16: \(989 \text{ TFLOP/s} / 3\.35 \text{ TB/s} \approx 295 \text{ FLOP/byte}\)). Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

Roofline Model

A visual and analytical tool that plots hardware performance ceilings (the “roofline”) and shows where workloads sit relative to them. The sloped region is Memory-Bound; the flat region is Compute-Bound; the inflection point is the Ridge Point. Introduced by Williams, Waterman, and Patterson (2009). MLSys·im implements a generalized roofline via the Iron Law. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

title: Glossary
text:
S

SLA (Service Level Agreement)

A target performance guarantee, typically specifying maximum acceptable latency and minimum throughput. For LLM serving, common SLAs target TTFT < 200 ms and ITL < 50 ms/token. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking, Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving

Speculative Decoding

An inference optimization where a small, fast “draft” model generates candidate tokens that are then verified in parallel by the full model. Reduces ITL by converting sequential autoregressive steps into a single parallel verification pass, at the cost of occasional rejected tokens. Slides: Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

SSoT (Single Source of Truth)

The principle that each specification (chip peak FLOP/s, grid carbon intensity, etc.) has exactly one authoritative location: the MLSys Zoo. All computations derive from the Zoo, eliminating inconsistencies from stale copied values.

Systolic Array

A grid of processing elements that rhythmically pass data to their neighbors, performing a multiply-accumulate at each step. The dominant dataflow architecture in ML accelerators: Google TPUs use systolic arrays for matrix multiplication, and NVIDIA Tensor Cores implement a similar systolic-like pattern. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

title: Glossary
text:
T

TCO (Total Cost of Ownership)

The full cost of a system over its lifetime: \(\text{TCO} = \text{CapEx}_{\text{amortized}} + \text{OpEx}\). Includes hardware purchase, electricity, cooling, networking, and labor. MLSys·im’s TCO solver computes this from hardware registry specs and regional energy costs. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure, Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

TDP (Thermal Design Power)

The maximum sustained power a chip is designed to dissipate under load, in Watts. Relevant for datacenter cooling capacity planning. An H100 SXM5 has a TDP of 700 W (an A100 has 400 W). Used in MLSys·im to compute energy consumption and TCO. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure

Tensor Core

A specialized hardware unit in NVIDIA GPUs designed for matrix-multiply-accumulate operations. Achieves much higher throughput than standard CUDA cores for ML workloads. The A100’s 312 TFLOP/s peak (FP16) comes from its tensor cores, not its CUDA cores. Functionally similar to a Systolic Array. Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

Tensor Parallelism (TP)

A distributed training strategy that splits individual matrix multiplications across devices within a node. Requires high-bandwidth intra-node connectivity (NVLink). Combined with Data Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism in 3D Parallelism. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

3D Parallelism

The combination of Data Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism, and Pipeline Parallelism to scale training across hundreds or thousands of GPUs. TP operates within a node (over NVLink), PP across a small group of nodes, and DP across the remaining replicas. The standard recipe for training frontier LLMs. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

Throughput

The number of samples (or tokens) processed per unit time: \(\text{Throughput} = \text{Batch Size} / \text{Latency}\). Maximizing throughput often conflicts with minimizing Latency. Larger batches increase throughput but also increase per-request latency. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking

TTFT (Time to First Token)

The latency from receiving a user query to generating the first output token in an LLM serving system. Determined primarily by the prefill phase, which is Compute-Bound. Target: <200 ms for interactive applications. See also ITL. Slides: Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

title: Glossary
text:
U

Utilization (\(\eta\))

The fraction of theoretical peak FLOP/s actually achieved in practice. Typical values: 30–50% for well-optimized training, 10–30% for inference. MLSys·im uses \(\eta\) as a parameter in the Iron Law; see the hardware registry for per-device defaults. Closely related to MFU. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

title: Glossary
text:
W

WUE (Water Usage Effectiveness)

Liters of water consumed per kilowatt-hour of energy. Relevant for datacenters using evaporative cooling. MLSys·im estimates water usage as: \(\text{Water (L)} = \text{Energy (kWh)} \times \text{WUE}\). Slides: Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

title: Glossary
text:
Y

Young-Daly Formula

The optimal checkpoint interval for fault-tolerant distributed training: \(\tau_\text{opt} = \sqrt{2 \times \delta \times \text{MTBF}_\text{fleet}}\), where \(\delta\) is the time to save one checkpoint and MTBF is the mean time between failures of the fleet. Named after Young (1974) and Daly (2006). Slides: Vol II Ch 7: Fault Tolerance



This glossary is updated with each MLSys·im release. If a term is missing, please open an issue.

title: engine.solvers.acceptance
text:
engine.solvers.acceptance
Agent evaluation solvers: what a set of graded trials supports about a configuration.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated trial counts, verdicts, and costs: the acceptance rate when some trials never resolve; a grader’s error rates against a reference assessment; how tasks and repeated runs share an evaluation budget; Wald and Wilson intervals; the task counts a precision or detection target needs; a paired candidate-against-baseline comparison (Newcombe’s method 10, McNemar’s exact test, and the variance pairing removes); the within-model spread of a leaderboard across scaffolds and the neighboring ranks it cannot separate; repeated runs of one task against new tasks; batch and sequential selection under one candidate cap; and the summary of a paired repeated-run evaluation. Repeated-run consistency over k recurrences is horizon compounding (HorizonCompoundingModel).





Name
Description




BinomialIntervalsModel
Wald and Wilson intervals for several success counts out of trials.


CappedSelectionCostModel
Batch against sequential selection of up to cap candidates under an exact checker.


PairedComparisonModel
A candidate against a baseline, one trial of each on the same tasks.


ProportionPlanningModel
How many independent tasks a precision or a detection target needs.


TaskMixConsistencyModel
All-pass probability of k runs: one task repeated against k new tasks.





engine.solvers.acceptance.BinomialIntervalsModel()
Wald and Wilson intervals for several success counts out of trials.
Wald collapses to zero width at x = 0 and leaves [0, 1] near the boundaries; Wilson keeps a nonzero width and stays inside, and the two nearly coincide near one half. The Wilson upper limit at x = 0 is z^2 / (n + z^2).



engine.solvers.acceptance.CappedSelectionCostModel()
Batch against sequential selection of up to cap candidates under an exact checker.
Both policies return a passing candidate with q = 1 - (1 - p)^cap. The batch generates and checks all cap; sequential selection stops at the first pass and starts q / p candidates on average. Charging every initiated trial to the accepted ones gives cap c / q against (c / p), where c is generation plus checking: sequential cost per accepted task does not depend on the cap, and only p lowers it.



engine.solvers.acceptance.PairedComparisonModel()
A candidate against a baseline, one trial of each on the same tasks.
Only discordant pairs move the difference; Newcombe’s method 10 gives its interval, and a noninferiority gate needs the lower limit above -tolerance. Lower half-widths shrink as 1 / sqrt(n), so the pairs that center the expected lower limit on the margin are n [(delta - lower) / (delta + tolerance)]^2 (even odds of clearing), and a true gain of zero needs the half-width inside the tolerance itself. The paired outcome has variance d - delta^2 per pair against p_c (1 - p_c) + p_b (1 - p_b) for two independent arms. McNemar’s exact test answers the separate equality question.



engine.solvers.acceptance.ProportionPlanningModel()
How many independent tasks a precision or a detection target needs.
One rate: the normal half-width z sqrt(p (1 - p) / n) shrinks as 1 / sqrt(n), and ceil(z^2 p (1 - p) / h^2) tasks reach a half-width h. Two independent arms at average rate p: about 2 (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 p (1 - p) / delta^2 tasks per arm detect a difference delta, so halving delta quadruples the count. The detection quantiles are the rounded planning values the caller states.



engine.solvers.acceptance.TaskMixConsistencyModel()
All-pass probability of k runs: one task repeated against k new tasks.
Repeating one randomly drawn task passes every run with E[p_i^k]; k independently drawn tasks all pass with (E[p_i])^k, which Jensen’s inequality places at or below it, strictly when task difficulty varies and k >= 2. Task types are equally weighted.







Name
Description




z_for_confidence
Two-sided standard normal quantile for a confidence level (1.96 at 0.95).





engine.solvers.acceptance.z_for_confidence(confidence)
Two-sided standard normal quantile for a confidence level (1.96 at 0.95).

title: physics.layers
text:
physics.layers
Layer-level counting laws for neural network architectures (added 2026-10-20).
Weight, multiply-add, and byte counts for one layer are products of its dimensions and live on the calculation scenarios (engine/scenario_types.py: DenseLayerScenario, ConvLayerScenario, RecurrentStepScenario). This module holds the few laws those counts compose with: how a stack of convolutions widens its view, how a depthwise separable factoring shrinks a convolution, and how a product of per-layer gradient gains decays with depth.





Name
Description

Product of depth per-layer gradient factors of average gain (plain stack, no skips).


calc_layers_for_receptive_field
Fewest stride-1 kernel-wide convolutions whose receptive field reaches field pixels.


calc_receptive_field
Side of the input window one output sees after layers stride-1 kernel-wide convolutions.


calc_resnet_bottleneck_macs
Multiply-adds per image of a bottleneck ResNet, by kernel size (added 2026-10-21).


calc_separable_cost_fraction
Depthwise separable cost over a standard kernel-by-kernel convolution (Howard et al. 2017).





physics.layers.calc_gradient_product(gain, depth)
Product of depth per-layer gradient factors of average gain (plain stack, no skips).



physics.layers.calc_layers_for_receptive_field(field, kernel)
Fewest stride-1 kernel-wide convolutions whose receptive field reaches field pixels.



physics.layers.calc_receptive_field(layers, kernel)
Side of the input window one output sees after layers stride-1 kernel-wide convolutions.
Each layer adds kernel - 1 pixels to the one-pixel start.



physics.layers.calc_resnet_bottleneck_macs(
    stages=((64, 3), (128, 4), (256, 6), (512, 3)),
    input_size=224,
    num_classes=1000,
    stride_on_3x3=False,
)
Multiply-adds per image of a bottleneck ResNet, by kernel size (added 2026-10-21).
The architecture of He et al. (2016), Table 1: a 7x7/2 stem, a 3x3/2 max pool, then stages of bottleneck blocks (1x1 to width, 3x3, 1x1 to 4 x width), a 1x1 projection on each stage’s first block, global pooling, and a fully connected classifier. The default ResNet-50 stages give 1.850 G of 3x3 and 3.858 G of total multiply-adds at 224x224. The original network strides the first 1x1 of a downsampling block (stride_on_3x3=False); torchvision’s v1.5 strides the 3x3 (about 4.09 G in total).
Returns {"7x7", "3x3", "1x1", "fc", "total"} in multiply-adds.



physics.layers.calc_separable_cost_fraction(kernel, out_channels)
Depthwise separable cost over a standard kernel-by-kernel convolution (Howard et al. 2017).
A depthwise step (one filter per input channel) and a pointwise 1x1 step cost 1/out_channels + 1/kernel**2 of the standard convolution’s multiply-adds or weights.

title: solvers.BatchingOptimizer
text:
solvers.BatchingOptimizer()
Finds the maximum batch size that satisfies a P99 latency SLA.
Searches the continuous batching design space using an M/M/c queueing model to find the optimal balance between throughput and tail latency.





Name
Description




solve
Determine the maximum batch size that satisfies a P99 latency SLA.





solvers.BatchingOptimizer.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    seq_len,
    sla_latency_ms,
    arrival_rate_qps,
    num_replicas=1,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
    max_search_batch=256,
)
Determine the maximum batch size that satisfies a P99 latency SLA.
Exhaustively scans batch sizes 1..max_search_batch. For each candidate b, the per-batch service latency is TTFT + ITL * seq_len from ServingModel, and the batch arrival rate is arrival_rate_qps / b (requests are grouped into batches). A candidate is feasible when the model fits in memory, the M/M/c queue is stable, and the queueing P99 meets the SLA. Among feasible candidates the largest batch wins, since throughput grows with batch size.

Analyzes Cluster Orchestration and Queueing (Little’s Law).
Caveat: This model uses a pedagogical M/D/1 queue (single server, deterministic service) to establish macroscopic wait-time bounds for dedicated, monolithic cluster workloads. For detailed multi-tenant job packing and preemption, a discrete-event M/G/c scheduler simulation would be required.

Physical-plant solvers: the stopping, actuation, heat, and power budgets of an embodied machine (added 2026-10-20).

Each model takes stated inputs and returns every intermediate a budget quotes, so a chapter, a slide deck, and a lab read the same arithmetic. The equations themselves live in physics/ (robotics/stopping.py, drivetrain.py, motors.py); these models only compose them into the budgets of one machine.

Upper bound on the per-trial failure rate after a failure-free campaign.





engine.solvers.plant.BrakingCeilingsModel()
The three ceilings on a credible deceleration (traction, tip-over, drive torque) and back-EMF headroom.
Composes calc_braking_limits for a wheeled base driven by direct-drive hub motors at a configured current limit, adds the rated-current torque ceiling and the inspected-floor traction ceiling (all weight on the driven wheels), and checks the terminal voltage braking and driving need at speed.



engine.solvers.plant.ContinuousDeratingModel()
Installed continuous torque relative to the catalog rating.
Continuous torque scales as sqrt((T_max - T_amb) / theta): a hotter ambient and a larger installed thermal resistance each cut it.



engine.solvers.plant.DiagnosticCoverageModel()
Diagnostic coverage that leaves at most target of a raw fault rate unmitigated, and the zero-miss injection campaign that demonstrates it (added 2026-10-20).
Rates are in FIT (faults per 10^9 hours). The raw rate is the sum of the strata; coverage C_diag = 1 - target / raw. Each injection misses with probability 1 - C_diag, so n zero-miss injections bound it at confidence C when n >= ln(1 - C) / ln(C_diag); the rule of three approximates n by 3 / (1 - C_diag). Drawn in proportion to the rates, each stratum receives its share of the n injections.



engine.solvers.plant.DriveBusModel()
A shared drive bus: sustained sag under a coincident load step, and the regenerative surge of a stop.
Sag Delta V = Delta I R_bus against the converter lockout; the step current that would spend the depleted pack’s headroom is (V_low - V_uvlo) / R_bus. A stop from speed v returns a share of (1/2) m v^2; into the bus capacitance alone, V_final = sqrt(V_full^2 + 2 E / C). Speed falls linearly at constant deceleration, so regenerated power falls linearly from 2 E / t_stop, and a chopper resistor at the clamp must satisfy R <= V_clamp^2 / P_peak.



engine.solvers.plant.ExponentialRareEventModel()
One rare exponential tail estimated by plain Monte Carlo, a zero-failure campaign, and cross-entropy importance sampling (added 2026-10-20).
The operational variable is exponential with mean; failure is a draw past threshold, so p = exp(-threshold / mean). Plain Monte Carlo needs (1 - p) / (p r^2) runs for relative error r; a zero-failure campaign needs ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - p)) clean runs to bound p. The cross-entropy method with elite_share reaches the threshold in a few levels; its exponential proposal gives the per-draw relative variance, the weighted runs for r, the share of proposal draws that fail, and the effective sample size.



engine.solvers.plant.FreshnessProfileModel()
A moving target’s freshness deadline against a capture-to-onset age profile.
The deadline is the tolerance left after the initial error, divided by the target speed: Delta t_fresh = (r_tol - e_0) / v. Stage percentiles are summed per percentile; the target’s travel at the median chain and at the system tail age is compared with the allowed error.



engine.solvers.plant.GearRatioCostModel()
Holding heat and reflected inertia of one motor holding one joint torque, per gear ratio.
Motor torque tau_m = tau_out / (eta N); copper loss (tau_m / K_m)^2 with K_m = K_t / sqrt(R_loss); reflected inertia N^2 J_in. Their product is tau_out^2 J_in / (eta^2 K_m^2), independent of N.



engine.solvers.plant.GearedRotorModel()
Reflected rotor inertia N^2 J_rotor, sized as a solid flywheel, and the inertia match.
A solid disk of radius r has J = m r^2 / 2, so m = 2 J / r^2. Joint acceleration for a fixed motor torque peaks at N* = sqrt(J_load / J_rotor); at N it is 2x / (1 + x^2) of that peak, x = N / N*.



engine.solvers.plant.HubDriveElectricalModel()
Electrical time constant, voltage-limited current ramp, and phase-short braking peak of a hub drive.
tau_e = L / R (line quantities, the same ratio as per phase for a star winding); at stall the back-EMF is zero, so the full bus voltage ramps the current at V / L: t = L I / V. Shorted windings brake hardest where the winding reactance equals its resistance: omega_e = R / L, which is omega_e / p at the wheel for p pole pairs. The same R / L, divided by 2 pi, is the winding’s current pole in hertz.



engine.solvers.plant.SpeedStepModel()
Braking travel added by raising the speed setpoint, and the delay that costs the same distance.
Braking travel grows as v^2; the added travel divided by the base speed is the pre-brake delay that would cost the same distance at the base speed.



engine.solvers.plant.StallDeratingModel()
Steady stall temperature with copper’s resistance feedback, and the hold the winding can sustain.
Steady state: dT = I^2 R_0 [1 + alpha (T_amb - T_0 + dT)] theta, linear in dT, so dT = c / (1 - g) with loop gain g = I^2 R_0 theta alpha (runaway if g >= 1). The sustainable loss at the limit is (T_limit - T_amb) / theta at the hot resistance R(T_limit).



engine.solvers.plant.ThermalBurstModel()
Burst horizons from a cold and a heat-soaked start, the average-power duty screen, and the periodic peak.
First-order lumped winding at fixed resistance: tau = theta C; the burst drives the winding toward T_amb + P theta; the duty screen holds the average loss to (T_ceiling - T_amb) / theta; the off-time is rounded up to 0.1 s and the resulting schedule’s periodic peak is checked against the ceiling.



engine.solvers.plant.ThrottledStageModel()
A compute-bound stage at a fraction of full clock: its time scales by the inverse clock ratio, and the added age is paid as travel at the stated speed.



engine.solvers.plant.ZeroFailureModel()
Upper bound on the per-trial failure rate after a failure-free campaign.
Poisson (rule of three):  p_upper = -ln(1 - C) / n
exact binomial:           p_upper = 1 - (1 - C)^(1/n)
With target_rate, also the clean trials that bound the rate at the target: ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - target)), and its rule-of-three estimate -ln(1 - C) / target (exact form and target added 2026-10-20).

The three ceilings on a credible deceleration (traction, tip-over, drive torque) and back-EMF headroom.
Composes calc_braking_limits for a wheeled base driven by direct-drive hub motors at a configured current limit, adds the rated-current torque ceiling and the inspected-floor traction ceiling (all weight on the driven wheels), and checks the terminal voltage braking and driving need at speed.



engine.solvers.plant.ContinuousDeratingModel()
Installed continuous torque relative to the catalog rating.
Continuous torque scales as sqrt((T_max - T_amb) / theta): a hotter ambient and a larger installed thermal resistance each cut it.



engine.solvers.plant.DiagnosticCoverageModel()
Diagnostic coverage that leaves at most target of a raw fault rate unmitigated, and the zero-miss injection campaign that demonstrates it (added 2026-10-20).
Rates are in FIT (faults per 10^9 hours). The raw rate is the sum of the strata; coverage C_diag = 1 - target / raw. Each injection misses with probability 1 - C_diag, so n zero-miss injections bound it at confidence C when n >= ln(1 - C) / ln(C_diag); the rule of three approximates n by 3 / (1 - C_diag). Drawn in proportion to the rates, each stratum receives its share of the n injections.



engine.solvers.plant.DriveBusModel()
A shared drive bus: sustained sag under a coincident load step, and the regenerative surge of a stop.
Sag Delta V = Delta I R_bus against the converter lockout; the step current that would spend the depleted pack’s headroom is (V_low - V_uvlo) / R_bus. A stop from speed v returns a share of (1/2) m v^2; into the bus capacitance alone, V_final = sqrt(V_full^2 + 2 E / C). Speed falls linearly at constant deceleration, so regenerated power falls linearly from 2 E / t_stop, and a chopper resistor at the clamp must satisfy R <= V_clamp^2 / P_peak.



engine.solvers.plant.ExponentialRareEventModel()
One rare exponential tail estimated by plain Monte Carlo, a zero-failure campaign, and cross-entropy importance sampling (added 2026-10-20).
The operational variable is exponential with mean; failure is a draw past threshold, so p = exp(-threshold / mean). Plain Monte Carlo needs (1 - p) / (p r^2) runs for relative error r; a zero-failure campaign needs ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - p)) clean runs to bound p. The cross-entropy method with elite_share reaches the threshold in a few levels; its exponential proposal gives the per-draw relative variance, the weighted runs for r, the share of proposal draws that fail, and the effective sample size.



engine.solvers.plant.FreshnessProfileModel()
A moving target’s freshness deadline against a capture-to-onset age profile.
The deadline is the tolerance left after the initial error, divided by the target speed: Delta t_fresh = (r_tol - e_0) / v. Stage percentiles are summed per percentile; the target’s travel at the median chain and at the system tail age is compared with the allowed error.



engine.solvers.plant.GearRatioCostModel()
Holding heat and reflected inertia of one motor holding one joint torque, per gear ratio.
Motor torque tau_m = tau_out / (eta N); copper loss (tau_m / K_m)^2 with K_m = K_t / sqrt(R_loss); reflected inertia N^2 J_in. Their product is tau_out^2 J_in / (eta^2 K_m^2), independent of N.



engine.solvers.plant.GearedRotorModel()
Reflected rotor inertia N^2 J_rotor, sized as a solid flywheel, and the inertia match.
A solid disk of radius r has J = m r^2 / 2, so m = 2 J / r^2. Joint acceleration for a fixed motor torque peaks at N* = sqrt(J_load / J_rotor); at N it is 2x / (1 + x^2) of that peak, x = N / N*.



engine.solvers.plant.HubDriveElectricalModel()
Electrical time constant, voltage-limited current ramp, and phase-short braking peak of a hub drive.
tau_e = L / R (line quantities, the same ratio as per phase for a star winding); at stall the back-EMF is zero, so the full bus voltage ramps the current at V / L: t = L I / V. Shorted windings brake hardest where the winding reactance equals its resistance: omega_e = R / L, which is omega_e / p at the wheel for p pole pairs. The same R / L, divided by 2 pi, is the winding’s current pole in hertz.



engine.solvers.plant.SpeedStepModel()
Braking travel added by raising the speed setpoint, and the delay that costs the same distance.
Braking travel grows as v^2; the added travel divided by the base speed is the pre-brake delay that would cost the same distance at the base speed.



engine.solvers.plant.StallDeratingModel()
Steady stall temperature with copper’s resistance feedback, and the hold the winding can sustain.
Steady state: dT = I^2 R_0 [1 + alpha (T_amb - T_0 + dT)] theta, linear in dT, so dT = c / (1 - g) with loop gain g = I^2 R_0 theta alpha (runaway if g >= 1). The sustainable loss at the limit is (T_limit - T_amb) / theta at the hot resistance R(T_limit).



engine.solvers.plant.ThermalBurstModel()
Burst horizons from a cold and a heat-soaked start, the average-power duty screen, and the periodic peak.
First-order lumped winding at fixed resistance: tau = theta C; the burst drives the winding toward T_amb + P theta; the duty screen holds the average loss to (T_ceiling - T_amb) / theta; the off-time is rounded up to 0.1 s and the resulting schedule’s periodic peak is checked against the ceiling.



engine.solvers.plant.ThrottledStageModel()
A compute-bound stage at a fraction of full clock: its time scales by the inverse clock ratio, and the added age is paid as travel at the stated speed.



engine.solvers.plant.ZeroFailureModel()
Upper bound on the per-trial failure rate after a failure-free campaign.
Poisson (rule of three):  p_upper = -ln(1 - C) / n
exact binomial:           p_upper = 1 - (1 - C)^(1/n)
With target_rate, also the clean trials that bound the rate at the target: ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - target)), and its rule-of-three estimate -ln(1 - C) / target (exact form and target added 2026-10-20).

title: solvers.ErrorFeedbackModel
text:
solvers.ErrorFeedbackModel
solvers.ErrorFeedbackModel()
A compressor that sends each value rounded to a whole unit, with error feedback.
Without a residual, every value below half a unit is lost. With error feedback the worker adds the carried residual e_t to the gradient, sends the rounded v_t, and keeps e_{t+1} = g_t + e_t - v_t; what is sent plus the last residual equals the true sum at every step.
Literature Source: Karimireddy et al. (2019), “Error Feedback Fixes SignSGD”.

    gpus_per_node,
    intra_node_bw,
    inter_node_bw,
    intra_node_lat=Q_('500 ns'),
    inter_node_lat=Q_('5 us'),
)
Calculates communication time for a Hierarchical AllReduce collective.
This models the standard topology of modern GPU clusters (e.g., NVLink within a node, InfiniBand across nodes). It operates in three phases: 1. Reduce-Scatter locally within each node (using fast intra-node BW). 2. AllReduce the smaller, partially reduced chunks globally across nodes (using slower inter-node BW). 3. AllGather the fully reduced chunks locally within each node.

With a single NIC shared by all g local ranks, the inter phase costs 2(n-1)/n * M / beta — g times this model’s phase-2 term — and this function understates the total accordingly.

Compute throughput penalty from oversubscription.
For an idealized workload with baseline step time T_base, oversubscribing the fabric stretches only the communication fraction::
T_new = T_base * [(1 - f) + f * r]
relative_throughput = T_base / T_new = 1 / ((1 - f) + f * r)
where: - f = communication fraction of baseline step time - r = N:1 oversubscription ratio (e.g., 2.0, 4.0)

    element_bytes,
    sustained_flops,
    link_bandwidth,
)
Smallest per-device sequence chunk whose attention compute hides the next K/V tile.
In ring attention each device computes attention for its n-token query chunk against one arriving key/value tile while the next tile crosses the link. Per tile, compute grows as n^2 d and transfer as n d s bytes (keys and values at s bytes per element), so the transfer hides when n >= s R / (2 B) for sustained rate R and link bandwidth B (Liu et al. 2023). Returns n in tokens. Added 2026-10-20.

)

Reduce-Scatter locally within each node (using fast intra-node BW). 2. AllReduce the smaller, partially reduced chunks globally across nodes (using slower inter-node BW). 3. AllGather the fully reduced chunks locally within each node.

title: engine.solvers.reinforcement
text:
engine.solvers.reinforcement
Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards: what a reward measures and what the loop costs.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated rates, counts, and durations: the share of an update’s accepted rollouts that failed, binary rewards centered on a fixed baseline, a shaped reward’s ordering condition, a turn valued by forked continuations and the tokens forking costs, group-relative coefficients, the per-token push of length normalization, the rollouts one informative group costs, an all-pass rule over repeated trials, the room a ratio clip leaves, a sandbox slot’s episode cycle, a group barrier, and a verifier pool. None models a trained network’s learning dynamics.





Name
Description




CenteredRewardModel
Binary terminal rewards centered on a fixed baseline: r - b.


ContinuationForkCostModel
Tokens generated when branches continuations are forked at chosen turns.


ForkValueModel
One turn valued by forking k binary continuations before and after it.


GroupBarrierModel
A synchronous group whose step waits for its slowest member.


GroupCoefficientsModel
Group-relative (GRPO) coefficients (r_i - mean) / (std + epsilon) of one group.


LengthNormalizationModel
Per-token push of two rollouts with the same coefficient under per-rollout averaging.


RatioClipModel
The probability ceiling a symmetric ratio clip 1 +/- epsilon sets on one token.


RepeatedVerificationModel
An all-pass rule over n independent trials of one candidate.


RewardCompositionModel
True and false accepts among one update’s rollouts under an imperfect verifier.


RolloutSlotCycleModel
A sandbox slot running one episode at a time, under a cold and a snapshot reset.


RolloutStepBudgetModel
One update’s generated tokens and the rollouts spent per informative group.


VerifierPoolModel
Verification workers for a stationary stream of completed trajectories.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.CenteredRewardModel()
Binary terminal rewards centered on a fixed baseline: r - b.
A positive baseline makes every failure’s centered score negative, so the update pushes every turn of a failed rollout down alike.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.ContinuationForkCostModel()
Tokens generated when branches continuations are forked at chosen turns.
Forking at every boundary costs 1 + m (H - 1) / 2 times the base trajectory, which grows with the square of the horizon in tokens.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.ForkValueModel()
One turn valued by forking k binary continuations before and after it.
Each fork’s sampled mean has standard error at most 1 / (2 sqrt k); the difference of two independent means at most sqrt 2 times that. The difference is resolved when it exceeds two difference bounds.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.GroupBarrierModel()
A synchronous group whose step waits for its slowest member.
Every slot is held until the barrier, so the reserved slot time is G x max and the busy share is mean / max.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.GroupCoefficientsModel()
Group-relative (GRPO) coefficients (r_i - mean) / (std + epsilon) of one group.
Every sampled token of rollout i carries coefficient i. The dispersion divisor (G or G - 1) and the stabilizer are part of the objective; a lone pass in a group of G binary rewards gets sqrt(G - 1) as epsilon goes to zero.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.LengthNormalizationModel()
Per-token push of two rollouts with the same coefficient under per-rollout averaging.
Each rollout’s loss is divided by its own length, so the shorter rollout’s tokens each move long / short times as far. A failure is pushed down hardest when it is short, so failures drift long.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.RatioClipModel()
The probability ceiling a symmetric ratio clip 1 +/- epsilon sets on one token.
A dominant token’s ceiling can exceed 1 (the clip does not bind), while a rare token may rise only epsilon p per update.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.RepeatedVerificationModel()
An all-pass rule over n independent trials of one candidate.
Graded once, a group of G incorrect candidates holds at least one false pass with probability 1 - (1 - q_bad)^G. Requiring all n trials to pass accepts an incorrect candidate with q_bad^n and rejects a correct one with 1 - q_good^n. Stopping at the first failed trial runs sum_{j<n} q^j trials on average.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.RewardCompositionModel()
True and false accepts among one update’s rollouts under an imperfect verifier.
tasks x group rollouts pass with probability p; the verifier accepts a pass with probability valid_accept_rate and a failure with false_accept_rate. Expected counts carry no rounding. The false share is Bayes’ rule over the accepts, so it moves with the policy’s pass rate as well as with the verifier.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.RolloutSlotCycleModel()
A sandbox slot running one episode at a time, under a cold and a snapshot reset.
Each episode is decisions x (model + tool) plus an assessment, then a reset. Capacity is slots / cycle. Faster resets raise capacity only by the reset’s share of the cycle (Amdahl’s law); the work floor remains.



engine.solvers.reinforcement.RolloutStepBudgetModel()
One update’s generated tokens and the rollouts spent per informative group.
A group of G independent binary attempts at pass rate p carries reward contrast with probability 1 - p^G - (1 - p)^G; a group without it moves no weights, so each informative group costs G / P(contrast) rollouts (infinite at p = 0 or p = 1, where no group carries contrast).



engine.solvers.reinforcement.VerifierPoolModel()
Verification workers for a stationary stream of completed trajectories.
By Little’s law the busy workers are the arrival rate times the service time per trajectory (every trial executes in this sizing case); the pool is that demand over the target utilization, rounded up.

title: solvers.ServingModel
text:
solvers.ServingModel()
Analyzes the two-phase LLM serving lifecycle: Pre-fill vs. Decoding.
LLM inference is not a single mathematical operation; it is a stateful process with two distinct physical regimes (Compute-bound Pre-fill and Memory-bound Decoding).
Literature Source: 1. Pope et al. (2023), “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference.” 2. Agrawal et al. (2024), “Sarathi-Serve” (chunked prefill scheduling). 3. Patel et al. (2024), “Splitwise” and Zhong et al. (2024), “DistServe” (prefill/decode disaggregation).
Formula contract: - TTFT is prefill compute over new prompt tokens plus dispatch overhead and, for disaggregated serving, KV-transfer time. - ITL is the decode lower bound: model weights plus KV cache streamed from decode memory bandwidth, plus the configured framework layer tax. - KV memory always covers the full sequence, even when prompt caching skips part of the prefill computation.





Name
Description




solve
Solves for LLM serving performance.

    model,
    hardware,
    seq_len,
    batch_size=1,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
    decode_hardware=None,
    network_bandwidth=Q_('100 GB/s'),
    draft_model=None,
    draft_acceptance_rate=0.7,
    cached_prefix_len=0,
    prefill_chunk_tokens=None,
)

title: engine.solvers.reliability
text:
engine.solvers.reliability
Reliability and checkpoint-interval solvers.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__); kept per-domain so the logic stays reviewable.





Name
Description




CheckpointIntervalModel
Young-Daly checkpoint interval and the share of wall time it wastes.


RecoveryBudgetModel
Cold-restart budget for one failure, and its cost per day at a failure interval.


ReliabilityModel
Calculates Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and optimal checkpointing intervals.


SeriesFailureModel
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.





engine.solvers.reliability.CheckpointIntervalModel()
Young-Daly checkpoint interval and the share of wall time it wastes.
tau* = sqrt(2 * write_time * MTBF) balances the write share write_time / tau against the rework share tau / (2 * MTBF); at the optimum the two are equal. Literature: Young (1974); Daly (2006). Added 2026-10-20.



engine.solvers.reliability.RecoveryBudgetModel()
Cold-restart budget for one failure, and its cost per day at a failure interval.
The budget is detection + restart + checkpoint load + warmup (RecoveryProfile.cold_restart_time); a job that fails every failure_interval pays it 1 day / failure_interval times a day, on every one of its n_devices. Rework since the last save is charged to checkpoint waste, not here. Added 2026-10-20.



engine.solvers.reliability.ReliabilityModel()
Calculates Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and optimal checkpointing intervals.
This model handles the reliability modeling of massive clusters, helping determine the ‘Goodput’ of long-running training jobs. It identifies the probability of a job failure before completion and calculates the Young-Daly optimal interval to minimize wasted compute time.
Literature Source: 1. Young (1974), “A First-Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” 2. Daly (2006), “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart-Dump Strategy.”





Name
Description




solve
Calculates reliability and checkpointing metrics for a fleet.





engine.solvers.reliability.ReliabilityModel.solve(
    fleet,
    job_duration_hours,
    checkpoint_time_s=60.0,
    avg_recovery_time_s=300.0,
)
Calculates reliability and checkpointing metrics for a fleet.











Name
Type
Description
Default




fleet
Fleet
The hardware cluster configuration.
required


job_duration_hours
float
Total job duration in hours.
required


checkpoint_time_s
float
Time to write one checkpoint in seconds (default 60s).
60.0


avg_recovery_time_s
float
Average time to recover from a failure in seconds (default 300s). Includes checkpoint reload, process restart, and re-warmup.
300.0









engine.solvers.reliability.SeriesFailureModel()
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.
Any single component failure stops the job, so failure rates add (a series system with independent, exponentially distributed failures). Each component is stated per node, with its MTTF and its count per node; its share per device is count / devices_per_node / MTTF. A redundant part that cannot fail the node singly (an N+M power supply) enters with count 0. Added 2026-10-20.

SeriesFailureModel
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.





engine.solvers.reliability.CheckpointIntervalModel()
Young-Daly checkpoint interval and the share of wall time it wastes.
tau* = sqrt(2 * write_time * MTBF) balances the write share write_time / tau against the rework share tau / (2 * MTBF); at the optimum the two are equal. Literature: Young (1974); Daly (2006). Added 2026-10-20.



engine.solvers.reliability.RecoveryBudgetModel()
Cold-restart budget for one failure, and its cost per day at a failure interval.
The budget is detection + restart + checkpoint load + warmup (RecoveryProfile.cold_restart_time); a job that fails every failure_interval pays it 1 day / failure_interval times a day, on every one of its n_devices. Rework since the last save is charged to checkpoint waste, not here. Added 2026-10-20.



engine.solvers.reliability.ReliabilityModel()
Calculates Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and optimal checkpointing intervals.
This model handles the reliability modeling of massive clusters, helping determine the ‘Goodput’ of long-running training jobs. It identifies the probability of a job failure before completion and calculates the Young-Daly optimal interval to minimize wasted compute time.
Literature Source: 1. Young (1974), “A First-Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” 2. Daly (2006), “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart-Dump Strategy.”





Name
Description

Calculates reliability and checkpointing metrics for a fleet.

    fleet,
    job_duration_hours,
    checkpoint_time_s=60.0,
    avg_recovery_time_s=300.0,
)

Type

Default

Fleet

required

required

engine.solvers.reliability.SeriesFailureModel()
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.
Any single component failure stops the job, so failure rates add (a series system with independent, exponentially distributed failures). title: engine.solvers.supervision
text:
engine.solvers.supervision
Responsible physical AI solvers: a detection gap in meters and joules, one assistant’s queue.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). The equations live in physics/statistics.py and physics/serving.py; these models compose them for one stated machine and site, so a chapter, a slide deck, and a lab read the same arithmetic (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




DetectionShortfallModel
A stop sized for the best-detected group, met by groups the detector sees less often.


SupervisorQueueModel
One remote assistant serving a fleet, as an M/M/1 queue.





engine.solvers.supervision.DetectionShortfallModel()
A stop sized for the best-detected group, met by groups the detector sees less often.
Each group needs N = ceil(ln p_miss / ln(1 - p_frame)) consecutive frames before detection counts. A group needing Delta N more frames than the reference loses Delta d = v T_frame Delta N before braking begins. The reference stop sheds all of v^2 just as it reaches the person, so the late stop arrives with v_impact = sqrt(2 a Delta d) and E = m a Delta d, valid while Delta d stays below the braking travel v^2 / (2 a).



engine.solvers.supervision.SupervisorQueueModel()
One remote assistant serving a fleet, as an M/M/1 queue.
Requests arrive at lambda = N r (N machines, r requests per machine-hour) and each holds the assistant for a mean s: utilization rho = lambda s, mean wait W_q = rho s / (1 - rho) (the M/G/1 wait ratio with exponential service), and the 99th-percentile wait from the Erlang C tail with one server.

title: engine.solvers.kv_cache
text:
engine.solvers.kv_cache
KV cache management solvers: what retained attention state costs a serving node.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on a model’s KV geometry and a node’s registry specs: the per-token payload and the pool left after the weights, the bytes per token each attention design keeps, full-cap reservation against paged blocks, the prefill a prefix hit avoids, chunked prefill against a monolithic one, keeping, moving, or dropping a paused request’s state, and block-rounded resident fit turned into a turn rate by Little’s law. None models attention traffic during a pass, link contention, or an engine’s scheduler; every rate is a memory-only or weight-only bound.





Name
Description




ChunkedPrefillModel
The decode gap a new prompt causes, run whole or in chunks.


KvAttentionDesignModel
Bytes each token keeps under multi-head, grouped-query, and latent attention.


KvBlockSharingModel
Block-rounded resident fit with and without a shared prefix, as a turn rate.


KvResidencyArchetypeModel
Sharing gain, residency tax, and resume cost for one agent workload.


PagedAllocationModel
Full-cap reservation against fixed-size blocks allocated on demand.


PausedKvStateModel
Keep, move, or drop a paused request’s KV state during a tool wait.


PrefixRebuildModel
The prefill a prefix-cache hit avoids, against one short suffix pass.





engine.solvers.kv_cache.ChunkedPrefillModel()
The decode gap a new prompt causes, run whole or in chunks.
T(N) = max(T_weights, 2 P N / R)
Run whole, the prompt sits between two decode steps, so every ongoing stream waits T(decodes) + T(prompt). Chunked, each iteration runs one chunk beside the decodes, so the gap is T(chunk + decodes) and the prompt finishes after prompt / chunk iterations. Weight work only.



engine.solvers.kv_cache.KvAttentionDesignModel()
Bytes each token keeps under multi-head, grouped-query, and latent attention.
The design is fixed in pretraining: MHA stores a key and value per query head, GQA shares each stored head among a group, and MLA stores one compressed latent per layer. Parameter count does not enter.



engine.solvers.kv_cache.KvBlockSharingModel()
Block-rounded resident fit with and without a shared prefix, as a turn rate.
B = floor(N_blocks / N_req),   B_shared = floor((N_blocks - N_common) / N_private)
lambda = B / W,   W = T_gen (+ T_wait if the state is kept)
Each request reserves its input and output allowance in whole blocks; a fraction of the pool is withheld as headroom. The gain from sharing approaches 1 / (1 - f) in a large pool.



engine.solvers.kv_cache.KvResidencyArchetypeModel()
Sharing gain, residency tax, and resume cost for one agent workload.
Unrounded resident fit with a shared prefix stored once; the residency tax 1 + T_wait / T_gen; and the two resume paths for a dropped or moved state, recompute 2 P S / R against reload S m_token / B_link.



engine.solvers.kv_cache.PagedAllocationModel()
Full-cap reservation against fixed-size blocks allocated on demand.
A reservation holds S_max slots from admission; a request ending at a mean of S_mean tokens fills S_mean / S_max of it. Paged blocks waste at most the unused tail of the last block; under capped exponential final lengths (a modeling assumption, calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens) the expected allocation sets a final-length snapshot count, not a live admission capacity.



engine.solvers.kv_cache.PausedKvStateModel()
Keep, move, or drop a paused request’s KV state during a tool wait.
T_reload = M / (n B_link),   T_recompute = 2 P S / R
Both grow linearly with the context, so their ratio does not depend on length. Keeping holds M x T_wait of memory time; moving frees the memory for the wait less the copy-out (on demand) or less the round trip (prefetch). Correlated returns serialize on the shared links.



engine.solvers.kv_cache.PrefixRebuildModel()
The prefill a prefix-cache hit avoids, against one short suffix pass.
T_rebuild = (2 P S + 2 L d S^2) / R,   R = n R_peak u
T_hit = max(W / (n B_mem), 2 P S_suffix / R)
A miss rebuilds the prefix’s linear and causal-attention work at the sustained rate; a hit runs one pass over the suffix, bounded by reading the weights once when the suffix is short.

title: solvers.EfficiencyModel
text:
solvers.EfficiencyModel()
Models the gap between peak and achieved FLOPS (Wall 3: Software Efficiency).
This model quantifies the software efficiency of a workload — the fraction of peak hardware FLOPS that the software stack actually converts into useful computation. It decomposes Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) by workload type, accounting for kernel fusion efficiency, SM occupancy, and memory access patterns.
Literature Source: 1. Chowdhery et al. (2022), “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” (First systematic MFU reporting for large Transformers.) 2. Dao et al. (2022), “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.” (FlashAttention MFU improvement.) 3. NVIDIA (2023), “Hopper Architecture Tuning Guide.” (SM Occupancy model.)

Description

physics.economics
Fleet economics and cloud cost models.

calc_fleet_tco
Total Cost of Ownership (CapEx + energy OpEx) for a hardware fleet.

Calculates the monthly cloud egress cost for sustained bandwidth usage.


calc_optimal_retraining_interval
Interval that minimizes calc_retraining_cost_rate: T* = sqrt(2 C / s).


calc_ownership_breakeven_utilization
Sustained utilization at which owning and renting cost the same over years.


calc_payback_period
Simple payback: the time for running-cost savings to repay an up-front cost.

Time at which cumulative rent overtakes owning: t = C_up / (r_rent - r_own).

physics.economics.calc_detection_delay_loss(
    annual_value,
    quality_drop,
    delay,
    year_length=None,
)
Value lost while a quality drop goes undetected: V_year * drop * (delay / year).
annual_value is one year’s value, quality_drop the fractional loss while the fault persists, delay the time to detection, and year_length the year it is measured against (default DAYS_PER_YEAR days).



physics.economics.calc_fleet_tco(unit_cost, power_w, quantity, years, kwh_price)
Total Cost of Ownership (CapEx + energy OpEx) for a hardware fleet.
Calculates the combined capital expenditure (hardware purchase) and operational expenditure (electricity) over a given lifespan.











Name
Type
Description
Default




unit_cost
Quantity
The purchase price of a single hardware unit (e.g., USD).
required


power_w
Quantity
The average active power consumption per unit (e.g., Watts).
required


quantity
int
The total number of units in the fleet.
required


years
Quantity or float
The total operating lifespan to cost out (NOT annualized — full CapEx is charged up front, no straight-line amortization). Bare floats are years of 365 days (8,760 hours, the convention every book LEGO cell uses).
required


kwh_price
Quantity
The local cost of electricity (e.g., $/kWh).
required









Name
Type
Description





float
The total cost of ownership in USD.






Device-level napkin model: energy is the device’s own draw — no PUE / cooling overhead, no maintenance. For facility-level TCO with PUE-loaded energy, straight-line amortization, and maintenance, use mlsysim.solvers.EconomicsModel.




physics.economics.calc_monthly_egress_cost(bytes_per_sec, cost_per_gb)
Calculates the monthly cloud egress cost for sustained bandwidth usage.











Name
Type
Description
Default




bytes_per_sec
Quantity
The sustained continuous data transfer rate (e.g., Bytes/s).
required


cost_per_gb
Quantity
The egress pricing tier from the cloud provider (e.g., $/GB).
required









Name
Type
Description





float
The total monthly cost in USD.






Uses a 30-day month convention (a common cloud-billing simplification), so a “month” here is exactly 2,592,000 seconds — not a calendar month and ~1.4% short of the 365/12 average.




physics.economics.calc_optimal_retraining_interval(run_cost, staleness_slope)
Interval that minimizes calc_retraining_cost_rate: T* = sqrt(2 C / s).
At T* one cycle’s staleness triangle (1/2) s T*^2 equals one run’s cost.



physics.economics.calc_ownership_breakeven_utilization(
    upfront_cost,
    fixed_cost_per_year,
    rent_per_year_full,
    years,
    use_cost_per_year_full=0.0,
)
Sustained utilization at which owning and renting cost the same over years.
Owning costs C_up + Y (F + u E), where F is running cost paid whether or not the fleet is busy and E is running cost that scales with use (energy drawn only while busy), both at full use. Renting the same capacity costs u Y R, with R the rent for every hour of a year. Setting them equal gives
u* = (C_up + Y F) / (Y (R - E)).



physics.economics.calc_payback_period(upfront_cost, annual_savings)
Simple payback: the time for running-cost savings to repay an up-front cost.
t = C_upfront / (savings per year), undiscounted (added 2026-10-20).











Name
Type
Description
Default




upfront_cost
Quantity
One-time capital cost (USD).
required


annual_savings
Quantity
Running cost avoided per year (USD/year); must be positive.
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Payback period in years.







physics.economics.calc_rent_crossover(
    upfront_cost,
    owned_cost_rate,
    rent_cost_rate,
)
Time at which cumulative rent overtakes owning: t = C_up / (r_rent - r_own).
Owning pays upfront_cost at time zero and then owned_cost_rate; renting pays rent_cost_rate from zero. Both rates are costs per unit time in the same units. Returns None when rent never overtakes (the owned running cost is at least the rent).



physics.economics.calc_retraining_cost_rate(interval, run_cost, staleness_slope)
Cost per unit time of retraining every interval: C / T + (1/2) s T.
The first term spreads one run over the cycle; the second is the average of the linearly growing staleness loss, the triangle (1/2) s T^2 per cycle.



physics.economics.calc_skew_cost(skew_rate, query_rate, cost_per_error)
Cost rate of training-serving skew: Rate_skew * Q * C_error.
skew_rate is the fraction of queries whose prediction skew makes wrong, query_rate the query volume per unit time, and cost_per_error the business cost of one wrong prediction. Returns cost per unit time.



physics.economics.calc_staleness_slope(
    query_rate,
    value_per_query,
    initial_accuracy,
    decay_rate,
)
Growth of value lost per unit time since the last retraining run: Q V A0 gamma.
For A(t) = A0 exp(-gamma t) and small gamma t, the value lost per day at age t is about Q V A0 gamma t; the slope is in value per time squared.

physics.economics.calc_skew_cost(skew_rate, query_rate, cost_per_error)
Cost rate of training-serving skew: Rate_skew * Q * C_error.
skew_rate is the fraction of queries whose prediction skew makes wrong, query_rate the query volume per unit time, and cost_per_error the business cost of one wrong prediction. Returns cost per unit time.



physics.economics.calc_staleness_slope(
    query_rate,
    value_per_query,
    initial_accuracy,
    decay_rate,
)
Growth of value lost per unit time since the last retraining run: Q V A0 gamma.
For A(t) = A0 exp(-gamma t) and small gamma t, the value lost per day at age t is about Q V A0 gamma t; the slope is in value per time squared.

title: physics.retrieval
text:
physics.retrieval
Retrieval from long-term memory: the equations behind a read and its index.
Pure arithmetic (added 2026-10-20). A read stages whole serialized records inside a token allowance; a lexical index ranks candidates with BM25; an exact vector scan streams every eligible vector, so bandwidth sets its floor; a typed traversal grows with depth; and similarity between two texts counts shared words, which is all a similarity-first deduplicator sees. The solvers in engine/solvers/retrieval.py compose these.

BM25 length term in the denominator: k1 (1 - b + b \|D\| / avgdl).

One query term’s BM25 contribution to a document’s score.

Nodes of an exact tree through depth (the seed is depth zero).

physics.retrieval.calc_bandwidth_fit_through_origin(bytes_streamed, seconds)
Least-squares bandwidth of measured scans on the line t = bytes / B.
Minimizing the squared time residuals over 1 / B gives B = sum(bytes^2) / sum(bytes t), in bytes per second.



physics.retrieval.calc_bm25_idf(documents, matching_documents)
BM25 inverse document frequency (the non-negative variant).
IDF(q) = ln(1 + (N - n(q) + 0.5) / (n(q) + 0.5))



physics.retrieval.calc_bm25_length_normalizer(length, average_length, k1, b)
BM25 length term in the denominator: k1 (1 - b + b |D| / avgdl).



physics.retrieval.calc_bm25_term_score(
    idf,
    frequency,
    length,
    average_length,
    k1,
    b,
)
One query term’s BM25 contribution to a document’s score.
IDF(q) f (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 (1 - b + b |D| / avgdl))



physics.retrieval.calc_full_tree_nodes(children, depth)
Nodes of an exact tree through depth (the seed is depth zero).
1 + c + c^2 + ... + c^d = (c^(d+1) - 1) / (c - 1)



physics.retrieval.calc_interface_bandwidth(width, transfer_rate)
Peak bandwidth of a memory interface: width x transfers per second.
width in bits and transfer_rate in bits per second per pin (one bit per transfer); returns bytes per second.



physics.retrieval.calc_lsh_candidate_probability(similarity, bands, rows)
Chance that two documents of Jaccard similarity share at least one band bucket.
A MinHash signature cut into bands bands of rows hashes each makes a pair a candidate when every hash of some band agrees: 1 - (1 - s^r)^b (Leskovec, Rajaraman, and Ullman, Mining of Massive Datasets, Sec. 3.4).



physics.retrieval.calc_lsh_threshold(bands, rows)
Similarity where the banding S-curve is steepest, approximately (1/b)^(1/r).



physics.retrieval.calc_minhash_standard_error(similarity, hashes)
Standard error of the MinHash estimate of Jaccard similarity from hashes independent hashes.
Each hash agrees with probability J, so the agreeing fraction has standard error sqrt(J (1 - J) / k); the largest, at J = 0.5, is 0.5 / sqrt(k) (added 2026-10-20).



physics.retrieval.calc_records_that_fit(allowance, envelope, record)
Whole serialized records that fit a retrieval allowance after its envelope.
n = floor((allowance - envelope) / (body + metadata))



physics.retrieval.calc_vectors_in_budget(
    budget,
    bandwidth,
    dimension,
    bytes_per_value,
)
Vectors an exact scan can stream within a time budget: t B / (d b).
Quantities in, a dimensionless float out; the scan’s arithmetic is ignored because it sits far below the host’s ridge point.



physics.retrieval.calc_word_overlap(first, second)
Distinct words two texts share, and the union, after lowercasing and stripping punctuation. Returns (shared, union, words_in_first, words_in_second); shared / union is the Jaccard similarity.

title: solvers.TailLatencyModel
text:
solvers.TailLatencyModel()
Analyzes queueing delays and P99 tail latency for deployed inference models.
Models inference servers as M/M/c queues to determine if the deployment can sustain the target arrival rate while meeting strict SLA latency bounds.
Approximations (deliberate, pedagogical): - p50_latency/p99_latency add the WAIT-time quantile to the MEAN service time. The true quantile of sojourn time (wait + service) is generally larger, because service time has its own variance. - Kingman’s (cv^2 + 1)/2 factor is derived for the MEAN wait (M/G/1); applying it to the P50/P99 wait quantiles is a further heuristic. Quote these fields as model estimates, not exact M/G/c percentiles.
Literature Source: 1. Dean & Barroso (2013), “The Tail at Scale.”





Name
Description




solve
Solves for P50 and P99 tail latencies under variable load.





solvers.TailLatencyModel.solve(
    arrival_rate_qps,
    service_latency_ms,
    num_replicas=1,
    service_time_cv=1.0,
)

physics.robotics.assurance
Statistical release gates, Clopper-Pearson bounds, and fleet hazard rates.





Name
Description




calc_clopper_pearson_lower_bound
Exact one-sided Clopper-Pearson lower confidence limit on a success probability.


calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound
Calculate exact Clopper-Pearson binomial lower confidence bound for zero-failure trials.


calc_empirical_testing_exposure
Calculate required zero-failure operating exposure to statistically bound a hazard rate.


calc_rule_of_three_bound
The rule of three: about 3/n bounds the failure rate after n clean trials at 95 percent.


calc_rule_of_three_trials
Clean trials the rule of three asks for a success lower limit: 3 / (1 - p_target).


calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate
Calculate end-to-end hazardous event rate for a physical AI system protected by a deterministic runtime safety shield.


calc_zero_failure_mission_count
Failure-free missions needed to bound a constant hazard rate, counted per mission.


calc_zero_failure_rate_upper_bound
Upper confidence bound on a per-trial failure rate after n_trials without failure.


calc_zero_failure_sample_size
Calculate required number of consecutive zero-failure trials to certify a target reliability lower bound.





physics.robotics.assurance.calc_clopper_pearson_lower_bound(
    successes,
    trials,
    confidence=0.95,
)
Exact one-sided Clopper-Pearson lower confidence limit on a success probability.
Solves P(X >= k | n, p) = 1 - C for p by bisection, X ~ Binomial(n, p). At k = n it reduces to (1 - C)^(1/n), the zero-failure bound.
Source: Clopper and Pearson, “The Use of Confidence or Fiducial Limits Illustrated in the Case of the Binomial,” Biometrika 26(4), 1934.



physics.robotics.assurance.calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(
    n_trials,
    confidence=0.95,
)
Calculate exact Clopper-Pearson binomial lower confidence bound for zero-failure trials.
Equation: p_L = (1 - C)^(1 / n)



physics.robotics.assurance.calc_empirical_testing_exposure(
    target_hazard_rate,
    confidence=0.95,
)
Calculate required zero-failure operating exposure to statistically bound a hazard rate.
Under a Poisson failure arrival process with constant rate lambda, the probability of observing zero failures over total exposure duration T is P(0) = exp(-lambda * T). To claim lambda <= lambda_target at statistical confidence C = 1 - alpha: exp(-lambda_target * T) <= 1 - C ==> T >= -ln(1 - C) / lambda_target
For 95% confidence (C = 0.95): -ln(0.05) ≈ 2.99573 ==> T ≈ 3.0 / lambda_target
Source: Littlewood and Wright, “Some Conservative Stopping Rules for Testing Software”, IEEE TSE, 1997; Kalbfleisch and Prentice, The Statistical Analysis of Failure Time Data, Wiley, 2002.











Name
Type
Description
Default




target_hazard_rate
Quantity or float
Target acceptable failure rate (e.g. 1e-6 / hour or 1e-9 / hour). If float, interpreted as failures per hour.
required


confidence
float
Statistical confidence level (default 0.95 for 95% two-sided/one-sided bound).
0.95









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Required continuous operating hours.







physics.robotics.assurance.calc_rule_of_three_bound(n_trials)
The rule of three: about 3/n bounds the failure rate after n clean trials at 95 percent.
The rounded form of calc_zero_failure_rate_upper_bound; it overstates the exact limit slightly. Source: Hanley and Lippman-Hand, JAMA 249(13), 1983.



physics.robotics.assurance.calc_rule_of_three_trials(target_lower_bound)
Clean trials the rule of three asks for a success lower limit: 3 / (1 - p_target).



physics.robotics.assurance.calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate(
    brain_hazard_rate,
    shield_coverage,
    shield_hw_failure_rate=None,
)
Calculate end-to-end hazardous event rate for a physical AI system protected by a deterministic runtime safety shield.
Equation: p_sys = p_brain * (1 - c_shield) + p_hw



physics.robotics.assurance.calc_zero_failure_mission_count(
    target_hazard_rate,
    mission_time,
    confidence=0.95,
)
Failure-free missions needed to bound a constant hazard rate, counted per mission.
Each mission of length t fails with probability lambda t (small); n clean missions bound it when (1 - lambda t)^n = 1 - C:
n = ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - lambda t)
Unrounded; at small lambda t it approaches the exposure wall divided by t.



physics.robotics.assurance.calc_zero_failure_rate_upper_bound(
    n_trials,
    confidence=0.95,
)
Upper confidence bound on a per-trial failure rate after n_trials without failure.
Under the Poisson approximation, P(0 failures) = exp(-p n); requiring it to stay at or above 1 - C gives p_upper = -ln(1 - C) / n. At 95 percent confidence -ln(0.05) = 2.996, the “rule of three”: p_upper ~ 3 / n.
Source: Hanley and Lippman-Hand, “If Nothing Goes Wrong, Is Everything All Right?”, JAMA 249(13), 1983 (the rule of three); added 2026-10-20.



physics.robotics.assurance.calc_zero_failure_sample_size(
    target_lower_bound,
    confidence=0.95,
)
Calculate required number of consecutive zero-failure trials to certify a target reliability lower bound.
Equation: n = ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(p_L))
