title: engine.solvers.context
text:
engine.solvers.context
Context-engineering solvers: what one agent request carries, and what it costs.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on serialized token counts: a budget by role against the window, one attention head’s softmax over fixed logits, a measured comprehension sweep, the input bill of a zoned layout under prefix reuse, compaction between two watermarks, the edits that retire a stale observation, and the cost per accepted task of a protected-field check. None models tokenization across joins, cache eviction, or a trained model’s attention.





Name
Description




AttentionDilutionModel
One head’s weight on a target key among keys whose logits stay fixed.


CompactionCadenceModel
Compaction between a trigger and a target watermark (hysteresis).


ContextBudgetModel
A request budgeted by role: S_sys + S_tools + S_state + S_obs <= S_max - K_max.


ContextInvalidationModel
Three edits that retire a superseded excerpt at the start of the trunk.


PrefixLayoutBillModel
Input bill of turns calls whose requests are ordered root, trunk, leaf.


ProtectedFieldCheckModel
Cost per accepted task with and without a protected-field check at each compaction.





engine.solvers.context.AttentionDilutionModel()
One head’s weight on a target key among keys whose logits stay fixed.
short_keys and long_keys count every key, the target included, at background_logit. The look-alike case counts competitors only: unrelated_keys at the background logit plus lookalike_keys at the higher lookalike_logit of text that shares the evidence’s identifiers. A sufficient condition for dilution, not a forecast of a trained model.



engine.solvers.context.CompactionCadenceModel()
Compaction between a trigger and a target watermark (hysteresis).
Each turn appends delta tokens; a pass fires on the first turn that reaches the trigger and resets the request to the target, so passes come every ceil((trigger - target) / delta) turns. The trigger is soft: the request can overshoot it by less than one append, and the output reserve must still fit. An optional alternate target prices a narrower gap.



engine.solvers.context.ContextBudgetModel()
A request budgeted by role: S_sys + S_tools + S_state + S_obs <= S_max - K_max.
Appending every tool result grows S_obs by delta per turn until the observation budget overflows, and resends the history, so the input bill grows quadratically. Selecting a fixed observation share keeps every request the same size and the bill linear. Bills assume no prefix reuse and, for the appending policy, a window large enough to admit every request.



engine.solvers.context.ContextInvalidationModel()
Three edits that retire a superseded excerpt at the start of the trunk.
Removing it or replacing it in place with a short marker changes the request right after the reused root, so every later token is prefilled again; appending a notice keeps the prefix and prefills only the notice, but leaves the stale tokens resident on every later call.



engine.solvers.context.PrefixLayoutBillModel()
Input bill of turns calls whose requests are ordered root, trunk, leaf.
With a volatile field first, no prefix is reused and every input token is billed at full price. Ordered by change rate, the first call is cold, each trunk rewrite prefills trunk and leaf, and every other call prefills only the leaf; reused tokens are billed at cached_fraction of the price. Assumes compatible cached state is retained; prices only input tokens.



engine.solvers.context.ProtectedFieldCheckModel()
Cost per accepted task with and without a protected-field check at each compaction.
Each of constraints is lost independently with loss_per_round in each of rounds; a lost constraint makes the task unacceptable, so acceptance is p_intact (1 - eps)^(n R). A check that detects detection of losses and repairs them leaves eps (1 - detection) per round and adds check_cost per round to the attempt.

title: physics.neural
text:
physics.neural
Neural computation: what a dense network costs, and what its activations and loss compute.
A dense (fully connected) network is a list of layer widths [n_0, n_1, ..., n_L]: layer l maps n_{l-1} inputs to n_l outputs with an n_{l-1} by n_l weight matrix and one bias per output. Every count here follows from the widths and the batch size alone (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




calc_cross_entropy
Cross-entropy loss with a one-hot label: -ln p of the correct class.


calc_dense_backward_flops
Backward-pass matrix work at batch B.


calc_dense_biases
Biases per layer: one per output unit, n_out.


calc_dense_forward_flops
Forward-pass operations at batch B, per layer.


calc_dense_inference_activations
Values inference must hold at once with rolling buffers: the largest


calc_dense_macs
Multiply-accumulates per example: one per weight.


calc_dense_params
Parameters of a dense network: sum((n_in + 1) * n_out).


calc_dense_saved_activations
Values training keeps for the backward pass: the input and every layer output, B sum(n_l).


calc_dense_traffic_values
Activation values that cross main memory in one forward pass.


calc_dense_weights
Weights per layer: one per connection, n_in * n_out.


calc_relu
Rectified linear unit, max(0, x).


calc_sigmoid
The logistic sigmoid, 1 / (1 + e^-x).


calc_sigmoid_slope
The sigmoid’s derivative, s(x)(1 - s(x)); its peak, at x = 0, is one quarter.


calc_training_state
Persistent training state of parameters values, one precision throughout.


calc_training_step_ops
Operations launched in one training step of a dense ReLU network of layers layers.





physics.neural.calc_cross_entropy(p_correct)
Cross-entropy loss with a one-hot label: -ln p of the correct class.



physics.neural.calc_dense_backward_flops(widths, batch=1)
Backward-pass matrix work at batch B.
Each layer computes its weight gradient (activations transposed times the error, 2 B n_in n_out) and, except the first layer, the error sent to the layer before it (error times weights transposed, the same size). The first layer has no earlier layer to send a signal to.
Returns (weight_gradient, input_gradient) totals.



physics.neural.calc_dense_biases(widths)
Biases per layer: one per output unit, n_out.



physics.neural.calc_dense_forward_flops(widths, batch=1)
Forward-pass operations at batch B, per layer.
matrix multiply: 2 B n_in n_out      (one MAC = 2 FLOPs)
elementwise:     2 B n_out           (bias add and activation)
Returns (matmul, elementwise), two lists with one entry per layer.



physics.neural.calc_dense_inference_activations(widths, batch=1)
Values inference must hold at once with rolling buffers: the largest adjacent pair, B max(n_{l-1} + n_l), since each output can overwrite its input once the next layer has read it.



physics.neural.calc_dense_macs(widths)
Multiply-accumulates per example: one per weight.



physics.neural.calc_dense_params(widths)
Parameters of a dense network: sum((n_in + 1) * n_out).



physics.neural.calc_dense_saved_activations(widths, batch=1)
Values training keeps for the backward pass: the input and every layer output, B sum(n_l).



physics.neural.calc_dense_traffic_values(widths, batch=1)
Activation values that cross main memory in one forward pass.
Each layer runs as its own kernel: the input is read once, the output is written once, and every hidden activation is written by one layer and read back by the next, B (n_0 + 2 sum(hidden) + n_L). The weights are read once on top of this.



physics.neural.calc_dense_weights(widths)
Weights per layer: one per connection, n_in * n_out.



physics.neural.calc_relu(x)
Rectified linear unit, max(0, x).



physics.neural.calc_sigmoid(x)
The logistic sigmoid, 1 / (1 + e^-x).



physics.neural.calc_sigmoid_slope(x)
The sigmoid’s derivative, s(x)(1 - s(x)); its peak, at x = 0, is one quarter.



physics.neural.calc_training_state(
    parameters,
    bytes_per_value,
    optimizer_bytes_per_parameter,
)
Persistent training state of parameters values, one precision throughout.
Weights and gradients take bytes_per_value each per parameter; the optimizer keeps optimizer_bytes_per_parameter more (two FP32 values for Adam, one for SGD with momentum). Returns (weights, gradients, optimizer).



physics.neural.calc_training_step_ops(layers)
Operations launched in one training step of a dense ReLU network of layers layers.
forward       L   (one matrix multiply each, bias and ReLU fused)
loss          1
backward      2L - 1   (a weight gradient per layer, an input gradient for all but the first)
ReLU masks    L - 1    (one per hidden layer)
update        1   (one fused optimizer step)
Total 4L.

title: engine.solvers.durability
text:
engine.solvers.durability
Durable-execution solvers: what a runtime pays to survive a crash (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers. Each model is arithmetic on stated inputs: one group commit’s work and waits, the bytes full snapshots and deltas write, checkpoint strides priced on a fixed crash trace with Young’s balance in turns, and the cost of keeping a trajectory’s recovery and replay data. None models a particular storage engine or workflow runtime.





Name
Description




CheckpointTraceModel
Checkpoint strides priced on one fixed crash trace, against Young’s balance in turns.


GroupCommitModel
Storage work per record against the wait each record sees in one group commit.


RetentionCostModel
What keeping one trajectory’s recovery and replay data costs, against one attempt.


SnapshotVolumeModel
Bytes written by full snapshots and by deltas over one monotonically growing trajectory.





engine.solvers.durability.CheckpointTraceModel()
Checkpoint strides priced on one fixed crash trace, against Young’s balance in turns.
A policy checkpoints at every multiple of its stride (and at the final turn). A crash after turn c restores the last checkpoint and rebuilds the c mod stride turns since it from the log; the policy’s total is its checkpoint pauses plus the restores plus the rebuilt turns. The balance stride sqrt(2 pause / (rate * cost)) uses the trace’s crash rate, once with the cost of rebuilding a logged turn and once with the cost of re-executing an unlogged one.



engine.solvers.durability.GroupCommitModel()
Storage work per record against the wait each record sees in one group commit.
One flush acknowledges batch_size records; the work charged to each falls as flush / batch_size, but every record still waits the whole flush, and the first arrival also waits the batch timer. Amortization raises throughput; it never shortens one record’s wait.



engine.solvers.durability.RetentionCostModel()
What keeping one trajectory’s recovery and replay data costs, against one attempt.
The log is turns * (envelope + payload); one workspace snapshot is added; the total is priced at an object-storage rate for the retention period and compared with the cost of one attempt.



engine.solvers.durability.SnapshotVolumeModel()
Bytes written by full snapshots and by deltas over one monotonically growing trajectory.
turns // stride checkpoints; full snapshots grow with the square of the checkpoint count, deltas linearly, so the ratio is (n + 1) / 2.

title: solvers.SynthesisSolver
text:
solvers.SynthesisSolver()
Given an SLA, synthesizes the required hardware specs (Wall 22: Inverse Solve).
This solver inverts the Roofline model to derive minimum hardware specifications required to meet a target latency SLA.
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” 2. Jouppi et al. (2017), “In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU.”





Name
Description




solve
Synthesize minimum hardware requirements from a latency SLA.





solvers.SynthesisSolver.solve(
    model,
    target_latency,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Synthesize minimum hardware requirements from a latency SLA.
Inverts the Roofline model: instead of asking “how fast does this hardware run the model?”, asks “what hardware would run the model in target_latency?”. Assumes a single full pass that streams every weight once (batch size 1, no weight reuse), so:

required_bw = weight_bytes / T_target [GB/s] — the bandwidth needed if the workload is memory-bound;
required_flops = total_ops / (T_target * efficiency) [TFLOP/s] — the compute rate needed if it is compute-bound;
compute_memory_ratio = required_flops / required_bw [FLOP/byte] — the hardware balance point a matching part should sit near.












Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Workload
The workload to serve; sets weight bytes and operation count.
required


target_latency
Quantity
The SLA latency target (any time unit; converted to seconds).
required


precision
str
Numerical precision; sets bytes per parameter.
'fp16'


efficiency
float
Expected software efficiency in (0, 1]; lower values inflate the required FLOPS to compensate.
0.5














Name
Type
Description





SynthesisResult
Required bandwidth, FLOPS, memory capacity, and the compute:memory balance ratio.

title: physics.robotics.estimation
text:
physics.robotics.estimation
State estimation and belief expiry: scalar fusion, inertial coasting, and error-bound growth (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




calc_belief_error_bound
Error bound of a belief after elapsed without new evidence.


calc_inertial_coast_errors
Heading and position error of an IMU integrated open loop for duration.


calc_quadratic_invalidation_horizon
Invalidation horizon of a belief whose error bound grows with velocity and acceleration terms.


calc_scalar_kalman_update
Gain and posterior variance of one scalar Kalman update.





physics.robotics.estimation.calc_belief_error_bound(
    initial_error,
    growth_rate,
    elapsed,
    growth_acceleration=None,
)
Error bound of a belief after elapsed without new evidence.
Equation: E(dt) = E_0 + v dt + a dt^2 / 2
v bounds the unobserved velocity and a the disturbance acceleration; a growth law bounded by a speed alone has a = 0.
Source: kinematics of a bounded disturbance (displacement under a velocity bound plus a constant-acceleration bound).



physics.robotics.estimation.calc_inertial_coast_errors(
    gyro_noise_density,
    gyro_bias,
    accel_noise_density,
    accel_bias,
    duration,
)
Heading and position error of an IMU integrated open loop for duration.
Equations: heading from white rate noise = N_g sqrt(T) heading from a constant offset = b_g T position from white accel noise = N_a sqrt(T^3 / 3) position from a constant offset = b_a T^2 / 2
Noise grows with the square root of time (a random walk, integrated once more for position); an offset grows with time, or its square for position, so offsets limit how long a robot can coast between fixes.
Source: Woodman, “An introduction to inertial navigation,” University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory Tech. Rep. UCAM-CL-TR-696 (2007), Secs. 4.2 and 4.3.










Name
Type
Description





dict
heading_noise, heading_bias (angles), position_noise, position_bias (lengths).







physics.robotics.estimation.calc_quadratic_invalidation_horizon(
    initial_error,
    growth_rate,
    growth_acceleration,
    error_limit,
)
Invalidation horizon of a belief whose error bound grows with velocity and acceleration terms.
Equation: a dt^2 / 2 + v dt + (E_0 - E_max) = 0 ; T_inv = the positive root
With a = 0 this is calc_linear_invalidation_horizon. A zero result means the initial error already spends the limit.
Source: first-passage time of the bound calc_belief_error_bound (definition of the invalidation horizon, T_inv = inf{dt >= 0 : E(dt) >= E_max}).



physics.robotics.estimation.calc_scalar_kalman_update(
    prior_variance,
    measurement_variance,
)
Gain and posterior variance of one scalar Kalman update.
Equation: g = P / (P + R) ; P+ = (1 - g) P
The gain is how far the estimate moves toward the reading, between 0 and 1; the posterior is tighter than either input. Both variances must share a unit.
Source: Kalman (1960), Trans. ASME J. Basic Eng. 82(1); Thrun, Burgard, and Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005), Table 3.1, in one dimension.










Name
Type
Description





tuple
(gain as a float, posterior variance in the unit of prior_variance)

Noise grows with the square root of time (a random walk, integrated once more for position); an offset grows with time, or its square for position, so offsets limit how long a robot can coast between fixes.
Source: Woodman, “An introduction to inertial navigation,” University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory Tech. Rep. UCAM-CL-TR-696 (2007), Secs. 4.2 and 4.3.










Name
Type
Description





dict
heading_noise, heading_bias (angles), position_noise, position_bias (lengths).







physics.robotics.estimation.calc_quadratic_invalidation_horizon(
    initial_error,
    growth_rate,
    growth_acceleration,
    error_limit,
)
Invalidation horizon of a belief whose error bound grows with velocity and acceleration terms.
Equation: a dt^2 / 2 + v dt + (E_0 - E_max) = 0 ; T_inv = the positive root
With a = 0 this is calc_linear_invalidation_horizon. A zero result means the initial error already spends the limit.
Source: first-passage time of the bound calc_belief_error_bound (definition of the invalidation horizon, T_inv = inf{dt >= 0 : E(dt) >= E_max}).



physics.robotics.estimation.calc_scalar_kalman_update(
    prior_variance,
    measurement_variance,
)
Gain and posterior variance of one scalar Kalman update.
Equation: g = P / (P + R) ; P+ = (1 - g) P
The gain is how far the estimate moves toward the reading, between 0 and 1; the posterior is tighter than either input. Both variances must share a unit.
Source: Kalman (1960), Trans. ASME J. Basic Eng. 82(1); Thrun, Burgard, and Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005), Table 3.1, in one dimension.










Name
Type
Description





tuple
(gain as a float, posterior variance in the unit of prior_variance)

core.provenance.Sourced()
Scalar with mandatory Provenance. Subclasses float so notebooks and generated calculations can divide and format values without extra coercion.
.. warning:: Provenance does NOT survive arithmetic. Any operation on a Sourced (x * 2, x / y, -x, round(x) …) returns a plain float — Python numeric dunders construct float results, and nothing re-attaches .provenance/.name/.description. (copy.copy raises TypeError because __new__ requires a provenance argument.) The audit trail therefore lives only on the registry leaf value itself. title: engine.solvers.trajectory
text:
engine.solvers.trajectory
Trajectory-planning solvers: joint rates, handoff deadlines, seams, swings, and jerk-limited stops.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). The equations live in physics.robotics (the two-link Jacobian and damped least squares, the S-curve and polynomial stops, the seam torque step, the spill bound); these models compose them for one stated arm, joint, base, or mission, so a chapter, a slide deck, and a lab read the same arithmetic (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




BrakingBlendModel
A bumpless transfer from cruise into braking, beside the step and the resident stop.


ChunkReplacementModel
Replacement latency, capture to admission, against the renewal period and the lease.


DynamicWindowModel
The dynamic window of a base over one renewal, and the classical admissibility test.


HandoffExposureModel
A per-handoff deadline budget read across a mission of K handoffs.


JerkLimitedStopModel
A delayed jerk-limited (S-curve) stop, beside the constant and polynomial stops it replaces.


SeamBridgeModel
A velocity gap at a chunk seam, closed in one servo tick or by a quintic bridge.


ShoulderSwingModel
The loaded shoulder: holding torque, effective inertia, and a rest-to-rest swing.


SpillLimitedStopModel
The stop of a machine carrying an open container, whose liquid caps the deceleration.


StaleAnchorModel
How far a moving reference runs past a pose sampled when a replacement was requested.


TrajectoryDeadlinesModel
The deadlines a trajectory record carries, and the cruise charged before its stop begins.


TwoLinkJointRateModel
Joint rates a tool speed asks of a planar two-link arm, exact and damped.





engine.solvers.trajectory.BrakingBlendModel()
A bumpless transfer from cruise into braking, beside the step and the resident stop.
At a change of authority the enforcer may blend the base’s command from cruise to the braking deceleration a with the fixed-endpoint quintic smoothstep. Its slope peaks at 1.875, so under the resident stop’s jerk bound j the window is T = 1.875 a / j (calc_smoothstep_blend_window), rounded up to whole permission ticks. The same change taken in one tick asks a jerk of a / tick. During the blend the speed falls by a T / 2 and the base travels v0 T - a T^2 / 7 (calc_smoothstep_braking_blend); full braking follows. The blended stop is set against an ideal step (v0^2 / 2a) and the resident S-curve stop; the reserve a blend uses is the largest growth of travel plus resident stop over its ticks (calc_blend_reserve_use). An arm joint’s torque change under a torque-rate ceiling gives its own window the same way (added 2026-10-20).



engine.solvers.trajectory.ChunkReplacementModel()
Replacement latency, capture to admission, against the renewal period and the lease.
L = observation age at dispatch + the dispatch-to-admission allocation; the inference pass and whole-plan validation sit inside the allocation. Admitting one plan every renewal period with L longer than that period keeps ceil(L / T_renew) requests in flight.



engine.solvers.trajectory.DynamicWindowModel()
The dynamic window of a base over one renewal, and the classical admissibility test.
Speeds reachable in the next window differ from the current one by at most a_max x window. The dynamic window approach admits an arc whose speed satisfies v <= sqrt(2 d a_b), a constant-deceleration stop within the distance d to the nearest obstacle (Fox, Burgard, and Thrun 1997, eq. 14), with no pre-brake delay, jerk ramps, or margins.



engine.solvers.trajectory.HandoffExposureModel()
A per-handoff deadline budget read across a mission of K handoffs.
With independent misses at probability p, all K handoffs are on time with probability (1 - p)^K and p K are late on average. Holding a mission budget eps_M by the union bound leaves each handoff eps_M / K, the quantile 1 - eps_M / K, deeper than p by the ratio p K / eps_M.



engine.solvers.trajectory.JerkLimitedStopModel()
A delayed jerk-limited (S-curve) stop, beside the constant and polynomial stops it replaces.
The machine travels v tau during the pre-brake delay, then stops along the double-S profile with deceleration bound a and jerk bound j (calc_scurve_stop_distance): above the plateau speed a^2 / j the stop is v^2 / (2 a) of braking plus v a / (2 j) of cruise over half a jerk ramp. Without a stated jerk bound, j is the peak jerk of the reference C2 polynomial stop (calc_c2_stop_suffix) at jerk_reference_speed (the entry speed by default), which stops in 0.75 v^2 / a. A localization bound and a protective margin, when stated, add to every required distance; the speed ceiling is the fastest entry speed whose delayed S-curve stop fits, with the jerk bound held fixed (calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity).



engine.solvers.trajectory.SeamBridgeModel()
A velocity gap at a chunk seam, closed in one servo tick or by a quintic bridge.
Closing a gap of delta in one tick asks the reflected rotor inertia N^2 J_rotor for J delta / dt of torque (calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump), reached in one tick, a torque rate of J delta / dt^2. The C2 bridge over T, with zero boundary accelerations and an endpoint on the incoming reference, is the quintic q(t) = a3 t^3 + a4 t^4 + a5 t^5 (solved from its 3x3 boundary system); its acceleration peaks at 1.5 delta / T mid-bridge and its jerk at 6 delta / T^2 at both ends, so torque falls as 1 / T and torque rate as 1 / T^2.



engine.solvers.trajectory.ShoulderSwingModel()
The loaded shoulder: holding torque, effective inertia, and a rest-to-rest swing.
Holding payload m at reach r costs m g r of torque; the payload and the reflected rotor inertia give J = m r^2 + J_refl (link masses omitted, a lower bound). Gravity, held at its horizontal value, makes the torque-limited acceleration (tau_max - tau_g) / J lifting and (tau_max + tau_g) / J braking; the binding acceleration is the smallest of those and the joint limit. The time-optimal (bang-bang) swing of D takes 2 sqrt(D / a) and steps torque by 2 J a at the switch point. A torque-rate limit bounds jerk at taud / J, and the jerk-limited swing is the double-S without cruise (calc_scurve_rest_to_rest_time).



engine.solvers.trajectory.SpillLimitedStopModel()
The stop of a machine carrying an open container, whose liquid caps the deceleration.
Under steady deceleration a the free surface tilts until the liquid rises R a / g at the wall; keeping it below the rim’s freeboard h_f caps the deceleration at g h_f / R (calc_quasistatic_spill_acceleration). The stop at that bound keeps the stop’s shape, so its jerk bound is rescaled with the deceleration (the reference polynomial’s peak at the entry speed); the carry speed is the fastest entry speed whose delayed stop fits.



engine.solvers.trajectory.StaleAnchorModel()
How far a moving reference runs past a pose sampled when a replacement was requested.
A joint turning at omega for the replacement delay moves omega x delay; at a lever arm r that is up to omega x delay x r of tool motion, the step backward a plan anchored at the stale pose would command.



engine.solvers.trajectory.TrajectoryDeadlinesModel()
The deadlines a trajectory record carries, and the cruise charged before its stop begins.
A replacement requested request_delay after the schedule origin, with a design-tail latency target and scheduling slack, is admitted at the preferred admission; the full reserve adds the decision-to-onset response. The matched stop must physically begin at the commitment instant, so admission closes one response earlier; the arm rests one stop time after commitment. Cruise from the blend deadline to commitment is charged before the stop.



engine.solvers.trajectory.TwoLinkJointRateModel()
Joint rates a tool speed asks of a planar two-link arm, exact and damped.
The weakest direction of the Jacobian at elbow angle q2 has singular value sigma_min; a tool speed v along it needs a joint-rate vector of norm v / sigma_min, and with two joints at least one component is that norm divided by sqrt(2). Damped least squares with damping lambda commands v sigma / (sigma^2 + lambda^2), never more than v / (2 lambda), and delivers the fraction sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + lambda^2) of the tool motion.

title: solvers.ScalingModel
text:
solvers.ScalingModel()
Analyzes the ‘Scaling Physics’ of model training (Chinchilla Laws).
This model determines the optimal model size (P) and dataset size (D) given a compute budget (C), following the compute-optimal training regime where D ≈ 20P.
Literature Source: 1. Hoffmann et al. (2022), “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” 2. Kaplan et al. (2020), “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” 3. McCandlish et al. (2018), “An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training.”

physics.memory.calc_activation_memory(
    n_layers,
    seq_len,
    batch_size,
    hidden_dim,
    n_heads=None,
    precision_bytes=2,
    strategy='selective',
)
Estimates the activation memory required for a Transformer model during training.
Implements the per-layer analytical bounds of Korthikanti et al. (2023), “Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models”, Sec. 4.1, whose constants are expressed in BYTES with FP16 (2-byte) activations baked in:

none (no recomputation): s*b*h*34 + 5*a*s^2*b
selective (recompute attention matrices): s*b*h*34
full (recompute everything; keep layer inputs): s*b*h*2

where s = sequence length, b = microbatch size, h = hidden dimension, and a = attention heads. The quadratic 5*a*s^2*b term is the attention softmax/dropout/score storage — dominant at long sequence lengths — and is exactly what selective recomputation discards. Activations stored at other precisions scale the FP16-based constants by precision_bytes / 2.
(Audit fix 2026-06-06: the previous implementation used 34/10/2 as precision-free coefficients AND multiplied by precision_bytes, double- counting the FP16 width at every strategy; its selective=10 matched no published convention; and the attention term was missing entirely.)

Type
Description
Default

required

required

required

physics.memory.calc_capped_exponential_scale(mean_tokens, max_tokens)
Solves for the exponential scale whose context-capped mean is mean_tokens.
Request lengths are modeled as S = min(X, S_max) with X ~ Exponential(mu): short requests are common, long ones are rare, and a request that would run past the context window is cut off at S_max. The capped mean is E[S] = mu * (1 - exp(-S_max / mu)), which rises monotonically from 0 toward S_max as mu grows, so exactly one scale matches any 0 < mean_tokens < S_max. At mean_tokens == S_max every request fills the window (the fixed-length limit) and the scale is infinite.
The exponential shape is a modeling assumption, chosen because it is the maximum-entropy distribution for a positive length with a known mean. It is not fitted to a serving trace.

Type
Description
Default

required

required

Activation memory of evenly spaced checkpointing, in units of one layer’s activations.
With k checkpoints over L equal layers, the forward pass keeps the k checkpoint activations and the backward pass rebuilds one segment of L/k layers at a time: k + L/k, smallest near k = sqrt(L) (Chen et al. 2016). (Added 2026-10-20.)

Bytes of a matrix in compressed sparse row (CSR) form.

Values and column indices are one each per nonzero; row pointers are one per row boundary, rows + 1 in all.

    layers,
    hidden_dim,
    vocab_size,
    mlp_ratio=4,
)
Weights in the matrix multiplies of a GPT-style decoder, by kind.
Each block has four weight matrices: the fused query-key-value projection (d x 3d), the attention output projection (d x d), and the two MLP matrices (d x r d and r d x d). The output layer projects d to the vocabulary (d x V). Biases, layer norms, and position embeddings are not matrix multiplies and are left out.

PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023, Sec. 4.2) hands a request fixed-size blocks on demand, so a request of S tokens holds ceil(S / p) blocks and wastes at most the unused tail of its last block. E[ceil(S/p)] = sum_{j=0}^{K-1} P(S > j p) = (1 - r^K) / (1 - r)
r = exp(-p / mu),  K = ceil(S_max / p)
The expected allocation is p * E[ceil(S/p)] and the expected internal fragmentation is 1 - mean / allocation. When mu >> p the tail averages about p / 2 tokens, so larger pages waste proportionally more even when S_max divides evenly by p. In the fixed-length limit (mean_request_tokens == max_seq_len) the allocation is ceil(S_max / p) * p, matching calc_paged_kv_cache_size.

physics.memory.calc_activation_memory(
    n_layers,
    seq_len,
    batch_size,
    hidden_dim,
    n_heads=None,
    precision_bytes=2,
    strategy='selective',
)
Estimates the activation memory required for a Transformer model during training.
Implements the per-layer analytical bounds of Korthikanti et al. (2023), “Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models”, Sec. 4.1, whose constants are expressed in BYTES with FP16 (2-byte) activations baked in:

none (no recomputation): s*b*h*34 + 5*a*s^2*b
selective (recompute attention matrices): s*b*h*34
full (recompute everything; keep layer inputs): s*b*h*2

where s = sequence length, b = microbatch size, h = hidden dimension, and a = attention heads. The quadratic 5*a*s^2*b term is the attention softmax/dropout/score storage — dominant at long sequence lengths — and is exactly what selective recomputation discards. Activations stored at other precisions scale the FP16-based constants by precision_bytes / 2.
(Audit fix 2026-06-06: the previous implementation used 34/10/2 as precision-free coefficients AND multiplied by precision_bytes, double- counting the FP16 width at every strategy; its selective=10 matched no published convention; and the attention term was missing entirely.)

physics.memory.calc_capped_exponential_scale(mean_tokens, max_tokens)
Solves for the exponential scale whose context-capped mean is mean_tokens.
Request lengths are modeled as S = min(X, S_max) with X ~ Exponential(mu): short requests are common, long ones are rare, and a request that would run past the context window is cut off at S_max. The capped mean is E[S] = mu * (1 - exp(-S_max / mu)), which rises monotonically from 0 toward S_max as mu grows, so exactly one scale matches any 0 < mean_tokens < S_max. At mean_tokens == S_max every request fills the window (the fixed-length limit) and the scale is infinite.
The exponential shape is a modeling assumption, chosen because it is the maximum-entropy distribution for a positive length with a known mean. It is not fitted to a serving trace.

title: engine.solvers.fine_tuning
text:
engine.solvers.fine_tuning
Fine-tuning solvers: what a serialized trajectory teaches, and what the update costs.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated counts: one serialized example’s positions under a target mask, one example per model call against one transcript, recorded transcripts split by role, a long trajectory’s weight under token and example averaging, padding against packing, one preference pair under the DPO loss, a distilled per-turn prefix against its bill, and a candidate policy’s release comparison. None models a trained network’s learning dynamics.

Description




LossNormalizationModel
One long trajectory’s weight in a batch under token and example averaging.


PerInvocationSerializationModel
One training example per model call against one stored transcript.


PreferencePairModel
One preference pair under the DPO loss, against its value at a zero margin.


SequencePackingModel
Variable-length examples padded to the longest against packed into fixed buffers.


TargetMaskModel
One serialized example’s positions under two target masks.





engine.solvers.fine_tuning.LossNormalizationModel()
One long trajectory’s weight in a batch under token and example averaging.
The batch holds the trajectory, split into focus_pieces records that each select every turn’s response once, and other_examples examples of other_targets selected targets each. Token averaging weights each example by its target count, so splitting changes nothing; example averaging weights each record once, so the trajectory’s share rises from 1/B to k/(B - 1 + k).



engine.solvers.fine_tuning.PerInvocationSerializationModel()
One training example per model call against one stored transcript.
When each of H turns adds about a tokens, call t carries t a tokens, so separate examples store a H (H + 1) / 2 tokens against a H for one transcript: the append-only resend triangle (calc_append_only_context with s0 = delta = a), an expansion of (H + 1) / 2.



engine.solvers.fine_tuning.PreferencePairModel()
One preference pair under the DPO loss, against its value at a zero margin.
At initialization the policy equals the reference, so both scores are zero, the loss is ln 2, the saturation factor is 1/2, and the coefficient is beta / 2. The logistic score depends on beta, so it measures fit to this comparison, not a success probability.



engine.solvers.fine_tuning.SequencePackingModel()
Variable-length examples padded to the longest against packed into fixed buffers.
Padding allocates N rows of the longest length, so occupancy is the mean length over the maximum. Packing places examples longest first into the first capacity-token buffer with room (first-fit decreasing). Occupancy counts context and targets alike; it is not measured throughput.



engine.solvers.fine_tuning.TargetMaskModel()
One serialized example’s positions under two target masks.
The example stores a prompt, a task, an optional rationale, the policy’s responses, and the observations. Targets are the responses minus the unselected ones (kept as context), with or without the rationale. The first stored position has no preceding position, so an unmasked token average divides by stored - 1 prediction terms; each target’s weight shrinks by (stored - 1) / targets.

solvers.EconomicsModel()
Calculates Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) including Capex and Opex.
Combines hardware costs, energy consumption, and maintenance into a single financial model for the fleet.

title: solvers.ParallelismOptimizer
text:
solvers.ParallelismOptimizer()
Searches for the optimal 3D/4D parallelism split (DP, TP, PP, EP).
Given a model architecture and a cluster size, this optimizer sweeps the integer design space of parallelism degrees to find the configuration that maximizes Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU).
Literature Source: 1. Narayanan et al. (2021), “Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM.”





Name
Description




solve
Search for the parallelism split (TP x PP x DP) that maximizes MFU.





solvers.ParallelismOptimizer.solve(
    model,
    fleet,
    batch_size,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
    max_tp=None,
    max_pp=None,
    overlap_comm=True,
    seq_len=2048,
    activation_recomputation=False,
)
Search for the parallelism split (TP x PP x DP) that maximizes MFU.
Exhaustive sweep over power-of-two TP and PP degrees with TP * PP * DP = total_accelerators. TP is capped at the node size by default (tensor parallelism needs NVLink-class bandwidth). Candidates are pre-screened for memory feasibility — per-GPU weights plus same-size gradients must fit in 90% of HBM capacity, with weights sharded by TP*PP — then each survivor is priced with DistributedModel, dropped if its replica’s training state (activations included) does not fit, and ranked by MFU = scaling_efficiency * efficiency. Pipelined candidates use one-sample microbatches (microbatch_count = per-replica batch), the schedule that minimizes both the bubble and in-flight activations.

title: solvers.ServingCapacityModel
text:
solvers.ServingCapacityModel()
Sizes an LLM serving deployment from a QPS and tail-latency target.
The model deliberately composes existing first-order pieces: ServingModel for TTFT/ITL, ContinuousBatchingModel for per-replica token capacity, and TailLatencyModel for queueing pressure. It is a capacity planner, not a request-level scheduler.





Name
Description




solve
Return the minimum replica count that satisfies the target P99.





solvers.ServingCapacityModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    qps,
    target_p99_latency_ms,
    max_seq_len=2048,
    mean_request_tokens=None,
    output_tokens=128,
    max_batch_size=32,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
    max_replicas=1024,
    service_time_cv=1.0,
)
Return the minimum replica count that satisfies the target P99.
Composes three first-order models and then scans replica counts upward (1, 2, …) until the estimated request P99 meets the target:

ContinuousBatchingModel sizes the per-replica active batch and token throughput under the memory wall, using paged allocation over the request-length distribution;
ServingModel (at that batch and the mean request length) gives TTFT/ITL, so the base request latency is TTFT + ITL * output_tokens;
TailLatencyModel (M/M/c) adds the P99 queue wait at each candidate replica count.

Estimated P99 = base request latency + P99 queue wait. Per-replica QPS capacity = token throughput / output_tokens.

title: physics.fairness
text:
physics.fairness
Fairness arithmetic: error-rate identities, the bias feedback model, and gap sample sizes.
Added 2026-10-20. The closed forms a fairness release gate rests on:

Chouldechova’s identity, which fixes a group’s false positive rate from its base rate, positive predictive value, and false negative rate;
the bias feedback model, a disparity multiplied by a feedback factor at each retraining cycle, and the cycle at which it crosses a release gate;
the per-group sample size that pins a gap between two groups’ rates.






Name
Description




calc_cycles_to_gate
Unrounded cycle count at which launch_gap * factor^k reaches gate.


calc_feedback_disparity
Disparity after cycles retraining cycles: gap(k) = gap(0) * factor^k.


calc_fpr_from_ppv
False positive rate implied by a group’s base rate, precision, and false negative rate.


calc_gap_samples_per_group
Per-group draws, equal groups, for a gap between two rates to have half-width half_width.





physics.fairness.calc_cycles_to_gate(launch_gap, factor, gate)
Unrounded cycle count at which launch_gap * factor^k reaches gate.
k = ln(gate / gap(0)) / ln(factor); the gate first fails at the next whole cycle above it. Requires a growing gap (factor > 1) that starts inside the gate.



physics.fairness.calc_feedback_disparity(launch_gap, factor, cycles)
Disparity after cycles retraining cycles: gap(k) = gap(0) * factor^k.
A factor above one grows a gap passed at launch; below one it decays.



physics.fairness.calc_fpr_from_ppv(base_rate, ppv, fnr)
False positive rate implied by a group’s base rate, precision, and false negative rate.
Equation (Chouldechova 2017, “Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact”): FPR = p / (1 - p) * (1 - PPV) / PPV * (1 - FNR)
With equal PPV and unequal base rates p, the false positive and false negative rates cannot both be equal across groups.



physics.fairness.calc_gap_samples_per_group(rate, half_width, z_critical)
Per-group draws, equal groups, for a gap between two rates to have half-width half_width.
The gap’s variance is the sum of both groups’ variances: h = z sqrt(p (1 - p) / n + p (1 - p) / n), so n = ceil(2 z^2 p (1 - p) / h^2), twice the single-rate count.

The gap’s variance is the sum of both groups’ variances: h = z sqrt(p (1 - p) / n + p (1 - p) / n), so n = ceil(2 z^2 p (1 - p) / h^2), twice the single-rate count.

title: solvers.MoERoutingModel
text:
solvers.MoERoutingModel()
Models first-order MoE routing imbalance and expert-parallel all-to-all cost.
Sparse models decouple memory from compute, but routing is rarely perfectly balanced. This model keeps the abstraction small: a single imbalance factor inflates the effective active experts and the routed-token communication volume. It does not simulate a router or token dispatcher.





Name
Description




solve
Estimate effective active parameters and optional EP all-to-all latency.





solvers.MoERoutingModel.solve(
    model,
    batch_size,
    seq_len,
    precision='fp16',
    ep_size=1,
    routing_imbalance_factor=1.0,
    fleet=None,
)
Estimate effective active parameters and optional EP all-to-all latency.
Single-factor imbalance model: a router that overloads hot experts behaves as if each token activated top_k * routing_imbalance_factor experts (capped at the model’s expert count), inflating active parameters and routed traffic by the same multiplier. The routed payload per step is batch * seq_len * hidden_dim * bytes_per_param * top_k * multiplier bytes, of which the fraction (ep_size - 1) / ep_size crosses ranks (a token’s target expert is local with probability 1/ep_size under uniform placement).

title: physics.numerics
text:
physics.numerics
Number formats: the range a binary floating-point or two’s-complement format holds.
The limits follow from the bit layout alone (IEEE 754-2019 for binary floating point; two’s complement for signed integers), so they are computed here rather than stored (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




calc_accumulator_headroom
About how many worst-case products of two signed operand_bits codes fit in a


calc_affine_scale
Step of an asymmetric (affine) integer grid over the clipping range [alpha, beta]:


calc_block_bits_per_weight
Stored bits per weight of a block format: (scale_bits + n code_bits) / n.


calc_dequantize
Real value a code reads back as: s (q - z).


calc_float32_bit_flip
value stored as an IEEE 754 binary32 word, read back after bit bit flips.


calc_float_decimal_digits
Decimal digits a binary float keeps: (f + 1) log10 2 for f stored fraction bits


calc_float_range
Largest finite, smallest normal, and smallest subnormal magnitude of a binary float.


calc_float_round
value stored in a binary float format, rounded to nearest (ties to even).


calc_float_spacing
Gap between value and the next larger number of a binary float format (one ulp).


calc_float_values
Every non-negative finite value of a binary float format, sorted (zero included).


calc_int_levels
Distinct codes of a bits-bit integer, 2^b.


calc_int_max
Largest value of a signed two’s-complement integer of bits bits, 2^(n-1) - 1.


calc_quantize
Code for x: clamp(round(x / s + z), qmin, qmax) (ties to even).


calc_repeated_add
start after adding update repeats times, rounding to the format after every add.


calc_symmetric_scale
Step of a symmetric signed grid that reaches max_abs: s = max_abs / (2^(b-1) - 1)


calc_zero_point
Integer that stands for real zero on an affine grid: qmin + round(-alpha / s).





physics.numerics.calc_accumulator_headroom(operand_bits, accumulator_bits)
About how many worst-case products of two signed operand_bits codes fit in a signed accumulator_bits register: 2^(a-1) // (2^(b-1) - 1)^2 (127 times 127 at INT8; about 133,000 in INT32).



physics.numerics.calc_affine_scale(alpha, beta, bits)
Step of an asymmetric (affine) integer grid over the clipping range [alpha, beta]: s = (beta - alpha) / (2^b - 1).



physics.numerics.calc_block_bits_per_weight(
    block_weights,
    code_bits,
    scale_bits,
)
Stored bits per weight of a block format: (scale_bits + n code_bits) / n.
One shared scale per block of n codes (llama.cpp’s Q4_0: 32 four-bit codes and one 16-bit scale, 4.5 bits per weight).



physics.numerics.calc_dequantize(code, scale, zero_point)
Real value a code reads back as: s (q - z).



physics.numerics.calc_float32_bit_flip(value, bit)
value stored as an IEEE 754 binary32 word, read back after bit bit flips.
Bit 31 is the sign, bits 30 to 23 the exponent, bits 22 to 0 the fraction. Returns (stored, corrupted): the value as stored, and the value after the flip. Flipping bit 30 of a weight below 2 multiplies it by 2^128 and leaves it finite (added 2026-10-20).



physics.numerics.calc_float_decimal_digits(fraction_bits)
Decimal digits a binary float keeps: (f + 1) log10 2 for f stored fraction bits plus the implicit leading bit (about 7.2 for FP32, 3.3 for FP16, 2.4 for BF16; added 2026-10-20).



physics.numerics.calc_float_range(exponent_bits, fraction_bits)
Largest finite, smallest normal, and smallest subnormal magnitude of a binary float.
bias              = 2^(e-1) - 1
largest finite    = (2 - 2^-f) 2^bias
smallest normal   = 2^(1 - bias)
smallest subnormal= 2^(1 - bias - f)
Returns (largest, smallest_normal, smallest_subnormal).



physics.numerics.calc_float_round(value, exponent_bits, fraction_bits)
value stored in a binary float format, rounded to nearest (ties to even).
A magnitude below half the smallest subnormal flushes to zero (underflow); one that rounds above the largest finite value becomes infinity (overflow).



physics.numerics.calc_float_spacing(value, exponent_bits, fraction_bits)
Gap between value and the next larger number of a binary float format (one ulp).
A number in the binade [2^E, 2^(E+1)) has neighbors 2^(E - f) apart; below the smallest normal the spacing stays at the subnormal step. An update smaller than half this spacing rounds away when added to value (added 2026-10-20).



physics.numerics.calc_float_values(exponent_bits, fraction_bits, ieee=True)
Every non-negative finite value of a binary float format, sorted (zero included).
ieee=True reserves the top exponent for infinities and NaNs (IEEE 754, and FP8 E5M2). ieee=False is the “finite” layout of FP8 E4M3 (Micikevicius et al. 2022): the top exponent holds normal values and only its all-ones fraction is NaN, which lifts the largest value from 240 to 448.



physics.numerics.calc_int_levels(bits)
Distinct codes of a bits-bit integer, 2^b.



physics.numerics.calc_int_max(bits)
Largest value of a signed two’s-complement integer of bits bits, 2^(n-1) - 1.



physics.numerics.calc_quantize(x, scale, zero_point, qmin, qmax)
Code for x: clamp(round(x / s + z), qmin, qmax) (ties to even).



physics.numerics.calc_repeated_add(
    start,
    update,
    repeats,
    exponent_bits,
    fraction_bits,
)
start after adding update repeats times, rounding to the format after every add.
Returns the stored value after each add, starting with start itself (repeats + 1 values). This is how a weight kept in a narrow format accumulates small optimizer updates (added 2026-10-20).



physics.numerics.calc_symmetric_scale(max_abs, bits)
Step of a symmetric signed grid that reaches max_abs: s = max_abs / (2^(b-1) - 1) (zero-point 0; the code -2^(b-1) goes unused).



physics.numerics.calc_zero_point(alpha, scale, qmin=0)
Integer that stands for real zero on an affine grid: qmin + round(-alpha / s).
Returns (exact, zero_point): the unrounded -alpha / s and the stored integer. Rounding is to nearest, ties to even, as Python and PyTorch round.

title: solvers.NetworkRooflineModel
text:
solvers.NetworkRooflineModel()
Analyzes the Distributed Performance Bounds (The Network Wall).
This model elevates the single-node Roofline analysis to the fleet scale. It calculates the Communication Intensity (CI) of a workload and identifies if the fleet is Compute-Bound (Wall 1) or Network-Bound (Wall 2).
Literature Source: 1. Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline Model.” (Theoretical basis) 2. Ghose et al. (2019), “A Survey of Communication-Efficient Distributed Training.”





Name
Description




solve
Solve for the fleet-scale performance bound (network roofline).





solvers.NetworkRooflineModel.solve(
    model,
    fleet,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Solve for the fleet-scale performance bound (network roofline).
Models one data-parallel training step as two independent ceilings — compute and gradient synchronization — and takes the slower as the binding latency (no overlap is assumed, so this is a lower-bound model). The conventions used:

communication intensity CI = training_ops / sync_bytes [FLOP/byte], with training_ops = 6 * P FLOPs per sample (Kaplan/Chinchilla forward+backward convention) and sync_bytes = 2 * P * bytes_per_param (ring all-reduce moves roughly 2x the gradient volume);
network ridge = fleet_peak_FLOPS / bisection_BW [FLOP/byte], the CI above which the fleet is compute-bound.

Description

required

required

Numerical precision; sets bytes per parameter and the FLOPS entry.
'fp16'

float
Software efficiency factor in (0, 1] applied to fleet peak FLOPS.
0.5

title: engine.solvers.model_call
text:
engine.solvers.model_call
Model-call solvers: what one call admits, samples, and costs, and what a trajectory resends.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated token counts and per-token floors: admission against a context window, temperature and top-p on a fixed logit vector, Bayes’ rule for a fallible check, and prefill plus decode time at the weight-transfer floors. None models queueing, batching, attention, or serving overhead.





Name
Description




CheckerPosteriorModel
Defects that survive a fallible check, by Bayes’ rule.


ContextAdmissionModel
Token-measured admission: a request fits when S <= S_max - K_max.


ModelCallModel
One model call at per-token floors: S * tau_prefill + K * tau_decode.


SamplingModel
Temperature and top-p on one fixed logit vector.


TrajectoryResendModel
Input a trajectory resends when every call carries the whole history.





engine.solvers.model_call.CheckerPosteriorModel()
Defects that survive a fallible check, by Bayes’ rule.
false_accept_rate is P(PASS | defective) and valid_accept_rate is P(PASS | valid). Rerunning the same check is not modeled: its errors are correlated with the first pass.



engine.solvers.model_call.ContextAdmissionModel()
Token-measured admission: a request fits when S <= S_max - K_max.
The serialized prompt (text plus any image charge) must fit in the context window with output_reserve tokens held back for the reply.



engine.solvers.model_call.ModelCallModel()
One model call at per-token floors: S * tau_prefill + K * tau_decode.
prefill_per_token is the compute floor 2P / R_peak and decode_per_token the weight-transfer floor P b / BW (see DecodeBoundModel). A shared prefix reused from cache leaves only the remaining prompt for fresh prefill. Optional: a deadline, and the success rates of the stages a reply must clear to be accepted.



engine.solvers.model_call.SamplingModel()
Temperature and top-p on one fixed logit vector.
Softmax at the base and the sharpened temperature, the probability left to every non-top token (the tail), and the top-p nucleus at the base temperature, renormalized.



engine.solvers.model_call.TrajectoryResendModel()
Input a trajectory resends when every call carries the whole history.
Turn t sends the first prompt S0 plus t - 1 appended blocks of D tokens (model output plus tool observation). Without reuse the total is H S0 + D H (H - 1) / 2; reusing each earlier prompt prefix leaves S0 + (H - 1) D of fresh prefill. Times are at the stated floors.

physics.robotics.stopping
Stopping envelopes, S-curve trajectories, and velocity bounds for Physical AI.





Name
Description




calc_blend_reserve_use
Largest growth, over a smoothstep blend’s ticks, of travel plus the resident stop.

Time to brake from velocity to rest at constant deceleration.

Calculate contact force rise, brake command force, and required arm deceleration upon latch contact.

Calculate maximum safe forward velocity admitted by physical stopping clearance.

Calculate dynamic stopping distance under non-zero control latency.

Highest cruise speed whose delayed S-curve stop fits the clearance.

Calculate the duration of a jerk-limited rest-to-rest move with no cruise phase.

Distance of a jerk-limited S-curve stop entered from zero-acceleration cruise.


calc_scurve_stop_time
Duration of the jerk-limited S-curve stop of calc_scurve_stop_distance.

Exit speed and travel of a fixed-endpoint smoothstep blend from cruise into braking.

Speed at which travel during the pre-brake delay equals braking travel.


calc_travel_between_speeds
Distance covered while speed changes uniformly between two recorded values.





physics.robotics.stopping.calc_blend_reserve_use(
    entry_velocity,
    deceleration,
    max_jerk,
    window,
    tick,
)
Largest growth, over a smoothstep blend’s ticks, of travel plus the resident stop.
At each permission tick i of a blend of length T from cruise into braking, u = min(i * tick / T, 1); the blended speed and travel follow from the once- and twice-integrated smoothstep:
A1(u) = u^6 - 3 u^5 + 2.5 u^4,   A2(u) = u^7 / 7 - u^6 / 2 + u^5 / 2
v(u) = v0 - a T A1(u),            x(u) = v0 T u - a T^2 A2(u)
use = max_i [ x(u_i) + d_S(v(u_i)) ] - d_S(v0)

Calculate the duration and distance of a C2-continuous stop from cruise.
A stop that begins and ends at zero acceleration, entered from constant velocity v_c, follows the minimum-order polynomial
q(u) = q_c + v_c * T * (u - u^3 + u^4 / 2),  u = t / T in [0, 1],
whose peak deceleration is 1.5 * v_c / T and whose distance is v_c * T / 2. Setting the peak equal to the credible deceleration a gives
T = 1.5 * v / a,    d = 0.75 * v^2 / a,
which is 1.5 times the constant-deceleration distance v^2 / (2 * a). The factor belongs to this polynomial, not to smooth stopping in general: its jerk q’’’ = -(6 v_c / T^2)(1 - 2u) peaks in magnitude at the ends,
j_peak = 6 * v / T^2 = (8 / 3) * a^2 / v,
and a jerk-limited S-curve with the same a and j_peak stops shorter (calc_scurve_stop_distance).
Source: derived here. The polynomial satisfies q’ = v_c, q’’ = 0 at u = 0 and q’ = 0, q’’ = 0 at u = 1; peak |q’‘| occurs at u = 1/2 (minimum of q’‘(u) = v_c / T * (-6u + 6u^2)); peak |q’’’| occurs at u = 0 and u = 1.

physics.robotics.stopping.calc_scurve_rest_to_rest_time(
    distance,
    max_acceleration,
    max_jerk,
)
Calculate the duration of a jerk-limited rest-to-rest move with no cruise phase.
A symmetric double-S profile that accelerates, then immediately decelerates. With t_j = a/j and x the time from the start of the jerk ramp to the end of the constant-acceleration plateau minus t_j (peak speed a*x):
plateau reached (x >= t_j):  D = a * x * (x + t_j),  T = 2 (x + t_j)
no plateau (D < 2 a^3 / j^2): D = 2 j tau^3,           T = 4 tau
Returns a dict with duration, peak_velocity, and reaches_max_acceleration. Works for linear or angular moves (distance in m or rad, rates to match).
Source: Biagiotti and Melchiorri, Trajectory Planning for Automatic Machines and Robots (Springer, 2008), ch. 3, double-S velocity profile.



physics.robotics.stopping.calc_scurve_stop_distance(
    entry_velocity,
    max_deceleration,
    max_jerk,
)
Distance of a jerk-limited S-curve stop entered from zero-acceleration cruise.
The stop drives acceleration from zero to -a at the jerk limit j, holds -a, and returns acceleration to zero at the jerk limit as velocity reaches zero (trapezoidal acceleration, the “double S” velocity profile). The profile is C2: position, velocity, and acceleration are continuous and jerk is piecewise constant.
if v >= a^2 / j:   d = (v / 2) * (v / a + a / j)
                     = v^2 / (2 a) + v * a / (2 j)
else:              d = v * sqrt(v / j)     (a is never reached)
In the first case the stop equals constant-deceleration braking at a plus cruise over half of one jerk ramp, a / (2 j). Under the bounds |a| <= a_max and |j| <= j_max this is the time-optimal stop, and for a stop that does not reverse it is also the shortest.
Source: Biagiotti, L. and Melchiorri, C., Trajectory Planning for Automatic Machines and Robots, Springer (2008; DOI 10.1007/978-3-540-85629-0), ch. 3, trajectory with double S velocity profile, specialized here to a stop from v to rest with zero boundary accelerations. Formula re-derived and checked against a discretized minimum-distance linear program.

no plateau (D < 2 a^3 / j^2): D = 2 j tau^3,           T = 4 tau
Returns a dict with duration, peak_velocity, and reaches_max_acceleration. Works for linear or angular moves (distance in m or rad, rates to match).
Source: Biagiotti and Melchiorri, Trajectory Planning for Automatic Machines and Robots (Springer, 2008), ch. 3, double-S velocity profile.



physics.robotics.stopping.calc_scurve_stop_distance(
    entry_velocity,
    max_deceleration,
    max_jerk,
)
Distance of a jerk-limited S-curve stop entered from zero-acceleration cruise.
The stop drives acceleration from zero to -a at the jerk limit j, holds -a, and returns acceleration to zero at the jerk limit as velocity reaches zero (trapezoidal acceleration, the “double S” velocity profile). The profile is C2: position, velocity, and acceleration are continuous and jerk is piecewise constant.
if v >= a^2 / j:   d = (v / 2) * (v / a + a / j)
                     = v^2 / (2 a) + v * a / (2 j)
else:              d = v * sqrt(v / j)     (a is never reached)
In the first case the stop equals constant-deceleration braking at a plus cruise over half of one jerk ramp, a / (2 j). Under the bounds |a| <= a_max and |j| <= j_max this is the time-optimal stop, and for a stop that does not reverse it is also the shortest.
Source: Biagiotti, L. and Melchiorri, C., Trajectory Planning for Automatic Machines and Robots, Springer (2008; DOI 10.1007/978-3-540-85629-0), ch. 3, trajectory with double S velocity profile, specialized here to a stop from v to rest with zero boundary accelerations. Formula re-derived and checked against a discretized minimum-distance linear program.











Name
Type
Description
Default




entry_velocity
Quantity
Cruise velocity at stop onset (e.g. m/s); zero gives zero distance.
required


max_deceleration
Quantity
Deceleration bound a_max (e.g. m/s^2).
required


max_jerk
Quantity
Jerk bound j_max (e.g. m/s^3).
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Stopping distance in meters.







physics.robotics.stopping.calc_scurve_stop_time(
    entry_velocity,
    max_deceleration,
    max_jerk,
)
Duration of the jerk-limited S-curve stop of calc_scurve_stop_distance.
if v >= a^2 / j:   T = v / a + a / j
else:              T = 2 * sqrt(v / j)
Source: Biagiotti and Melchiorri (2008), ch. 3, double S velocity profile; see calc_scurve_stop_distance.





Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Stopping time in milliseconds.







physics.robotics.stopping.calc_smoothstep_braking_blend(
    entry_velocity,
    deceleration,
    window,
)
Exit speed and travel of a fixed-endpoint smoothstep blend from cruise into braking.
Equation: a(t) = -a_b alpha(t / T), alpha(s) = 10 s^3 - 15 s^4 + 6 s^5 v_exit = v0 - a_b T / 2 (the integral of alpha over [0, 1] is 1/2) d_blend = v0 T - a_b T^2 / 7 (the integral of (1 - s) alpha over [0, 1] is 1/7)
The quintic smoothstep has zero first and second derivatives at both ends, so the commanded deceleration rises from zero to a_b with continuous jerk (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Type
Description





dict
exit_speed (m/s) and travel (m).







physics.robotics.stopping.calc_stopping_crossover_speed(
    total_latency,
    max_deceleration,
)
Speed at which travel during the pre-brake delay equals braking travel.
Equation: v * tau = v^2 / (2 * a) => v* = 2 * a * tau
Below v*, delay travel is the larger term of the elementary stopping budget; above it, braking travel is.
Source: equates the two terms of calc_safe_stopping_distance (OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Sec. 3.4, Eq. 3.14 and Example 3.10).











Name
Type
Description
Default




total_latency
Quantity
Pre-brake delay tau (e.g. ms or s); zero gives v* = 0.
required


max_deceleration
Quantity
Braking deceleration a (e.g. m/s^2).
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Crossover speed in m/s.







physics.robotics.stopping.calc_travel_between_speeds(
    start_velocity,
    end_velocity,
    duration,
)
Distance covered while speed changes uniformly between two recorded values.
Equation: x = (v_start + v_end) / 2 * t
With equal speeds this is the delay travel v * tau of the stopping budget; with two recorded speeds it is the trapezoid estimate of the distance covered between them.
Source: x = (v0 + v) / 2 * t for constant acceleration (OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Sec. 3.4, Eq. 3.11 with Eq. 3.12).
